One of Fairphone’s few software customizations is called Moments, which you can toggle with the brightly colored side switch. Moments can help limit distractions by hiding most of your apps behind a minimalist UI. It’s just a full-screen app overlay rather than a completely custom home experience, though. If you don’t fancy the digital well-being approach to mobile tech, you can remap that switch. Using it as a flashlight toggle is nifty, for example.
The camera may be the biggest compromise if you switch from a Google or Samsung phone. The hardware is typical for the mid-range, with a 50 MP Sony 700C joined by a 13 MP OmniVision OV13B10. That third lens on the back is actually a window for a time-of-flight sensor that helps with focus. With ample light, both rear sensors produce good images, and the primary even does fine in some more challenging conditions.
Capture speeds are long, though, making it hard to get clear images of moving subjects. Colors look a bit flat, too, and autofocus speed seems on the slow side. There’s a 32 MP selfie camera, which looks a touch dimmer than most devices in this price range.

With support increasing for making electronics more repairable, other companies may need to start moving in Fairphone’s direction. In Europe, regulators are preparing to require removable batteries, and more US states are enacting right-to-repair laws. The Fairphone CTO stresses that other OEMs have what they need to make phones more repairable.
“We’re producing our phones on the same production lines as our competitors, and often with many of the same components,” said Hatton. “It’s actually quite a small industry when you’re in it, and there is very little room for one of our competitors to say it’s impossible when on the next production line over it is happening.”

The UN general assembly will vote on Friday on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size.
Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said the resolution was sponsored by Togo and backed by countries including the African Union’s 54 other member states. He did not specify the total number.
“This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality,” he said.
UN resolutions are non-enforceable but if the vote passes, it could lead to an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology, given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance.
The layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later it remains the global standard.
Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory.
“You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption.
Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”.
Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This, they say, has reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks.
One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map.
Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign is promoting the use of the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums.
Some analysts agree too. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”.
He added: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.”
Togolese authorities hope the vote will go the same way as another African Union-backed decision at the UN this year. In March a Ghana-sponsored resolution to describe the slave trade as “gravest crime against humanity” passed, with 123 states voting in favour. Three states voted no and 52 abstained.
Ghana’s success has given supporters of the map cause to believe in a favourable outcome. Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution.
Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say, why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.”
He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

BRICS Chief Justices' Forum begins in Delhi; CJI Surya Kant to hold bilateral meetings
New Delhi, The BRICS Chief Justices' Forum, bringing together chief justices, presidents of supreme courts and senior judicial leaders from BRICS member states and partner countries, commenced here on Friday.
The forum, being hosted by the Supreme Court till September 6, will see Chief Justice of India Surya Kant hold bilateral meetings with senior judicial leaders from BRICS member states and partner countries.
"The forum will provide a platform for dialogue among the participating judiciaries and for exchange of views on contemporary issues relating to justice delivery, international dispute resolution, technology and sustainable development," the Supreme Court said in a statement issued on Thursday.

The Supreme Court, in a statement, said that substantive sessions will focus on four key areas: mediation and international commercial disputes, cross-border enforcement of arbitral awards, artificial intelligence and the judiciary, and judicial leadership and sustainable development.
The mediation session would examine it "as a strategic mechanism for resolving international commercial disputes in a globalised economy," it said. Likewise, the issue of cross-border enforcement of arbitral awards would be dealt with in the second session, and the jurists would deliberate upon the challenges in enforcement and the prospects for greater procedural harmonisation.

South Korea is reviewing a possible deployment of military assets to the strait of Hormuz amid pressure from Donald Trump over Seoul’s reluctance to provide support in the region, according to domestic media reports.
Citing unnamed government and military sources, the reportspublished on Thursday and Friday said preparations were under way and that the government intended to seek parliamentary approval for a new deployment. The reports, which appeared in major South Korean outlets, said the exact scale and timing have not been agreed.
But the presidential office pushed back, telling the Guardian that such reports were “different from the facts” and that “nothing related to the matter has been decided”, though it said the review was “continuing”.
An official said: “Our government has been closely discussing with the international community ways to make practical contributions for the speedy restoration of free navigation in the strait of Hormuz and peace and stability in the Middle East.”
According to reports, the assets under consideration include a P-8 Poseidon aircraft, which would mark South Korea’s first overseas deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft, and a naval logistics support ship to provide rear support.
One outlet, Seoul Broadcasting System, additionally reported that an explosive ordnance disposal team from the navy’s underwater demolition unit was part of the package.
Any new deployment in principle would require review by the national security council, a cabinet resolution and approval from the national assembly.
South Korea is highly dependent on the strait of Hormuz, importing more than 90% of its primary energy, including roughly 70% of crude oil through the waterway.
In 2020, the government of the then president Moon Jae-in expanded the mandate of an existing anti-piracy unit off the coast of Somalia to cover the strait of Hormuz, rather than seeking parliamentary approval for a new deployment.
South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, in March told parliament that any deployment to the strait would require the national assembly’s consent given how different the mission would be from the unit’s existing anti-piracy mandate.
The reports come amid growing strains in the US-South Korea alliance. Trump has repeatedly complained in public that Seoul turned down his request for help over Iran, claiming in August that South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had told him “No, thanks” despite the US stationing tens of thousands of troops on the peninsula.
Days later, he ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises to be scaled back, shortening the drills by six days.
Relations between the two allies have also been strained by delays implementing a $350bn investment package Seoul agreed with Washington last year, reports that the US had restricted intelligence sharing with South Korea, and by a dispute over a data breach at the South Korean e-commerce company Coupang.
Separately, Seoul has expressed interest in taking part in any renewed US-North Korea diplomacy, as Trump signals openness to another meeting with Kim Jong-un.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Associate professor Kate Adamala has been busy. Her lab at the University of Minnesota takes chemicals and dead, isolated biological parts — like DNA, membranes, ribosomes — and puts them together into “synthetic” cells to see if they will come to life…or at least act alive.
Can synthetic cells save the world?
The lab-made cell pushing the boundaries of life, explained.
This summer, Adamala’s lab had a tremendous breakthrough. They made synthetic cells that can feed, grow, and divide. She decided to name them SpudCells, and says that they prove that one day building a fully living lab-made cell will be possible.
Adamala’s dream, and the dream of other synthetic biologists like her, is to make all the medicine, materials, and fuel we need with synthetic cells like these. Instead of relying endlessly on petrochemicals, Adamala believes we could program cells to generate these materials in a lab for a more self-reliant and renewable future.
As Adamala explains: “I live in the Midwest, so we’ve got a lot of prairie grass. Why can’t I take that prairie grass and ferment it into a plastic toy? It’s totally possible. The atoms are there. We just…don’t have a living organism that would be willing and able to do that.” The synthetic cell could eventually be that organism.
Living cells can move atoms around with pinpoint precision without creating a lot of toxic waste along the way. The only problem is that natural biological cells are too hard to control.
Scientists still don’t actually understand how natural cells do everything they can do. “I’m scared of cells,” Adamala says. “I don’t believe that we’ll ever be able to understand a complex living cell. So my approach is I think we can build ourselves a cell.”
For Unexplainable’s three-part Life From Scratch series, I spoke with some of the leading voices of synthetic cell biology. From making the world’s first living cell with synthetic DNA to racing to build safeguards against a technology that could kill the world, this series explores the potential promise and scary risks of synthetic cell biology.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Adamala about her lab’s big breakthrough, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast — and the whole series — so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and more. You can also watch a video version of this conversation on Netflix.
What’s the big research that you shared with the public this summer?
We made a cell that can feed, grow, and divide out of nonliving, chemical components. People have been making cells from dead chemicals for a long time now, but none of them were able to realize those key functions of life. This is the first time synthetic cells have been able to grow and replicate based on their own instructions.
Before, we could make a synthetic cell and tell it to grow by adding things to it, but the SpudCells grow because they feel like it, because the proteins inside them tell them to grow.
So it can grow, it can eat, and it can divide. Are they alive?
I don’t think they’re alive. Even though they do all those functions that we think only life does, they’re not doing any of it very well.
They have to be fed pretty much every building block that they need. Life needs to figure out how to survive, and the cells that we made, even if on the surface level they look like they fulfill the functions of life, there is no robustness in there. If the conditions are not absolutely perfect, they will just stop.
This seems like it should be a simple question, but from our conversation, I get the sense that maybe it’s a little bit more complicated than it seems. What makes something alive?
That’s a very good question, and I think the best answer I can give is a quote from US Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart. He said, “I will know it when I see it.” It’s not a scientific definition, but there is no good scientific definition of life.
There is a NASA definition of life that NASA has been using when they look for life in the universe, and that definition says “a self-replicating chemical system that’s capable of Darwinian evolution.”
Okay.
And according to the NASA definition of life, you’re dead and I’m dead because I’m not self-replicating. For me to replicate, I need my husband. So that just shows you that definitions of life are very inaccurate, very context-dependent.
There’s just not a good definition of life that would cover everything that we instinctively consider alive, and exclude everything that we would all agree is not alive. Everyone defines life according to some different principles.
Why call these cells SpudCells?
We wanted to invoke Sputnik. It was the first artificial satellite, and it was actually a pretty bad satellite — it didn’t really do any of the things that fancy modern satellites do — but it basically opened up the Space Age.
It showed people that it’s possible to escape the gravity well. If we can put a satellite in orbit, maybe we can put people in orbit. And if we can put people in orbit, maybe we can escape orbit, go to the moon, and then go past the moon. It showed what’s possible. And that’s how I see the role of a SpudCell.
So it’s almost like a proof of concept?
Exactly. It’s a proof of concept that you can put chemicals together into a cell. By itself, it’s not a really good organism, but will hopefully show people that you can put together chemicals into something that can grow, divide, undergo selection, and that opens up this age of biology to me.
How do these SpudCells do all of these things differently than a natural cell?
The process of eating is very similar to how bacteria and other simple cells eat. So when they see something edible that’s pretty big, they will just kind of take it in. And that’s what SpudCell does.
Sort of like two soap bubbles joining together?
Exactly. Two soap bubbles, one of them is bigger, one of them is smaller, and they join together, and the smaller one brings in the food.
The division though, that’s a different story. The division is actually very different from how natural cells divide. The spud is genetically encoded, so the genome of the cell directs making the proteins. And if there’s enough proteins on a membrane, the cell starts dividing.
Does it feel like you’ve reached a milestone with this project?
Definitely. It’s a huge milestone because it shows us it’s possible.

Google Maps’ Ask Maps turns travel planning into a chat. It can build full itineraries, answer questions about places, suggest personalized nearby spots, plan surprise trips, and compare routes, travel times, costs, and transport options using Maps data.
Almost every app, website, or product has AI features now. While most AI implementations were forced, some of them are genuinely useful. I really loved the AI integration in Notion, where it simplified the hardest part of creating databases. Very recently, Hostinger’s implementation of the support agent is very useful for performing actions with just simple natural prompts. Finally, the Google Maps “Ask Maps” feature is what I really liked as the best AI implementation after those.
For those who are unaware, Google has rolled out the “Ask Maps” feature in Google Maps, which lets you chat with the application just like any LLM.
In simple words, you can chat with Google Maps for directions, information about places, calculate distances between places, basically everything you already do with Google Maps but in a more conversational format.
Table of Contents
5 Ways ‘Ask Maps’ Makes Google Maps Much More Useful
The best part of this implementation is that it works all the time and is very reliable. If you use Google Maps or even Apple Maps, I highly recommend trying this feature.
Since Google Maps is also available for iPhones, it is my default map app on the iPhone too. If you are using an older version, you can update Google Maps to the latest version by clicking on the links below.
Once you are done, here is everything you need to know about the Ask Maps feature, how to use it, and five unique ways to get the most out of it.
Plan Complete Trips With Accurate, Real-Time Information
There are plenty of AI trip planners out there that are very reliable, but Google Maps has a significant edge over them with its huge, real-time, and accurate amount of data.
I believe most of those applications also use Google Maps data for place suggestions, but you get everything for free with accurate details inside Google Maps.
And since this is an AI feature, just like any AI chat, you can have as many conversations as you want and personalize it the way you want.
You can ask everything about places, time, reviews, how much time it’s going to take, best alternatives, timings, and everything else while planning a trip.
For the best output, you can just copy and paste the prompt below with your details into Google Maps to get a detailed plan of whatever trip you are planning.
The best part is, Google also offers a preview of your destinations on the real map. You can see the list of all the places you are going to visit, the route you want to go through, and much more.
Since this can be a continuous conversation, you can follow up with new plans or any changes to your plans; it will automatically calculate and replan your entire journey based on the changes you want.
Prompt to Plan a Complete TripPlan a complete trip from [starting location] to [destination] for [number of days or dates].
My preferences:
- Budget: [budget]
- Traveling with: [solo/family/friends/couple]
- Interests: [nature, food, beaches, temples, shopping, nightlife, photography, etc.]
- Preferred transport: [car/public transport/walking/bike]
- Preferred pace: [relaxed/moderate/packed]
Create a day-by-day itinerary using places available on Google Maps.
For every place, include:
- Why it is worth visiting
- Best time to visit
- Opening hours
- Approximate time needed there
- Distance and travel time from the previous stop
- Best transport option
- Rating and important review highlights
- Estimated cost if available
- Nearby restaurants or food options
- Good alternatives if the place is closed or crowded
Arrange the places in the most practical order so I don’t waste time traveling back and forth.
At the end, show all the places on a route and give me a short summary of total travel time, approximate distance, and the most important things I should know before starting the trip.
Ask Anything About a Place Before You Visit
Another most useful feature for me in Google Maps is “Ask about a place.”
Previously, before Ask Maps, Google introduced “Ask about this place,” where you could just ask anything, and based on the reviews, it would answer your questions.
But ever since Ask Maps introduced it, you can just have conversations about any place, including learning about the place and what others think about it using real user reviews.
Not just that, you can also ask anything about multiple places, compare them, and much more.
For instance, you can ask how much time it would take to get to a certain point, what the timings, holidays, and do’s and don’ts are, what the negative reviews say, what recent incidents have happened around that place, the closest alternatives to that place, and everything else and much more.
The best part is it takes real data as input and answers your questions.
Prompt to Ask Everything About a PlaceTell me everything I should know before visiting [place name].
Use the latest information available in Google Maps and organize the answer clearly.
Include:
- What the place is known for
- Why people visit it
- Current opening and closing hours
- Best time of day to visit
- Best days to visit
- Entry fee or other costs if available
- How long people usually spend there
- Parking availability
- Public transport options
- Accessibility information
- Food and restaurants nearby
- Restrooms and other useful facilities
- Things I should carry
- Important rules, restrictions, or things visitors should avoid
- Common complaints from reviews
- Most positive things recent reviewers mention
- Whether it is suitable for families, kids, elderly people, couples, or solo visitors
- Safety or practical concerns
- Nearby places I can combine with this visit
Also suggest 3 good alternatives nearby and explain why I might choose each one instead.
Find Personalized Places Near You
Google Maps’ “Near me” feature is very helpful to quickly find places in your location, such as restaurants, living places, public transport, and much more. But this gets even better with personalized results using the “Ask Maps” feature.
Previously, the “Near Me” feature showed the exact same results for everyone, with no option to customize or personalize them. But with the “Ask Maps” feature, you can personalize locations and get dynamic results based on your needs.
For instance, if you only want a list of affordable hotels near you, you can simply ask Google Maps to show you just those. Plus, you can ask for locations that are currently open, locations that are a particular distance away from you, or even locations with specific needs. And again, the possibilities are endless. You can customize it the way you want.
Prompt to Find Personalized Places Near YouFind the best [restaurants/hotels/cafes/parks/attractions/etc.] near me based on these requirements:
- Maximum distance: [distance]
- Budget: [budget]
- Minimum rating: [rating]

- Preferred features: [parking, family-friendly, quiet, AC, outdoor seating, WiFi, etc.]

Do not just give me the most popular places.
Compare the best options using Google Maps information and reviews.

Nvidia has agreed to acquire Hugging Face, which makes online developer tools and maintains a massive library of open-source data sets, for nearly $13 billion. While the deal had been rumored for weeks, the companies made it official Thursday morning.
The deal signals Nvidia’s seriousness about being steeped in the software side of generative AI development as well as in infrastructure. Nvidia already offers customers a suite of free, customizable open-weights AI models, known as Nemotron. As part of its announcement, Nvidia committed to maintaining Hugging Face’s current open standards, suggesting that the chipmaker is positioning itself as an even greater resource for developers looking to access cutting-edge, nonproprietary tools.
The move also underscores Nvidia’s position that open-weights models are better for the tech industry than closed, proprietary AI models like those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic. Earlier this month, Nvidia rallied more than 80 companies to sign an open letter asking the US government to defend open-weight AI models. Nvidia also launched an initiative called SAFE, or Shared AI Findings Exchange, that encouraged tech companies to “confidentially collect and analyze AI incidents and near misses, identify recurring control failures and publish evidence-based operating recommendations that reduce systemic risk.”
“Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in the press release announcing the deal. “AI advances faster when people can build together.”
Nvidia’s embrace of open-source software and open-weights AI might seem like an abrupt turn, especially given that CUDA, the software layer for its highly coveted GPUs, is itself proprietary. But as frontier AI labs and some of the large hyperscalers, including Amazon and Meta, seek to build their own custom chips, Nvidia has begun to position itself as a maker of not just GPUs but also high-performance CPUs, and has widened its software offerings in order to keep developers building on Nvidia’s platforms.
Business Insider previously reported that the two companies were in talks, and The Information later reported that a deal had been reached.
Hugging Face was founded a decade ago by three French entrepreneurs in New York City, who wanted to launch an AI “companion” app. That didn’t catch on, but the team’s efforts to build their own natural language processing (NLP) tools inspired their next move: making complex tech tools more accessible to developers. Hugging Face eventually became a platform for developers to freely share source code, data sets, and, in the generative AI era, large language models.
“Open-source AI is at an inflection point,” wrote Hugging Face cofounder and CEO Clément Delangue in a post on X announcing the acquisition. “Thanks to the community, we’ve shown that it can be a complement, and even an alternative, to closed-source APIs. But for it to happen at larger scale, it needs more compute, more support, more collaboration and more visibility.”
According to PitchBook data, Hugging Face had raised nearly $400 million in venture capital funding as of December 2025. Some of its backers include Betaworks, Lux Capital, Sequoia Ventures, Coatue, and Addition. Notable individual investors include Greg Brockman, Richard Socher, and the NBA player Kevin Durant.
Hugging Face has more recently been front and center after its platform was hacked by AI agents from OpenAI. The incident sparked a broader conversation across the tech industry about the safety, security, and manageability of the autonomous agents being touted by top AI companies.
In a 2023 interview with CNBC Delangue predicted that the number of developers working with AI models would soar, and estimated that within five years, “you’re going to have like 100 million AI builders. And if all of them use Hugging Face all day, every day, we’ll obviously be in a good position.”
Obviously, Nvidia seems to agree.

Indian families seeking permanent US residency through family-sponsored categories got relief as cut-off dates moved forward substantially this month, but there was little change for professionals keen on getting EB-1 visas.
The visa bulletin for September stated that the Final Action Date for China and India advanced from December 15, 2018, to January 22, 2020 for the F-1 categories that cover unmarried adult sons and daughters of US citizens.
The September bulletin is the last for the current financial year, and new annual visa numbers will become available from October 1. The US federal government's fiscal year begins on October 1 and ends on September 30 of the following year.
"High demand and number use by aliens chargeable to India in the EB-1 visa category may necessitate making the category unavailable in the coming weeks if India's pro-rated limit in the EB-1 category is reached before the fiscal year ends. This situation will be continually monitored, and any necessary adjustments will be made accordingly," the visa bulletin said.
The EB-1 category covers priority workers, including individuals with extraordinary ability, outstanding professors and researchers, and certain multinational corporate leadership roles.
For September, the EB-1 final action date for India is October 15, 2022. In general, an applicant must have a priority date earlier than the listed cutoff for an immigrant visa number to be available for final action, subject to other eligibility requirements.
The fiscal year 2026 limit for family-sponsored preference immigrants is 226,000.
The worldwide level for annual employment-based preference immigrants is 186,317, while the per-country limit for preference immigrants is set at seven per cent of the total annual family-sponsored and employment-based preference limits, i.e., 28,862. The dependent area limit is set at two per cent, or 8,247.
The Final Action Date for the F2A category, which covers spouses and minor children of lawful permanent residents, also advanced by one month for most countries, including China, India and the Philippines, moving from July 22, 2026, to August 22, 2026.
The F2B category, which covers unmarried adult sons and daughters of permanent residents, is one of September's biggest beneficiaries.
For most countries, including China and India, the Final Action Date advanced from January 1, 2018, to August 22, 2019 – nearly 20 months of forward movement in a single Visa Bulletin.
For the F3 category, covering married sons and daughters of US citizens, the Final Action Date advanced from May 15, 2012, to October 22, 2014 – approximately 29 months forward.

In September 2026, a rumor spread that a U.S. airman's widow was denied death benefits because he died in the context of the war in Iran, which Congress hadn't officially declared. 
The rumor appeared on Facebook, Reddit and X. 
The meme included two images: one of a young man smiling as he posed in front of a U.S. flag and another of a couple posing on a tarmac, in which the man wore Army fatigues and a woman with long blonde hair smiled in his arms. The meme read:
This is Major Alex Klinner, a U.S. Air Force airman from Alabama. He was killed in Iran on March 12 during Trump's ILLEGAL "Operation Epic Fury" war.
On Sunday, his widow exposed that Trump is REFUSING to give her death benefits, as Trump never actually formally declared war.
Let that sink in. Trump and Republicans are too weak to actually declare war as the Constitution demands, and they're leaving dead soldiers' families holding the bag.
BEYOND DEPLORABLE!
Several Snopes readers shared the meme via email, asking us to verify its claims.
The rumor stems from an Instagram post by a woman named Libby Klinner, whose bio says she is the "surviving spouse of Maj. Klinner," a former teacher and a mother to a toddler and twins. On Aug. 29, 2026, she posted a video of herself rocking a baby, with on-screen text that read "The Air Force recently told me that because we haven't officially declared war, my kids and I aren't eligible for some benefits."
A review of Klinner's Instagram feed indicated she lost her husband Alex Klinner, who had been deployed to the Middle East, on March 12, 2026. According to a March 14 announcement from the U.S. Department of Defense, Maj. John A. Klinner died two days earlier in a plane crash in Iraq, 12 days after the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran. (A separate post by Klinner said her husband went by his middle name, Alex, though his first name was John.)
On Sept. 1, 2026, Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata said on X that someone had reached out to Klinner and her family "to confirm they have received all of the entitlements they are owed," though he did not specify if these included the alleged missing benefits Klinner referred to in her post.
Snopes found no reason to doubt Klinner's assertions. However, we were unable to independently verify details about the benefits in question without access to documentation or correspondence between Klinner and the Air Force. As a result, we also could not confirm whether Klinner was denied benefits because Congress hadn't declared war on Iran. For these reasons, we've left the claim unrated.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force told Snopes via email that they had spoken with Klinner to ensure she is receiving the benefits she's entitled to and to answer her questions. We reached out to Klinner for further confirmation and await a response.
Klinner's claims about missing benefits
Klinner regularly posted on Instagram until March 11, talking about the difficulties of a loved one's deployment and sharing teaching tips. On March 14, she shared several photos of her husband, saying he had died. Her next post was dated May 9, asking her followers to support the families of other service members who died in the March 12 plane crash. The text in her images discussed grief and her husband's death.
On Aug. 29, Klinner posted on Instagram a video of her rocking a baby with the caption "Six months of a war we can't call a war..." (archived).
"The Air Force recently told me that because we haven't officially declared war, my kids and I aren't eligible for some benefits," the video's on-screen text read. "So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we're left with are being dictated by semantics and public perception."
"The missing benefits are combat pay-related and were missing from his final paycheck," the caption said.
On Aug. 31, Klinner posted again, saying the director of Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations told her the agency was launching an audit into her benefits to ensure that she receives everything to which she is entitled, but provided no further details (archived).
We reached out to Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations but did not receive a response by the time of publication.
Officials' response
In an email to Snopes on Sept. 2, the Air Force spokesperson said officials had talked to Klinner on Aug. 31:
We understand this matter has been difficult for Mrs. Klinner and her family, and we are committed to addressing her concerns with care and respect. Department of the Air Force officials spoke with Mrs. Klinner on Monday [Aug. 31] to ensure she is receiving all eligible benefits she and her family are entitled to, as well as ensure all her questions are fully addressed. We remain committed to providing clear information and continued support to Mrs. Klinner, as well as all the families of the Airmen who died in the KC-135 crash.

A massive landslide has partially blocked the Chaulani River in Nepal’s Darchula district, prompting authorities to place downstream communities on alert amid fears that continued debris could choke the river and trigger sudden flooding.
The landslide occurred at Bhattar in Api Himal Rural Municipality, with debris spilling into the river and affecting its flow. The district administration office, Darchula, warned that further landslides could completely block the river, raising the risk of a sudden breach and flash floods downstream.
Authorities have urged people living along the riverbanks to remain vigilant and take precautionary measures. Security personnel have been deployed to warn residents and remain on standby for emergency response.
Sudurpaschim Chief Minister Khagraj Bhatta also directed local authorities and security agencies to maintain high alert and prepare for any emergency. The administration has issued emergency contact numbers for flood and disaster assistance.
The Armed Police Force said the river was flowing at a normal level for now, but personnel from the Nepal Chameliya Hydropower Security Base in Balanch had been mobilised to monitor the situation and alert nearby communities.
The Chaulani, also known as the Chamelia, originates in the Api Himal region and eventually joins the Mahakali River, which forms part of the Nepal-India border.
The warning comes as Nepal is still dealing with the impact of severe flooding and flash floods in several areas, with rescue and recovery efforts continuing after recent floods left communities displaced and caused deaths and extensive damage. The latest river blockage has added to concerns that further heavy rain could turn an already unstable situation into another flash-flood emergency.

Srinagar, Sep 4: An IndiGo flight operating from Navi Mumbai to Srinagar came into contact with a Visual Docking Guidance System (VDGS) pole while being positioned at Bay No. 06 at Srinagar Airport on Friday morning.
According to Srinagar Airport, IndiGo flight 6E 225 (VT-NOG) was involved in the incident at around 9:02 am during the parking process.

'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
- Published
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.
"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.
Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.
Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.
The expulsions show no sign of stopping.
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.
"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.
It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.
"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.
The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.
The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.
The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."
He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.
The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.
The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"
He answers his own question: "Nothing."
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

Hardly a year goes by without me whistling the Guild Wars 2 loading theme, rewatching clips of the original to soak up that Pre-Searing Ascalon nostalgia, or subjecting my wife to yet another Grawl impression. (Gui-la-la!)
That's how monumental ArenaNet's MMORPG has been in my life. So you can understand my excitement when the game developer announced Guild Wars 3 earlier this summer, with a beta set to launch in late 2027.
I spent countless hours playing Guild Wars in middle school and high school, and an ungodly amount of time playing Guild Wars 2 with my roommates in college. Guild Wars always felt like the dark horse in the MMORPG world, never reaching the scale and attention of World of Warcraft or Final Fantasy XI, yet maintaining a massive user base with a cult-like following. (It uniquely did not require a monthly subscription.) You wouldn't hear anyone talking about it in the school cafeteria like you would the other two titles (I was not a Cool Kid). Still, it always had a grand scale of wonder, adventure, and lore that drew me in—props to my older brother for discovering the game and its many discs, and building a PC to run it.
Guild Wars 3's setting predates the events of Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, which means you don't really need to know anything about the series to dive in. It marks the first time the franchise is heading to console with a PlayStation 5 release alongside PC. And while developers typically wind down support for predecessor titles ahead of a sequel, ArenaNet plans to maintain both the original Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2 for years to come. (It recently released the original game as Guild Wars Reforged with system enhancements and a mobile port.)
Details on the game—built on Unreal Engine 5 and in development for 4 years—are limited, but ArenaNet gave me a brief glimpse of early alpha footage showcasing gameplay components that have me excited to jump back into the world of Tyria.
Joy of Movement
Gliding is already a movement mechanic in Guild Wars 2, but when you stop and start running, the transitions are awkward and slow. All of that is becoming more fluid in Guild Wars 3, alongside some new range of movements. In some ways, it brings the game closer to an action RPG.
You can jump into a ravine, start gliding, and now wall-run to reach your desired destination, all in a series of fluid movements with no awkward transitions, though there is a stamina bar as a limiter. Colin Johanson, ArenaNet’s studio head, says this unlocks “truly expressive and free-formed joy of movement.” Much of this centers on character momentum—using speed, weight, and directional inertia—a philosophy massively multiplayer online games have historically avoided due to network latency and server-client synchronization issues.
Momentum doesn't only affect how you get around, but combat as well. For example, you can build up speed to ram into enemies and smash them into cliff walls to stun them—they can do the same to you—or use momentum to kick them off a ledge, King Leonidas-style. (What happens to their loot if they fall off a cliff? ArenaNet hasn't figured that out just yet.)
While the basic movement mechanics are the same across all character classes, each class has a unique spin on it. The Warrior class, for example, can sprint up a wall and use downward momentum to plunge their weapon and slam the ground, causing area-of-effect damage to nearby enemies.
I recall enjoying many of the collaborative fighting mechanics when Guild Wars 2 first debuted—like an Elementalist dropping a fire ring on the ground so an ally could shoot arrows through it to inflict burning damage. That's still a crucial component in GW3.
Warriors can angle their shield to act as a launchpad for allies, catapulting them into the air for elevated strikes. Rangers have an ability that creates an ice vortex, and a Warrior can jump in, ride the vortex's lift high, then plummet down to cause big (icy) damage. Some of these moves are GW3's new “contextual skills," which only show up during specific contextual windows. If a Warrior is in the air, that's when they can use the skill to bomb down and hit the ground with power.
In one encounter against spiders, a Warrior set his weapon on fire, which in turn lit his allies' weapons. They sliced through the spiders quickly, and the fire also spread through the webs to clear them out. Players can adjust and customize their builds on the fly in the open world, though some build aspects are restricted until they're back in main hub locations.
“Customizing your build to defeat different enemies more easily is also an important part of the Guild Wars franchise,” Johanson says. “It's one of the key pillars of Guild Wars 1, and we're bringing it back more heavily in the combat system in Guild Wars 3.”
Conditions you place on enemies are multiplayer stackable, so if one player starts freezing an enemy, the cold effect builds, and the enemy's animation slows down; their attacks are slower. As more people put more cold on the enemy, they'll move slower and slower until they become a block of ice that blocks their moves for a short period. If the enemy is low on health, a character with a knock ability like a Warrior can slam into the ice block and, if it kills the enemy, shatter them into tiny ice cubes, causing damage to nearby foes.
There's lots ArenaNet didn't talk about in this gameplay showcase, like the spirit mounts from the game's initial teaser—Johanson says there will be more to share in the future. Also, how will PS5 players, who can't really take advantage of the game's text-based chat systems on PC, communicate? But he confirmed that there will be a player-versus-player (PvP) mode, along with “high-trust coordinated dungeon-like experiences.” In general, combat will feature a “heck of a lot less” user interface over the screen than a traditional MMO.
ArenaNet says the scale is different compared to Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, with the former sitting at the smaller scale of the MMO market and the latter sitting on the opposite end. “Internally, we call Guild Wars 3 more of a meaningful MMO, where it's more about each player on-screen really matters and makes a difference,” Johanson says.
That's because GW3 uses an evolved version of the megaservers from GW2, allowing for fewer loading screens and an open-world cap of roughly 20 players in active combat zones—a number that scales up significantly higher in social hubs, like cities and towns.
“We've seen very few new MMOs in the last decade, and the overwhelming majority of us are still playing the same games from 10 to 20 years ago,” Johanson says. “We see MMO fans constantly clamoring for something new and saying this genre desperately needs something new to move it forward right now, and I think that is when ArenaNet is at its best.”
Expect a slow trickle of information over the next year as the beta launch for Guild Wars 3 approaches. Until then, I'm going to dust off Guild Wars 2, which has been seeing its own sudden influx of new players. As the Norn say, “May the spirits guide you.”

Gloria Steinem’s Feminism for All
The activist and writer, who died yesterday at the age of 92, steadfastly fought for her belief that women could change the world together.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Throughout most of Gloria Steinem’s life, two versions of her existed. Publicly, Steinem was a figurehead: the glamorous co-founder of Ms. magazine, a totem for second-wave feminism and a bull’s-eye for its detractors, gorgeously inscrutable behind her curtains of streaked hair and tinted glasses. Privately, she was a workhorse: someone who hid behind her accessories, felt she’d come to the women’s movement late (in her mid-30s), and spent much of the rest of her life hustling to make up for it. If these two identities came into conflict—the persona and the person, the superstar feminist who was terrified of public speaking—Steinem, who died yesterday at the age of 92, simply pushed on. Her politics and her life both revolved around her steadfast commitment to the idea that all women are human beings deserving of equal opportunity, and that uniting around this concept could change the world.
Steinem has said she was radicalized in 1969, around her 35th birthday, when, as one of the founding journalists working for Clay Felker’s New York magazine, she covered an abortion-rights “speak-out” in Greenwich Village, where she learned that as many as one in three American women had terminated a pregnancy. The statistic shocked her, if not the procedure—a little more than a decade earlier, when Steinem was 22 and a recent Smith College graduate, she’d had one herself. Years later, the way she’d been led to cordon it off as a private incident got stuck in her brain. It was, she later wrote in her 2015 memoir, My Life on the Road, a “click of consciousness—namely, that I had been silent and silenced.” (She dedicated that book to the London doctor who had performed her abortion.) She realized that, like so many other women, she’d “been made to feel at fault, not realizing there were political reasons why female humans were not supposed to make decisions about our own bodies.” For New York, Steinem wrote a report titled “After Black Power, Women’s Liberation,” one of the first major dispatches on a national movement that was starting to take form.
In her article, Steinem set out her thesis that for the women’s movement to be effective, it would have to be inclusive, bringing together different factions and activist groups. Throughout the 1960s, feminism had manifested most publicly as an expression of discontent among middle-class white women in the suburbs, while Black feminists worked on the fringes of the civil-rights movement and domestic workers struggled to be recognized by labor organizers. In 1963, Betty Friedan published The Feminine Mystique, a book that exposed the pervasive unhappiness of so many overeducated, underemployed housewives. By 1969, it had become clearer to many activists that forming alliances on behalf of all women might, as Steinem wrote, “forge the final revolutionary link.”
Feminists were rallying around the idea that the personal is political, something Steinem knew intimately. Her mother, Ruth, had been a reporter and an editor for a newspaper in Toledo, Ohio, and her paternal grandmother had been one of the first Jewish women elected to public office in the United States. Before Steinem was born, her mother had had a nervous breakdown, and she became addicted to the chloral hydrate prescribed to her by a doctor. Her father, a traveling antiques salesman, took the family on the road for much of every year. When Steinem was roughly 10, her parents separated, and she was left to care for Ruth alone, bringing her toast and coffee while her mother lay in bed “with eyes closed and lips moving in occasional response to voices only she could hear,” as Steinem would later describe it. Steinem didn’t blame her mother for an intensely difficult childhood, seeing Ruth’s life as proof of how unequally women were suffering.
“The middle-class, educated and disillusioned group gets larger with each college graduation,” Steinem wrote in 1969. But she saw, too, that women for whom work was a need, not an opportunity, were equally deserving of representation. When she was asked to speak publicly about women’s liberation after her New York report was published, she decided to take a friend, Dorothy Pitman Hughes, with her. “Right away we discovered that a white woman and a black woman speaking together attracted far more diverse audiences than either one of us would have done on our own,” she wrote in her memoir. She formed lifelong partnerships and friendships with some of the 20th century’s most influential activists—Florynce Kennedy, Wilma Mankiller, bell hooks—and was the treasurer for the legal fund for the defense of Angela Davis.
At the end of 1971, Steinem, with a collective of writers and editors, launched Ms., a magazine that debuted as a 40-page insert tucked inside New York. The idea for a feminist publication came about during meetings when people in the movement lamented that they couldn’t get meaningful stories about women published. Steinem suggested a newsletter. Brenda Feigen, who’d co-founded the Women’s Action Alliance with her, countered with the idea of a glossy magazine, a product that seemed familiar enough to appeal to women who weren’t already aligned with the cause. Even from the beginning, there were fractures between those who saw the insurgent potential of a mainstream feminist magazine and those who wanted something more radical. “We came out against marriage and motherhood,” the feminist writer Vivian Gornick said of the latter faction, in a 2011 oral history of Ms. “Gloria was uptown; we were downtown. She hung out with Establishment figures; we had only ourselves.” (Steinem pushed back later by saying that the only reason she lived uptown was that she couldn’t afford a place in the Village. She herself never had children and joked that she married in 2000, at the age of 66, only to help secure the immigration status of her husband, the entrepreneur and activist David Bale; Bale died of cancer three years later.)
The first full issue of Ms., published in January 1972, featured an image reimagining the Hindu goddess Kali as a housewife, each of her eight arms clutching a different household item while tears stream down her face. Inside the magazine were articles on sisterhood among feminists and raising children without adhering to traditional gender roles, as well as a groundbreaking statement signed by 53 women—Steinem, Anaïs Nin, and Billie Jean King among them—noting that they had had abortions. All 300,000 printed copies sold out in eight days. Mailbags jammed with letters began arriving at the office. The magazine was broadly mocked in mainstream publications, on TV news, and even in the White House: President Richard Nixon was caught on tape deriding Steinem to Henry Kissinger.
Anyone co-opted as a figurehead becomes vulnerable to charges of grandiosity, but the vitriol directed at Steinem for much of the ’70s and ’80s was almost unprecedented. In 1963, while trying to establish herself as a freelance writer, she’d worked undercover at Playboy’s Bunny Club in Manhattan, detailing how women were subjected to internal gynecological examinations, and were routinely groped and otherwise harassed under horrific working conditions. The report caused a stir, but it also cast Steinem in many people’s minds as a lightweight who used her looks to get ahead. Because Ms. often struggled to sell ads, Steinem was obliged to fundraise for donations to keep the magazine going, appearing in public as a spokesperson for feminism in a way that galled other women in the movement. Steinem’s sphinxlike distance—she hid behind her hair, she said, because she’d always been sensitive about the roundness of her face—also fueled her detractors. “Gloria has all the irritating qualities of a saint,” Liz Smith wrote in 1971, according to Vanity Fair. By 1975, radical feminists publicly had distanced themselves from Ms., whose politics the writer Ellen Willis described as “a mushy, sentimental idea of sisterhood designed to obscure political conflicts between women.”
In her memoir, Steinem was sanguine about experiencing decades of what a Ms. article described as “trashing,” or “the dark side of sisterhood.” Needing approval, she wrote, “is a female cultural disease, and often a sign of doing the wrong thing.” What often gets obscured in any discussion of feminist infighting is the scale of what the women’s-liberation movement managed to achieve during the 1970s: landmark legal victories regarding reproductive rights, sex discrimination in the workplace, and access to education; the establishment of dozens of shelters across the country for women who were victims of domestic abuse; the passage of the Equal Rights Amendment, although it was never ratified.
For Steinem, the most significant moment in her life was the 1977 National Women’s Conference in Houston, an event Steinem later described as “the most important event nobody knows about.” In 1971, she’d worked with three female representatives, Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, and Patsy Mink, to establish the National Political Women’s Caucus. Now Abzug was drafting all three women to help support the unimaginable: an official platform for women in America, voted on by delegates for diverse groups from all over the country. Steinem was asked to be a “token” by groups from the so-called Minority Women’s Plank, to record their concerns and conflicts and draft language that could be combined into a single text. “Before Houston, I had known that women in small groups could be courageous and loyal to each other and respect each other’s differences,” Steinem recalled in her memoir. “After Houston, I’d learned that women could do this in large numbers, across chasms of difference, and for serious purpose.” She was prouder of her role at the conference than of anything else she’d ever done.
For the rest of her life, and the rest of her career as an activist and a writer, she maintained this belief in what women are capable of when they can find common ground. “We are linked,” she once said, “not ranked.” She felt that true feminism would ultimately liberate everyone, not least men. And she was adamant that in-person meetings, in which people could gather to listen to one another, were crucial for bringing about change and fostering community. She continued to host “talking circles” at her home into her 90s, discussing reproductive health, inclusivity, and AI over the past year, and she placed her apartment in a trust so that others can continue her work there in the years to come. She saw herself fundamentally as an activist, not a theorist, and believed that the diversity of the women’s movement was also its strength. “I think I’ve wasted some of my time, but used most of it well, and have realized that my life is not separate from other people’s lives or from the universe,” Steinem told Interview in 2011. “I think our moments of happiness really come from a feeling of unity.”

Fruit flies aren’t exactly famous for their brainpower; you’ve probably drowned more than one in a wine glass left too long on the patio table. And yet, working with roughly 140,000 neurons—a brain smaller than a poppy seed—Drosophila can sort through a huge range of smells in a fraction of a second, and then retain the memory of that scent for a long time.
In this, they do much better than current “electronic noses.” Even the most advanced ones on the market tend to be expensive, painfully narrow in what they can detect, and quick to forget an odor the moment they learn a new one.
So why not just copy the fly? That’s the question a growing number of researchers have been asking—including Kevin Max and Yang Shen at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology, whose new algorithm, Spi-Fly, is described in a paper recently published in the journal Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering.
A rather obscure sense
Smell is a strange sense, mechanically speaking.
Vision and hearing both reduce to a single physical dimension you can plot on a graph—wavelength—which makes them relatively tidy to study. Odor molecules, by contrast, can’t be reduced to any single physical dimension. Biology had to find a messier solution instead: hundreds of different receptor proteins, each shaped to grab onto specific molecular features, firing in combinations that the brain then has to decode. It’s a system so combinatorially complex that it took until 1991 for Linda Buck and Richard Axel to even identify the receptor gene family behind it, work that won them a Nobel Prize in 2004.
Despite the difficulties in our understanding of smell, “electronic noses” exist on the market. Companies like Alpha MOS, Aryballe, and Odotech sell them for food-quality control, environmental monitoring, and security screening.
What these noses are bad at is generalizing. A device with software that is tuned to sniff out spoiled olive oil isn’t the same as a device that flags a specific explosive at an airport checkpoint. Retooling one for a new task usually means retraining its software almost from scratch.
Two technical bottlenecks sit behind that limitation. First, these systems typically need a mountain of hand-labeled examples before they can reliably tell one smell from another. Second, teaching them a new odor tends to scramble what they already knew, a problem researchers call “catastrophic forgetting”—the electronic equivalent of forgetting how to ride a bike right after learning to swim.
Odor barcodes
Fruit flies—and plenty of other insects—don’t have this problem, despite their minuscule brains. How do they tell odors apart and remember them with so little brainpower to work with? The secret, according to the paper’s authors, is something called sparse coding.
Think of it as the fly’s brain assigning a barcode to every smell. Its olfactory system relies on roughly 2,000 specialized cells, called Kenyon cells, that receive sparse, randomly wired signals passed on from the fly’s odor receptors. Those Kenyon cells all report to a single relay point: the anterior paired lateral neuron, or APL (actually a symmetrical pair of them, one per brain hemisphere). The APLs respond by firing strong, global inhibition back at every Kenyon cell at once, silencing nearly all of them. The cells that remain active after that crackdown are what Max and Shen call the barcode for that particular odor.
Spi-Fly picks up the story only after a sensor has already done its job—everything here happens in simulation, using pre-recorded sensor data, and the algorithm itself has nothing to do with capturing the smell in the first place.
In Max and Shen’s work, sensor readings become a stream of spikes, projected sparsely and randomly onto a hidden layer that stands in for the Kenyon cells, with neurons inhibiting each other instead of relying on a single APL-like referee. From there, the hidden layer connects to an output layer, one neuron per labeled odor, waiting to learn which barcode belongs to which smell.
A simple rule
What actually gets learned is the connection between a barcode and its label, following a simple, decades-old neural network rule: Every time a hidden neuron fires alongside the correct answer, that link gets a little stronger.
Nothing more. There’s no need for backpropagation, the technique co-invented by 2024 physics Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton that trains most modern neural networks by working backward through every layer to calculate exactly who’s to blame for a mistake.
In their tests, the simplified system works. On a set of odors picked up by common gas sensors, Spi-Fly peaks after just three exposures to each one, while backpropagation needs roughly 70 to get there.
Feed the network new odors a couple at a time—a stress test for catastrophic forgetting—and Spi-Fly barely blinks, holding onto old smells with almost no accuracy loss, while backpropagation crashes down into near random-guessing territory.
There’s another practical hurdle: memory. The whole point of designing a network this simple is to eventually run it on neuromorphic chips—a fast-developing technology that builds hardware that mimics the brain directly by processing spikes instead of running conventional software. Those chips typically don’t have much memory to work with. Any algorithm running on one has to make do with a fraction of what a regular computer takes for granted. Spi-Fly degrades far less than backpropagation does under those constraints.
There’s a ceiling, though, as Max himself admits. “If the sparse code layer contains 100 neurons, and each odor is represented by 5 neurons, the theoretical upper limit of odor capacity is ‘100, choose 5,’” he explained in an email—roughly 75 million possible “barcodes.” But real-world noise erases nearly all of that headroom. “The same odor is almost never represented by the same sparse code in two exposures, due to noise, airflow conditions, etc.,” Max wrote. “Given the parameters of our model, it should be able to represent a couple hundred odors, but it also depends on what type of odors, and the similarities between them.”
Same story with the tests themselves: Every one of them, like the rest of the study, ran entirely in simulation, using single, isolated odors—nothing like the tangle of competing smells a device would meet in an actual kitchen, forest, or airport terminal. There’s no guarantee Spi-Fly would hold up once real molecules start interfering with each other outside a computer.
A disputed comparison
Then there’s EPL net, which the paper singles out as its closest competitor. It manages middling results on the gas sensor dataset, but performs poorly on the synthetic Drosophila data. Max attributes that gap to, among other reasons, timing: EPL net samples odors in discrete snapshots, mimicking how animals actually sniff, while Spi-Fly reads a continuous stream, discarding nothing.
Thomas Cleland, a Cornell psychology professor who co-designed EPL net, disputes the comparison itself. In his account, EPL net and Spi-Fly were never built to solve the same problem. EPL net is meant to filter out sudden, unpredictable background odors, the smell equivalent of a stranger’s cigarette smoke drifting into the room, for example. It does so by using one-shot learning rules and wasn’t designed to learn the gradual, repeatable variation Spi-Fly is trained on. “EPL and Spi-Fly are based on different layers of the olfactory system and are built for different noise models,” he writes in an email. He’s blunt about the upshot: In his view, the comparison doesn’t tell you much of anything.
Spi-Fly exists purely as code, tested against prerecorded datasets rather than an actual whiff of anything. The next step is folding it into the odor-sensing hardware Max and his collaborators are building at TU Eindhoven and Kiel University—real, physical neuromorphic chips, manufactured with all the tiny inconsistencies that come from actually being built rather than simulated.
Max does not put a date on it, only promising that there’s more to come soon. For now, though, the fly you watched drown in your wine glass still wins.

A third-party investigative panel set up by Nidec said Friday that it has identified 844 cases of misconduct involving some of the company’s products, such as changes to materials, manufacturing processes and designs without customer approval.
The panel was set up in May after the major Japanese motor maker disclosed more than 1,000 suspected cases of quality irregularities committed between 2020 and 2025 in its home appliance, automotive, information technology and other businesses.
The third-party body comprising outside experts said in a report that inappropriate decisions had accumulated “under pressure from various business processes, including performance targets, cost reduction and delivery deadlines,” which led to the formation and entrenchment of an “unsound state.”
Toshihiko Itami, chairman of the investigative committee and a lawyer, told a news conference that “misconduct on this scale in an area that lies at the core of manufacturing is extremely serious.” He stressed that the company “must take the matter seriously and implement corrective measures.”
The report called on Nidec’s current management to centralize the management of quality-related information and establish investigation frameworks involving an independent in-house team and outside experts.
Nidec said in a statement that the company sincerely acknowledges the reported issues, adding that it will return to the basics of monozukuri (manufacturing) and shift toward quality-centered management.
