A US Army commander wrote in a new opinion article that a recent combat training exercise against Ukrainian soldiers showed that armor like infantry fighting vehicles and tanks can still survive and make a difference on battlefields swarming with drones, but troops have to be able to adapt, to flexibly change how they move, hide, and fight.
During the simulated battle, his troops saw how persistent drone surveillance exposed their movements and put their combat vehicles at risk. But the soldiers also learned and adapted, the commander said.
On Friday, Capt. Allan W. Watson, the commander of Blackhawk Company, 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment, wrote an op-ed in Task and Purpose about an April exercise. The exercise, held at Hohenfels Training Area in Germany, pit Watson's soldiers against Hohenfels' dedicated opposition force, the 1st Battalion, 4th Infantry Regiment, with support from the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Force's 412 Regiment.
The Ukrainian unit, known as "Nemesis," brought real combat experience fighting with and against drones to the training, presenting a demanding test for American soldiers. Reconnaissance drones tracked their movements, and US forces didn't have the counter-drone capabilities they wanted, Watson wrote.
Watson's soldiers responded by changing how they used their armored vehicles. They hid their Bradleys in gullies and among the trees, leveraged the terrain to mask their maneuvers, avoided predictable routes that they knew the Ukrainian hunters expected them to try, and deliberately considered how the force looked to overhead drones.
"More than once," he wrote, "I found myself standing sideways in the turret of our Bradley, barking orders as our platoons traversed 40-degree slopes, finding new routes to an objective."
"The enemy still found us," Watson wrote in the op-ed. But "even with drone reconnaissance, the enemy had to use traditional ground reconnaissance and infiltration techniques. While a drone could identify us from above, only troops on the ground could exploit the information."
Throughout the fight, the US forces lost Bradleys and tanks, which Watson said was expected in a high-pressure event like this, an exercise meant to resemble a real armed conflict.
For Watson, those losses didn't condemn his armored assets to irrelevance; rather, the training exercise demonstrated that armor still provides tremendously valuable mobility, protection, and firepower as long as it is put to use with the drone threat in mind.
"Our armor did not make us more vulnerable," he wrote, "it made us mobile, protected, and dangerous."
Officials and top war watchers have debated the value of armored vehicles against drones and uncrewed systems since the beginning of the Ukraine war, as reports from the front and video footage of drones blowing up tanks and armor across the battlefield circulated online.
The asymmetric threat raised concerns that the proliferation of cheap drones, both surveillance and attack, had made heavy armor too vulnerable, making it less relevant for future fights.
Watson's account of his experiences paints a more complicated picture, acknowledging that uncrewed systems represent a growing threat to armored combat vehicles but emphasizing that the threat hasn't yet made them obsolete. The debate goes on.

Tottenham Hotspur, a professional soccer team that’s part of the Premier League, has saved over 85 percent in licensing fees by replacing its stadium’s VMware instance with Hewlett-Packard Enterprise’s (HPE’s) Morpheus VM Essentials (VME) virtualization software.
Tottenham hasn’t disclosed which VMware products it used or how much it previously paid the Broadcom firm.
The soccer organization confirmed this week to The Register that it has moved its stadium’s server, storage, and networking infrastructure to HPE solutions delivered through HPE’s hybrid cloud management platform, GreenLake. That is all “underpinned by” VME and HPE’s OpsRamp software for hybrid and multi-cloud environments, Rob Pickering, Tottenham’s CTO, told the publication, with HPE in charge of the hybrid cloud-managed service.
Tottenham is almost done with a broader redesign of its stadium’s data center and network infrastructure, The Register reported. The stadium has a data center with six aisles that uses HPE’s ProLiant Compute Gen12 server hardware and Alletra Storage MP. In an announcement this week, HPE noted that Tottenham is using “solutions including HPE Morpheus software and HPE OpsRamp software… to manage a complex, multi-site environment more efficiently while modernizing virtualization platforms and reducing operational overhead.”
“We’re at the right time of our replacement cycles to be looking at those decision points,” Pickering told SDxCentral this week.
“For at least as long as my career in technology, hypervisor has been one of those very unsexy things that you bought from one person and you just sort of got on with it. And you know, with VMware, a 400-pound gorilla in that space, they took some decisions that I think run counter to both the system integrator side and the customer side.”

US and allies want IAEA board to report Iran to UN Security Council, diplomats say
Iran is the only country to enrich uranium to 60% without making a bomb, and the IAEA calls that stockpile “a matter of serious concern”.
VIENNA: The US and its allies Britain, France and Germany are pushing other countries on the UN nuclear watchdog's board to pass a resolution next week reporting Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, diplomats said on Friday (Sep 4).
If passed, the resolution would follow up on one adopted on June 12 of last year declaring Iran in breach of its non-proliferation obligations for not fully cooperating with an investigation into uranium traces found at undeclared sites.
The US launched an air war against Tehran on February 28 in which, together with Israel, it destroyed or badly damaged Iran's uranium-enrichment facilities.
Iran has not let International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors return to the bombed sites since then or verify what remains of its stocks of enriched uranium, some of which was enriched to up to 60 per cent purity, a short step from weapons grade.
A resolution by the IAEA's 35-nation board reporting Iran to the Security Council would also be the culmination of a standoff over IAEA access to those sites, since the board has passed two resolutions in the past year demanding Iran declare its enriched uranium stocks and grant the IAEA full access to verify them.
A draft text for the resolution has yet to be formally submitted to the board, and negotiations between countries over the exact wording are ongoing, diplomats said. A draft is usually formally submitted early in the week of a board meeting.
As a party to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), Iran has the right to develop nuclear technology, including enrichment, for peaceful purposes. Iran says it would never produce nuclear weapons.
It is, however, the only country to enrich to 60 per cent without making a bomb. The amount it has enriched to that level is "a matter of serious concern" to the IAEA.
The IAEA believes well over 200 kg of that highly enriched uranium has survived the bombardments and is held in a tunnel complex at Isfahan and at the Natanz facility.

The head office of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency has been hit in a Russian drone attack, sending plumes of black smoke rising into the air in the heart of Kyiv.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he had instructed the SBU to deliver an “appropriate, tangible response” to the strike, while the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described it as a “major escalation”.
The streets around the SBU headquarters were cordoned off shortly after Friday’s attack, with armed officers patrolling the area.
Numerous ambulances and emergency services vehicles were stationed around the site, which is close to St Sophia Cathedral, a Unesco world heritage site.
“Unfortunately, a Russian drone hit the central building of the SBU on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, opposite the St Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram. “The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building.”
Kyiv has been under a barrage of daily drone and missile attacks from Russia for over a week. Zelenskyy on Friday called for Russia to halt its attacks during a visit of US negotiators to the city on Sunday.
Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors which can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones which can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept.
It is rare for government buildings in central Kyiv to be reached by Russian strikes, especially in broad daylight. The explosion from the hit on the SBU building could be heard from several blocks away.
The incident is likely to intensify the escalating attacks that Moscow and Kyiv have been launching at each other in recent weeks in efforts to destroy each other’s resilience and morale. It will also raise questions about Kyiv’s ability to defend its key infrastructure against Russia.
Sybiha said the attack was “a major escalation that demands resolute responses” and called on international partners to “unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime”.
At least nine people were injured in Friday’s strike, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
Stanislav Zavertailo, the co-owner of the nearby Zavertailo cafe, said one of his customers was injured in the strike, which sent shockwaves through his premises, shattering all the windows.
“It’s a normal cafe,” he said. The customer was “eating one of our famous poppy seed rolls” when the attack occurred, he added.
Staff and customers rushed into an underground shelter after the strike, fearing a double-tap attack, a tactic which Russia has employed, in which a second drone is sent in soon after the first, hitting emergency service workers.
An hour later, there had been no second strike, but Zavertailo said he did not feel at ease. “We are all waiting for another attack,” he said.
The SBU is responsible for coordinating complex operations against Russia, including last year’s Operation Spiderweb which destroyed aircraft worth billions of pounds inside Russia.
Friday’s hit was “awful” said a Zavertailo cafe employee who had recently emerged from the underground shelter. As “a person who lives in Ukraine for all this time, it’s just hard”.
The strike came two days before Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv for the first time.
US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year invasion have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards the war with Iran.

Emotional Taylor steps on to the scales one final time

Katie Taylor has taken her final week as a professional boxer in her stride.
Each media event has been ticked off with the kind of composure and poise she has displayed in the ring for over two decades.
Dublin blessed Taylor and opponent Flora Pili with some early autumn sun as they weighed in at Trinity College before Saturday's undisputed light-welterweight battle at a sold-out Croke Park.
Taylor has not missed weight once in her 26-fight career and she was not going to buck the trend as she was greeted by adoring fans - many whom have followed her career since she won Olympic gold in 2012.
The announcement of the weights - both coming in just under the 10st (63.5kg) limit - was almost immaterial.
All 80,000 tickets for Saturday's undisputed light-welterweight fight have been long snapped up and demand for Friday's ceremonial weigh-in proved just as high.
Supporters packed into Trinity College, a seat of higher learning founded in 1592 by Queen Elizabeth I, to catch a glimpse of the queen of Irish sport.
Women were not permitted to study at Trinity College until 1975 but Taylor, who has smashed barriers for women in and out of the ring - was the star attraction.
Trinity's old library is an attraction in its own right, home to the Book of Kells - an illustrated manuscript, which contains the four Gospels of the New Testament in Latin - but those in its grounds were there for their own piece of history on this final fight week of Taylor's illustrious career.
The 40-year-old, two-weight undisputed champion, may not be a huge fan of the fight week obligations and making weight is certainly an aspect to the sport that will not be missed, but this was an opportunity to soak it all in one last time.
Pili has been the perfect guest all week, complimentary and polite, but the Frenchwoman is not here to be a tourist and there was an air of confidence as she hit the scales.
The 29-year-old has stitched together a perfect record of 12 wins and has an opportunity to raise her own reputation if she can pull of a major upset.
It is Pili's biggest night, an opportunity to catapult herself into the upper echelons of the fight game, but an also occasion she has never experienced and looked a little bemused as she stepped on to the scales.
As violinists played Irish folk song 'Óró, sé do bheatha 'bhaile' [Óró - you are welcome home], Taylor appeared to a rapturous reception and the fighters went through the formalities, all smiles and handshakes.

With under 60 days until the midterms, there is still plenty of time to change the entire political map
The Iran war, Elon Musk’s cash and who decides to spend money in Texas could all be curve balls this cycle, Eric Garcia writes
On Thursday, the House of Representatives decided to cancel votes for the last two weeks of September, meaning that after next week’s break for Labor Day and Rosh Hashanah, the House will only be in business for four days until the midterm elections.
Right now, Republicans are going to need all the help they can get ahead of November. Midterms have a certain rhythm: two years after electing a president, voters either feel the administration has not lived up to its promises or seen them implemented and they now have buyer’s remorse.
All signs seem to show that for President Donald Trump and Republicans in the Senate and House of Representatives. Trump now boasts a 33 percent approval rating. He’s bleeding with Hispanic voters who had broken for him in 2024 and even more telling, he is starting to fall with white voters without college degrees and rural voters.
But every once in a while, a curveball can come along. In 1998, after Republicans impeached Bill Clinton but failed to convict him, Republicans actually lost House seats. In 2002, in the aftermath of the September 11 terrorist attacks, Republicans earned a solid majority in the House and Senate. And most recently, in 2022, when the Supreme Court killed the right to an abortion in the Dobbs v. Jackson decision, Republicans only barely won the House while Democrats held numerous governorships and netted a Senate seat.
And then, sometimes, a wave is so big that the minority party can win in an unexpected place. Here are some twists that could help shape what the political future of the nation will look like after November:
An end to the Iran War
There really is only one thing that could move the voting public to be more favorable to Trump and the GOP: ending the war in Iran. Despite what the administration says, the U.S. adventure in Iran is a war and it has caused the price of gas to rise exponentially.
The resulting inflation has outpaced wage growth. At this point, the only thing that would matter to voters is an end to the war that reopens the Strait of Hormuz and therefore increases the global supply of oil.
This seems unlikely. On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance told reporters that “I wouldn’t call it a war” when asked if it would be over before the midterms. But every day that drags on reminds voters that Trump caused their gas prices to rise.
Trump or John Thune blinks in Texas
Perhaps the ugliest Senate primary this year came in Texas when Trump endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, leading to Cornyn’s humiliating defeat.
Paxton’s numerous scandals–which led to him being impeached but acquitted in the Texas legislature–and allegations of infidelity have made Democrat James Talarico competitive. Polling shows Talarico either in the lead or in a statistical tie in a state that has been a Republican lock for years.
But so far, neither the National Republican Senatorial Committee nor the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Majority Leader John Thune, have ponied up. Trump has praised Paxton and raised money for him, but he has yet to deploy resources from MAGA Inc., his super PAC that has a more than $400 million cash pile. Contrast that with Talarico’s $30 million fundraising haul in the most recent quarter.
If any of them decide to deploy resources, this could be the thing that saves Paxton. Otherwise, he might be toast as a candidate.
Will Elon Musk’s moneybomb backfire?
After Elon Musk’s public falling out with President Donald Trump and leadership of the government cost costing, Musk has mostly returned to the Republican fold. This week, his America PAC dropped $800,000 to support Republican candidates running for both House and Senate. In particular, he spent a little less than $250,000 for Paxton and against Talarico.
He also dropped the $170,000 for Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and against her Democratic opponent Troy Jackson.
Collins is in the toughest race of her career, though she has a history of outperforming polls. But perhaps recognizing how unpopular Musk is in a blue state like Maine, she immediately distanced herself from Musk.
“I wasn't aware of that donation, I knew he was going to get involved in political campaigns but I had not heard that there was a specific donation,” she told reporters in Maine.
Musk’s campaign cash has a history of backfiring. Last year in Wisconsin, he dropped millions during the state’s supreme court race just for the liberal candidate to win in a rout. If Republicans in purple or even light red districts are tied to Musk, they could wind up with a target on their back given how unpopular he is with many voters.
Which race will shock everyone?
Every election has a sleeper result nobody expects. In 2018, Democrat Kendra Horn shocked nearly everyone when she flipped Oklahoma’s 5th district and in 2024, the unthinkable happened when Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. Bob Casey, whose father was one of the most beloved governors in the state, lost his seat.
Other times, that race signals a larger shift: Ron DeSantis’s squeaker for governor in 2018 opened the door to Florida going from the perpetual swing state to a solid red state.
In that same year, Kyrsten Sinema’s race began a streak of Democrats winning Senate seats in Arizona.
Some potential shockers include Democrat Adam Hamilton, a pastor, beating Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas based on the toll Trump’s tariffs placed on farmers - and the disappointment some have voiced over that decision.
Republican Rep. Anna Paulina Luna in Florida has proven to be uniquely vulnerable as she underperformed Trump in 2024 in the district and could lose her seat.
In Iowa, Democratic state legislator and former paraolympian Josh Turek trails behind Rep. Ashley Hinson’s for the state’s Senate seat. But under the right circumstances, it could flip. And in Colorado, Rep. Lauren Boebert has raised a pittance of money despite being a nationally recognized figure.
There are plenty of possibilities - and plenty of time - for curveballs that can cause massive swings in the midterm races. Now, we will start seeing them as campaigns begin their home stretches.

The face of American feminism
Gloria Steinem, who died Wednesday at 92, defined feminism in the US. Where will that movement go next?
Gloria Steinem — the one-woman powerhouse who, in many ways, defined modern feminism in the United States — died Wednesday at 92 after six decades of activism.
Steinem was a journalist and advocate who first rose to prominence in the late 1960s, just as the women’s liberation movement exploded. She co-founded Ms. magazine, a trailblazing publication that mainstreamed once-taboo topics like sexual harassment, wage inequity, and the unfair division of household labor.
As an advocate, Steinem also led protests, worked to elect more female politicians, and lobbied for abortion rights, employment protections, and the long-deferred Equal Rights Amendment.
The ERA, which would create a constitutional guarantee of equal rights for women, has never officially been adopted, despite being ratified by the required number of states. Many of the other causes Steinem championed, however, are now at least firmly part of mainstream cultural and political debate.
Later in life, as the feminist movement evolved, Steinem continued to serve as a kind of elder statesperson. (We’ll break down how exactly it evolved in just a minute.) Much of her recent writing and speaking focused — for obvious, depressing reasons — on the importance of hope and persistence in social justice movements.
“Hope is a form of planning,” she told Vogue on her 90th birthday, in 2024. “If you don’t imagine what could be, you’re already defeated.”
Heads up: Vox is off tomorrow and Monday for the Labor Day holiday. And speaking of labor…can I interest you in supporting all the work that goes into this newsletter? For a limited time, you can become a Vox member — and invest in the journalism that helps you think more deeply about the world — for just $30/year. Read more and sign up here.
Go a little deeper
Steinem was the single-most recognizable face of American feminism, but she represented a distinct wave of it that future generations of feminists built on. American feminism is a sprawling, evolving, multifaceted movement — and its history is often broken down into four distinct periods.
- First wave: 1848 to 1920: You might better know the feminists of this era by the name “suffragists”: The troublesome campaigners who fought for women’s right to vote. This “wave,” as it’s popularly dubbed, began with the Seneca Falls convention in New York and ended with the passage of the 19th Amendment, after which momentum died down a bit.
- Second wave: 1963 to the 1980s: The movement revived with the publication of Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique in 1963. It also broadened its focus beyond political rights, taking on reproductive freedom, workplace and cultural sexism, sexual harassment, and women’s financial independence. Steinem was maybe the quintessential second-wave feminist.
- Third wave: 1991 to the 2000s: Feminism slumped a bit in the ’80s, deflated by Reagan-era conservatism and a backlash that cast feminists as bitter, bra-burning man-haters. But the Anita Hill case in 1991 revived mainstream attention to workplace harassment, discrimination and women’s exclusion from positions of power.
- Fourth wave: 2008(ish) to present: The current generation of feminism places greater emphasis on intersectionality and trans inclusion. But its defining trait is probably how very online it is. The fourth wave kicked off with blogs like Jezebel and Feministing and picked up steam through hashtags like #MeToo, #TimesUp, #StandWithWendy, and #YesAllWomen.
In fairness, not everyone is terribly enamored with the “waves” framework. But for those of us trying to get the gist of recent history — or to take stock of what has and hasn’t changed, on the occasion of Steinem’s death — it can be a helpful way to get oriented. Vox has lots of further reading if you want to get into the nuances.

➨ Talk to your aging parents about their Apple Watches. Wearable devices like the Apple Watch can serve as alert systems that help keep older people safe. But before you buy a fitness tracker or a smart camera to keep an eye on your loved one, have a serious chat with them about their wishes and privacy.

Flock cameras are officially banned on state roads in Florida
Florida joins a growing list of cities and states responding to the license plate reader backlash.
Florida's Department of Transportation has officially banned police from placing license plate readers on state roads, according to a one-page memorandum from DOT Chief Operating Officer Will Watts. The decision is an early example of state regulators responding to the growing animus directed at automatic license plate reader (ALPR) providers like Flock Safety, and one that isn't exclusive to Florida.
"While Florida law limits the issuance of permits for LPR systems to law enforcement agencies," the memorandum says, "the recent exponential increase in deployments along our roadways, coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians' sovereignty and quality of life."
Per the memorandum, permits for license plate readers are immediately revoked and police have within 30 days of August 31 to remove them from state roads. Florida's Department of Transportation says it will also "use its discretionary authority to cease the issuance of all future requests for LPR systems within its jurisdictional authority."
The license plate reader ban was made at the behest of Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who said in August 2026 that use of the technology was "out of control" in the state. Removing cameras from state roads is an attempt to address the problem. As DeSantis noted on a podcast episode promoting his stance, though, changing DOT rules doesn't impact the 98 percent of ALPRs that are installed on local roads and private property. Both Jacksonville and Okaloosa county sheriffs have also committed to removing ALPRs from their jurisdiction. Removing (or reining in) the rest of the license plate readers in the state will either require more social pressure, or ideally, new laws.
Automatic license plate readers have been around for decades — you may have encountered one running a stop light or using a toll road — and states have grown to rely on them for a wide variety of different law enforcement tasks. That could include finding stolen vehicles or missing people, along with the more nebulous goal of developing leads in ongoing criminal investigations. For example, a little over a week before Florida's ban, license plate readers were used to find a murder suspect who fled Florida for West Virginia.
Flock, the ALPR company that's faced the most backlash in 2026, has ample examples on its website as to how ubiquitous cameras could help states and cities handle things outside of police work, too, like letting firefighters survey a fire before they arrive. The problem most people have with ALPRs is the idea of constantly being surveilled, and the already documented ways Flock's own cameras have been misused. The company has attempted to address those issues with software updates to its platform and policy changes that limit the amount of time it stores footage captured with its cameras, but the continued public outcry and ongoing vandalism of license plate readers seems like it's finally provoking regulators to respond.
Outside of Florida's ban, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its contract with Flock in July. Earlier in August, two counties in Ohio also paused their use of Flock cameras because of reports of alleged misuse. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott went as far as pausing funding for state agencies trying to acquire Flock hardware. Most of these changes are focused on Flock specifically rather than the use of license plate readers in general, but they do suggest willingness to at least consider different approaches to public safety.

Germany's far-right poised for power in state election
HALLE, GERMANY — Everywhere Ulrich Siegmund goes, an influencer follows — streaming live from the campaign trail. Siegmund is the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) candidate running for governor in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
But Siegmund needs neither influencers nor journalists. The 35-year-old former marketing man is a TikTok star in his own right and his party is comfortably leading polls Sunday's state election, which could make the AfD the first far-right party to lead a German state government since World War II.
Siegmund has almost half as many followers on the platform as people eligible to vote in this small state. He makes a point of taking time to answer their questions personally, often from the comfort of his back porch.
In every video, he's dressed in a flawlessly ironed white polo shirt or starched white dress shirt — the uniform of Germany's newly professionalized far-right.
His carefully coiffed side parting is as immaculate as his smile, something which distinguishes him from the rest of his party whose members tend to grimace rather than grin. But Siegmund's broad smile rarely cracks, even when he speaks his mind about the party's biggest issue, immigration and the mass deportation of migrants. The incongruity is striking. The polished, affable politician is also a proponent of one of the hardest-right positions in contemporary European politics.
In a recent TikTok post, Siegmund asserts that it is "unacceptable that our doctors are leaving for Switzerland, Norway, or elsewhere because they cannot tolerate the conditions here, while we bring in doctors from India or other places to replace them."
The AfD's platform states that "culturally foreign" health workers often fail to meet German medical standards and "endanger patient well-being."
Siegmund refrains from going into such detail on camera and he keeps his campaign speeches snappy — full of pep talk rather than policy.
The real detail is something former AfD supporter Hannes Kreschel addresses instead.
The 23-year-old law student attends AfD election rallies to talk to voters on camera. Over a beer and bratwurst, he points out disparities between the AfD's carefully crafted campaign and its actual policies, particularly its economic policies which, he argues, only add up for the financially well-off.
Some chats are more constructive than others, he says. "They try to hit the microphone and they try to hit me," Kreschel says. "Of course we're confronting them with facts, but I try to be nice because I think you should separate the people from their talking points."
Kreschel posts the exchanges on his own channels which, while popular, do not get the same traffic as the AfD candidate. But he's convinced that if he can change his mind about the AfD, others can too.
Kreschel voted for the AfD in the past to stick it to those in power. But when he read their policies, he realized the Alternative for Germany is not a viable alternative for him.
"I figured out that this is not the country I would like to live in," Kreschel explains in reference to the Alternative for Germany's anti-immigration, nationalistic vision. "I would like to live in an open country which is friendly and not full of hate."
But other voters in the city of Halle, where Kreschel lives, don't see hate; they see reason and hope.
Waiting in line to grab lunch at a market stall on the city's main square, Alexander Winsek says he's weighing up whether to vote for the AfD, adding that it would be his first time.
"I think the AfD has some very good ideas, like limiting the influx of migrants," Winsek says.
But the 49-year-old aviation engineer says he doesn't agree with all of the AfD's positions: "I'd like to stay in NATO, I'd like to keep the euro, and I'm not exactly pro-Russia", he stresses.
But Winsek says Ulrich Siegmund may swing it for him because he's significantly different from others in the AfD who, he points out, are all doom, gloom and threats.
Siegmund, he says, is can-do and refreshingly optimistic. "He's younger than all the others and stands out from the crowd," adding that Siegmund is the breath of fresh air democracy needs.
At the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg, Marcel Lewandowsky researches what makes a democracy resilient and is the author of the book What Populists Want.
Lewandowsky says it's wrong to assume that AfD voters want an autocratic leader. "We can see in the polls that the greatest share of AfD voters is pro-democracy," he points out, adding that the same share of AfD voters "also believes democracy is not functioning in Germany."
He says the AfD promises its voters "real" democracy — a pledge, he adds, with which other political parties struggle to compete. "The more they want to defend democracy against the AfD," Lewandowsky argues "the more they seem like the establishment that doesn't want to share their state, their government, their institutions with the silent majority which the AfD claims to represent."
And the AfD's anti-establishment appeal is no longer confined to eastern Germany; at the federal level, the party is also polling first. A win in Saxony-Anhalt would be a major breakthrough for a party that has been classified as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence authorities in several German states.
But influencer Kreschel, who recently posted a video of AfD campaigners asking him to leave an election rally, says the party's promise to give voice to ordinary Germans does not extend to those who disagree with it.

‘We’re students' A team, decide amongst yourself': CJP's Abhijeet Dipke reacts to ‘B team’ allegations
Abhijeet Dipke claimed that different political parties were working on the issue of government schools and students and questioned by the BJP objected to it.
Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke responded to allegations that the political satirical outfit acted in collusion with some political party during the Jantar Mantar protest and said satirically that the parties should decide amongst themselves whose ‘B team’ CJP is.
He said that for him, CJP is ‘A team’ of students.
"Maharashtra Chief Minister says that I am B team of Congress, and some say that I am B team of Aam Aadmi Party. I feel all these people should sit together and decide whose B team I am. According to us, we are students' A team," Dipke said while talking to reporters.
CJP, which was founded as a satirical political outfit, is now working as a pressure group with a larger team across India. The Jantar Mantar protest led by the outfit forced the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as education minister over irregularities in NEET-UG exam.

Dipke said that the campaign should get support across the political spectrum instead of being viewed as a step taken by any one political organisation.

Retail sugar price drops 3.85% to ₹62.57/kg in a week: Govt data
A retailer typically holds 10-15 bags of sugar, each weighing 50 kg. Only once fresh stock is procured at the lower rate will retail prices adjust accordingly.
New Delhi, Sep 3 (PTI) The average all-India retail price of sugar has declined by 3.85 per cent to ₹62.57 per kg in a week, following recent government measures including allowing imports and tightening of stockholding norms for bulk users and dealers, according to official data.
The retail price of the sweetener declined from ₹65.08 per kg a week ago. However, the prices are still ruling 27 per cent higher than the previous month's level of ₹49.33 per kg.
The average wholesale price of sugar too dropped to ₹57.62 per kg on September 2 from ₹60.39 per kg a week ago, as per the data maintained by the consumer affairs ministry.
The drop in wholesale price takes time to reflect in the retail market because retailers who bought stock at the earlier, higher rates are unwilling to sell at a loss and will continue pricing their existing inventory at the older rate until it is exhausted, according to sources.
A retailer typically holds 10-15 bags of sugar, each weighing 50 kg. Only once fresh stock is procured at the lower rate will retail prices adjust accordingly.
"It takes at least ten days to reflect changes in the retail price," an industry source said.
To check a sudden rise in sugar prices, the government took a series of measures, including allowing import of 10 lakh tonnes of sugar, and tightening of stock holding norms for bulk users and dealers.
The Centre has blamed mills for "jacking up" prices, insisting the country has ample sugar stocks - even as production estimates for the 2025-26 marketing year (October-September) have been revised down to 306 lakh tonnes, from an earlier projection of 343 lakh tonnes.
Annual domestic demand is pegged at around 280-285 lakh tonnes.

In Tamil Nadu, 107 high-load Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (CEmONC) centres will have to set up mini-fortress-like storage facilities to guard one-gram gold rings meant for newborns under Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay’s ‘Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam’. Vault-like secure storage facilities will be put in place at all these health facilities to ensure safe custody of the gold rings.
The State Health Secretary has written to the Engineer-in-Chief and Chief Engineer (Buildings), Public Works Department (PWD) to put in place safety enclosures for the storage facilities at these centres. With the scheme all set to be launched on September 15, 2026 PWD has been asked to expedite and complete the works on or before September 5.
The proposed setup includes steel grill enclosures for the steel bureau/storage cupboards, cupboards anchored to the floor and wall and lockable gates to ensure the safe and secure custody of the gold rings. An approved model of the grill layout around the steel cupboard along with specifications has been shared with the PWD.
Under the scheme, a one-gram gold ring will be provided to every eligible newborn born in government health institutions through a network of 107 high-load CEmONC centres.
The Health Secretary listed several measures to ensure the safe custody of the gold rings at these hub institutions. This included a secure, restricted storage room surrounded by buildings on three sides, sealed windows and a cupboard firmly anchored to the floor and wall using cement/concrete. The cupboard is also to be enclosed with metal grills on three sides, while the storage room should not open into an isolated or easily accessible area and its door may also be grilled.
Listing out technical specifications, the communication said the safety enclosure for the steel bureau/storage cupboard should be made using mild steel square rods. The enclosure will cover the top and two sides, while the front will have an openable mild steel grill gate. The structure will be securely fixed using mild steel flats, with proper welding and finishing. The cupboard will also be anchored to a reinforced cement concrete bed to ensure stability.
In line with this, the official requested the PWD to fix the mild steel grill gate around the storage cupboard at all 107 institutions as per the approved design and specifications. The work may be taken up on priority basis and completed at the earliest to ensure safe and secure custody of the gold rings and facilitate uninterrupted implementation of the scheme in all the designated hubs.
The Health Secretary requested the PWD official to issue necessary instructions to all district-level PWD engineers/divisional engineers to coordinate with the respective medical college hospitals, district headquarters hospitals and sub-district hospitals and complete the work expeditiously on or before September 5.

D2C beauty and personal brand SUGAR Cosmetics has raised ₹144.47 Cr ($15.3 Mn) in a fresh equity round from VC firm A91 Partners, as per the startup’s MCA filings accessed by Inc42. It allotted 1.12 Lakh Series D7 CCPS to A91’s entity A91 Emerging Fund III at an issue price of ₹12,871. The CCPS will compulsorily convert into equity shares upon listing of the startup or one day prior to the expiry of 20 years from issue date. The startup’s board of directors passed the resolution at its meeting held on September 1. The startup has raised the fresh capital at a significant valuation cut. Its post-money valuation with the round, which seems to be its Series D equity round, is in the range of ₹550-600 Cr ($58-64 Mn), as per Inc42’s calculations. This implies a hefty 75-80% cut from the ₹2,600-2,700 Cr valuation it commanded back when it had raised funds in November 2024. The startup’s pre-money valuation for the round stood at ₹433.6 Cr. SUGAR’s peak valuation was about ₹3,000 Cr ($500 Mn) back in 2022. Inc42 has reached out to the startup for their response on the development. The story would be updated in case they respond. Notably, SUGAR’s net loss for the fiscal year FY25 nearly doubled to ₹135 Cr from ₹68.4 Cr. Its operating revenue also plunged by about 20% to ₹404.4 Cr in FY25, compared to ₹505.1 Cr in FY24. At the same time, its EBITDA losses more than doubled to ₹116 Cr in FY25 as against ₹48.5 Cr in FY24. To note, SUGAR is yet to report its financial performance for the fiscal year FY26. “The company has demonstrated a sustained and worsening pattern of financial deterioration over the past two financial years,” wrote Sayali Deshkar, the registered valuer, in a valuation report attached with the filings dated June 30, 2026. SUGAR’s economics were impacted mainly by its aggressive offline expansion. As per an ET report, the startup had to shut 30-40% of the physical stores that it opened due to the losses incurred per store. Inc42 has reached out to the company with questions and the story will be updated with their response. Founded in 2015 by the husband-wife duo of Vineeta Singh and Kaushik Mukherjee, Mumbai-based SUGAR sells beauty and personal care products on its own website, in physical stores, and through ecommerce platforms. To date, the startup has raised $90 Mn from investors like Elevation Capital, A91 Partners, Anicut Capital, and IndiaQuotient. SUGAR operates four brands – SUGAR, POP, ENN, and Quench Botanics – and competes with listed companies like Nykaa and Mamaearth as well as the likes of Renee Cosmetics. The stakes are high with India entering the D2C 3.0 era where D2C brands are expected to command more than two-thirds of the overall gross merchandise value (GMV) across ecommerce by 2031. Beauty and personal care is one of the most funded segments within the D2C ecosystem, with this space drawing over $1.1 Bn in funding across 201 deals between 2015 and Q1 FY26.

Donald and Crocombe get England white-ball call-ups
- Published
England have named the uncapped Aneurin Donald and Henry Crocombe in their squads for the white-ball series against Sri Lanka.
Derbyshire opener Donald has been included in the 16-player squad for the three-match T20 series, while Sussex seamer Crocombe makes the 16-man line-up for the three one-day internationals.
Donald scored 489 runs in 12 matches captaining Derbyshire Falcons in the Vitality Blast and hit the most sixes in this year's competition with 37.
He also helped Trent Rockets to the final of the Hundred, which the 29-year-old's side lost to Manchester Super Giants.
Crocombe, 24, has taken hat-tricks in his past two County Championship matches and has three five-wicket hauls this season.
England men's national selector Marcus North said the pair are "two promising players who have earned their places on the back of impressive performances in domestic cricket".
He added: "Aneurin has had an exceptional season for Derbyshire in the Vitality Blast and also with Trent Rockets in The Hundred while Henry is a player we have had an eye on all summer."
Meanwhile England all-rounder Jacob Bethell will again be absent after he "underwent successful surgery on his injured knee earlier this week".
He is targeting the white-ball series against Australia in November for his comeback.
Bethell sustained his injury in the ODI series against India in the summer and missed the Test series against Pakistan.
He is also expected to be absent for an ODI tri-series against hosts Pakistan and Sri Lanka in Lahore and Rawalpindi in October.
Batter Phil Salt is unavailable because of a right quad injury, while bowler Jamie Overton is in both squads after missing the white-ball series against India earlier with a thigh injury.
What about Brydon Carse?
Durham seamer Brydon Carse has not been included in either squad to face Sri Lanka.
The 31-year-old was dropped for the second Test of the current series against Pakistan after he was briefly arrested following an incident outside a Derby nightclub on 22 August.
Derbyshire police are continuing to investigate an allegation of assault in connection with that incident.
"Whiile Brydon was available for selection, he has not been picked for the Sri Lanka series squad," said the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB).
"Given recent events, we feel it is important for him to work through the issues that led to the Derby incident and take time for a proper reset. This decision does not prejudge the outcome of any investigation."
There are not expected to be any updates from the police imminently, while the Cricket Regulator will wait until that investigation is completed before looking into the incident.

A parliamentary committee has recommended a review and the rationalisation of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) limits governing the operation and acquisition of existing private hospitals, warning that aggressive corporatisation and the influx of foreign capital could push up healthcare costs and undermine the affordability of medical care.
The growing presence of foreign capital in private hospital chains was facilitating the acquisition of cost-effective, mid-sized hospitals by larger corporate entities, the committee said, and warned that such “aggressive corporatisation” was transforming healthcare from a public service into a “purely capitalistic enterprise”, with the potential to inflate the cost of medical procedures and trigger price increases across the healthcare ecosystem.
Foreign investment in private hospitals will make treatment unaffordable: RJD
The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare, headed by Samajwadi Party (SP) Rajya Sabha MP Ram Gopal Yadav, presented the 176th report on ‘Affordability and Accessibility of Healthcare Facilities in Public and Private Sector’, which distinguishes between foreign investment in hospital operations and investment in healthcare manufacturing.
Foreign capital should be encouraged in the manufacture of medical devices, consumables and specialised medicines for rare diseases, the report said, while its application in the direct operation and acquisition of hospitals needed greater scrutiny.
The report recommended that the government strictly review and rationalise FDI limits concerning the operational management and acquisition of existing healthcare facilities, while creating incentives to redirect foreign investment towards domestic manufacturing of medical technologies and pharmaceuticals.
The committee also argued that a strong public healthcare system could act as a market regulator by providing an affordable alternative to private care. Efficiently managed public hospitals, it said, could exert competitive pressure on private providers and help bring down healthcare costs.
It has recommended the establishment of autonomous, efficiently managed public multi-speciality hospitals in every revenue division to reduce patients’ dependence on major cities, and minimise travel for tertiary care.
The panel’s recommendations come against the backdrop of a widening public-private cost gap. Citing the 80th round of the National Sample Survey, the committee said the average cost of hospitalisation was ₹50,508 in private hospitals, compared with ₹6,631 in government hospitals. It has separately called for mechanisms to standardise and cap the cost of essential treatments, diagnostics, and routine procedures in private hospitals.
The committee has simultaneously proposed incentives — including tax holidays, soft loans, subsidised land and concessional electricity — to attract private investment in multi-speciality hospitals in tier-2, tier-3 and rural areas. It has suggested that public-private partnerships be used to extend advanced medical technologies and specialised services to underserved regions.
Private hospitals receiving government incentives should also consider cross-subsidisation, with revenues from higher-paying patients, including international patients, helping subsidise treatment for poorer patients, the committee said.
It has further recommended raising the mandatory reservation of beds for Below Poverty Line (BPL), Economically Weaker Section (EWS), and AB-PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana) beneficiaries from 10% to 20%, citing weak enforcement of existing obligations on private hospitals.
The committee has also called for hospital-level ethics committees to examine professional fees and for stronger regulatory oversight of public-private partnerships to ensure that commitments to provide affordable care are honoured.
It has proposed a single-window mechanism to ease regulatory approvals for healthcare facilities in smaller cities and called for greater empanelment of private hospitals in aspirational and remote districts under AB-PMJAY.
The thrust of the recommendations is that private and foreign capital should supplement rather than substitute public investment in healthcare, with incentives linked to affordability, geographical access, and services for vulnerable populations.

Komal Nahta, one of India’s prominent trade analysts, has returned with a new season of his podcast Game Changers: The Music Series, which features conversations with singers, composers and musicians about their journeys, influences and experiences in the music industry. The latest episode featured musician Adnan Sami, who reflected on his early years in music and how his identity as a pianist gradually expanded to include singing.
Adnan Sami recalls early music days: “If Kishore Kumar and Rafi Sahab could sing my music, it would be so great!”
Speaking about whether he considers himself a musician or a pianist, Adnan Sami said that he has always primarily viewed himself as a pianist. He recalled developing an interest in music at a young age and beginning his journey with the instrument when he was five. Adnan said, “I consider myself a pianist first. I always had a dream, since childhood, to be a pianist and a music composer. I started playing the piano at the age of five, and by the age of seven, I had composed my first piece of music. At the age of 15, I started making music and demos. I used to think, ‘If Kishore Kumar and Rafi Sahab could sing my music, it would be so great.’ After a while, people started saying that the music sounded good in my voice. I never took it seriously, but when more people, apart from my parents, started complimenting me, especially my cousins, I started believing it.”
Adnan further explained that his transition into singing was initially driven by circumstance rather than a deliberate decision to pursue another musical identity. He said that he began lending his voice to his own compositions because he could not find other singers willing to record them. “I started singing my songs because no one else wanted to sing them. Necessity is the mother of invention. In the beginning, when people introduced me as a singer; I felt weird, as I still considered myself a pianist. Then, with time, I got used to it,” he added.
Over the course of his career, Adnan Sami has established himself as a pianist, composer and singer, with his work spanning Indian film music and independent music. His conversation with Komal Nahta offers insight into the early stages of that journey and the circumstances that shaped his eventual career as a singer.

For many small-to-medium-sized businesses (SMBs), VMware has become too expensive.
Broadcom’s acquisition of the virtualization firm brought the end of perpetual license sales and the arrival of pricey, stacked, subscription-based bundles that priced out many SMBs.
The most obvious is VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), VMware’s flagship private cloud bundle that has been Broadcom’s primary focus since taking over VMware. Many SMBs find that VCF is unaffordable and stuffed with unnecessary offerings. However, numerous customers have reported online that VMware sales representatives have still pushed them toward VCF, with some claiming that sales reps have told them that the lower-priced edition of VMware’s virtualization platform, vSphere Standard, was no longer available.
Speaking with The Register this week, Paul Turner, VCF’s chief product officer, said Broadcom’s new sales incentives encouraged the sales team to push VCF.
“We corrected this,” Turner told the publication. He admitted that sometimes VMware had “too big a focus on VCF.”
vSphere Standard update
VMware will release an “updated version” of vSphere Standard “soon,” The Register reported. More information will likely come in October during VMware’s Explore conference in Frankfurt, Ram Velaga, president of Broadcom’s Infrastructure Software Group, told The Register.
VMware hasn’t updated vSphere Standard since 2022 despite an updated version of vSphere arriving with VCF 9 in 2025. This was because, Turner said, VMware was prioritizing improving VCF’s security.
Velaga said that VMware prioritized VCF in an effort to promote private clouds as a more affordable alternative to the public cloud, which are easier to manage. “People could get distracted” if VMware introduced a low-end virtualization product then, the executive said.
Broken trust
Dean Colpitts, CTO of Canadian managed services provider Members IT Group (MITG), which VMware cut from its reseller program after 19 years of partnership last year, told Ars that MITG is not doing any VMware business now and won’t in the future.
I was shocked how unapologetic and straight faced the CEO was when he explained what Broadcom was all about during company wide townhall after acquisition. "We are not in business of developing new technologies. We are in business of acquiring mismanaged great technologies and monetizing them". I think that tells you everything you need to know. I still can't believe regulators let the deal go through.

Bessemer Venture Partners-backed digital payments startup Innoviti managed to cut its net loss by over 57% YoY to ₹26.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹62.1 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. The startup managed to cull its loss despite its top line taking a hit during the fiscal, falling by 16.7% to ₹118.9 Cr in the year under review as against ₹142.6 Cr in FY25. During the fiscal, Innovit’s revenue from services fell by 17.8% YoY to ₹101.5 Cr. Of this, ₹97.3 Cr came from offline revenue, which shrank 20% from ₹121.4 Cr in the previous year. Its online revenue doubled to around ₹4.2 Cr. Additionally, the startup registered an operating revenue of ₹17.4 Cr from lease rentals in FY26. This figure also came down by about 9% from ₹19.1 Cr in the year-ago period. Apart from its operating revenue, it also reported ₹3.3 Cr in other income, bringing its total income for FY26 to ₹122.2 Cr. In its filing with the MCA, accessed by Inc42, the startup said that it expects to turn EBITDA positive in FY27, aided by operational improvements, cost-efficiency measures, and new customer additions. Founded in 2002 by Rajeev Agrawal and Amrita Malik, Innoviti offers three core products: sales acceleration software Innoviti Genie, revenue assurance software Innoviti Unipay and payment collection app Innoviti Link. The startup claims to process over ₹80,000 Cr of gross transaction volume (GTV) annually from across 2,000 Indian cities and over 20,000 merchants. Earlier this year, Innoviti received the certificate of authorisation by the RBI to operate as a payment aggregator (PA), permitting it to operate as a PA for both online and offline payments. It had earlier received RBI authorisation for online payment aggregation in March 2024. It has raised over $115 Mn in funding to date from investors like Bessemer Venture Partners, Catamaran Ventures, Alumni Ventures, FMO, and others. Most recently, it raised a $11.4 Mn Series M funding round in February. Innoviti has also been looking to make its public market debut for a few years now. In August 2024, it had said it would go for an IPO within a year. It then repeated the sentiment in January 2025 but is yet to make any headway in the public markets direction. Where Did Innoviti Spend In FY26? Innoviti managed to slash losses by paring its expenses by nearly 28% in the year under review. Pregnant woman and her unborn child die after her hair got caught in a go-kart
Baylee Johnson, 24, was 15 weeks pregnant with her son, Johnny, when the fatal incident occurred near Sumter, South Carolina
A 24-year-old South Carolina woman and her unborn son have died following an incident in Sumter County where her hair became entangled in a go-kart.
Baylee Johnson was 15 weeks pregnant when the incident occurred in the area of Skinner Road on August 23, Sumter County Coroner Robbie Baker reported to local news outlet WIS 10. Her hair caught in a sprocket of the vehicle, causing severe injuries.
Johnson was transported to McLeod Regional Medical Center in Florence, where she died eight days later on Aug. 31, surrounded by her family.
Johnson and her boyfriend, Justin Lowder, had recently learned they were expecting a baby boy, whom they named Johnny. She had also recently secured her dream job as a medical assistant at Prisma Health OB/GYN–Sumter.
In her obituary, Johnson was remembered for her devotion to others and her lively, humorous nature.
“Caring for others came naturally to Baylee — but so did making them laugh,” the family wrote. “And if there is one thing everyone who knew Baylee could agree on, it is that she was funny. So funny.
“Baylee was silly, spontaneous and completely carefree. She would dance anywhere, sing as loudly as she wanted and never give a second thought to who might be watching — or how crazy she looked while doing it. She did not simply walk into a room; she brought life into it.”
Her obituary noted that she enjoyed hunting, fishing, go-kart racing, reading her Bible and spending time with her family, her dogs Ruby and Roscoe, and her nieces and nephew.
“Baylee loved Johnny deeply,” the tribute read. “She dreamed about him, talked about him, prayed for him and was already planning the life she wanted to give him. From the moment she learned he was there, Baylee was his mama, and Johnny was completely and unconditionally loved.”
Her family expressed gratitude to the community and hospital care team for their support during her final days.

Mumbai: A passenger association's claim that four commuters fell from a running local at the same spot in Kalwa over three days has brought the safety concerns in the Kalwa-Mumbra section back into focus. The Mumbai Rail Pravasi Sangh has alleged that overcrowding and the closure of access to Kalwa Carshed-bound trains have turned the area into a danger zone. It has sought an investigation into the incidents and action within 15 days, warning of a protest if the issue is not addressed.
Central Railway, however, said the Carshed lines had been unauthorisedly used by commuters to board trains and that this practice had now been stopped. The railway said it had advised officials to check the matter, while noting that only one case of a commuter falling from a train had been reported a few days earlier.
Safety concerns at Kalwa-Mumbra
The association also alleged that commuters were experiencing jerks at the spot and demanded that the issue be investigated.
In its response, Central Railway said the RPF and GRP had been asked about the reported incidents. It also requested the Pravasi Sangh to bring such cases to its notice immediately so that appropriate action could be taken.
The railway further said that on some occasions, associations were involved in organising or participating in such events, a remark that adds another dimension to the dispute over unauthorised boarding.
Demand to revive Parsik station
The latest concerns have also revived the demand for Parsik Station as a suburban halt.
At the Suburban Railway Users' Consultative Committee (SRUCC) meeting held on July 24, Mumbai Rail Pravasi Sangh representative Siddhesh Desai sought a feasibility study into reviving the historic railway point. The Principal Chief Operations Manager (PCOM) asked the division to examine the proposal.
Desai had earlier raised the issue in a grievance filed in December 2025, arguing that the absence of a designated station between Kalwa and Mumbra was forcing commuters to depend on Carshed-bound trains or travel to Thane to board services passing Kalwa.
He said this was creating avoidable crowding at Thane, increasing travel time and exposing commuters to safety risks.
Heritage and commuter concerns
Desai also pointed to the historical significance of Parsik Point, which, according to GIPR records cited in his grievance, was the final stop of India's first trial train in November 1852.
He said reviving the station could preserve this heritage while addressing present-day commuter hardships. He also sought a safety and commuter-impact study, along with modernisation of Parsik Station as a suburban halt.
Railway measures and future plans
The demand comes amid concerns over overcrowding in the Kalwa-Mumbra section, where the distance between the two stations is among the longest in the Mumbai suburban network.
Desai said commuters standing near train doors remain exposed to risk during the journey and that allowing safe boarding of Carshed-bound trains at Kalwa or Parsik could reduce pressure on Thane.
Central Railway had earlier rejected the demand to allow general passengers to enter the Kalwa Carshed, citing safety and security restrictions applicable to railway carsheds, workshops and other operational premises.
In its response to the 2025 grievance, the railway said a pedestrian bridge was being constructed from Kalwa West to Kalwa station to prevent track crossing. Once opened, the safety wall would be fully closed to stop trespassing.
The railway also said it was considering increasing the number of 15-coach suburban trains, with platform-lengthening work under way at Kalwa and other stations.
It added that RPF personnel were carrying out regular patrolling, monitoring and crowd-management measures in the Kalwa-Mumbra and Thane areas, particularly during peak hours.
Also Watch:
Parsik revival proposal pending
The latest SRUCC discussion has put Parsik's revival back on the table, but the proposal remains at the feasibility-examination stage.
For now, the immediate concern is whether commuters can be prevented from taking unsafe boarding routes while a longer-term solution to overcrowding is considered.

Rahul Gandhi vs C Joseph Vijay: Can TVK chief do what Arvind Kejriwal could not?
Pallavi / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Sep 04, 2026, 16:20 IST

Vijay's national ambitions: Can the TVK chief succeed where Kejriwal failed?
The honeymoon period between Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) and its coalition partner, the Congress, appears to be over. Barely months after the two parties came together to form the government, they are already sparring over a question that is ostensibly about the 2029 Lok Sabha election: Who should be the opposition's prime ministerial face - Rahul Gandhi or Vijay?What began as statements and counter-statements between the two party leaders has quickly acquired a sharper political edge.TVK PWD minister Aadhav Arjuna pitched Vijay as a potential national leader, arguing that the country's highest political office should go to a leader from Tamil Nadu. On the other hand, state minister S Rajesh Kumar said Congress ministers in the Tamil Nadu cabinet would resign if TVK did not support Rahul Gandhi as the PM candidate in 2029.
The confrontation spilled into the assembly as well. Congress Legislature Party leader and MLA Tharahai Cuthbert was shifted on August 31 from the section allotted to TVK legislators to the front row of the opposition benches.But beneath the immediate fight over Rahul versus Vijay lies a much bigger question: Does Vijay intend to remain a powerful Tamil Nadu leader, or does he see the state's 2026 mandate as the launchpad for a national political project?And if the latter is the plan, can he succeed where Arvind Kejriwal could not?
Vijay's extraordinary first step
The scale of Vijay's rise explains why the 2029 debate has surfaced so early.The April 2026 Tamil Nadu assembly election ended nearly six decades of dominance by the DMK and AIADMK.
TVK, only two years old, emerged as the largest party with 108 seats in the 234-member assembly. The DMK won 59 and AIADMK 47, while Congress secured five seats, with the remaining seats going to smaller allies.TVK was therefore not merely a new party that performed better than expected. It emerged as the central political force in an election that disrupted the state's traditional two-party equilibrium.There was, however, one problem: 108 seats were still short of the 118 required for a simple majority.That made Congress indispensable.Vijay eventually formed the government with the support of MLAs from Congress [5], VCK [2] and IUML [2], along with outside support from the Left parties [4]. The MDMK, which has two MLAs, later extended its support.Congress moved away from its long-standing association with the DMK and backed a TVK-led government along with smaller allies, taking the coalition's strength to 121. Vijay was sworn in as CM on May 10.Congress had submitted its letter of support after the election, making it clear that its support would be conditional on TVK keeping "communal forces" out of the alliance.
Vijay emerged as the disrupter-in-chief in Tamil Nadu elections.
The 234-member assembly currently has seven vacancies following the resignation of six AIADMK MLAs and Vijay vacating his second seat, Trichy East. The effective strength of the House is therefore 227, bringing the majority mark down to 114.The political equation is unusual. Congress is the junior partner, with only five seats, but its support helped Vijay cross the majority mark. At the same time, TVK's 108 seats give Vijay overwhelming dominance within the coalition.That inversion may be at the heart of the present tension.Congress had been with the DMK in the pre-poll alliance and had never secured a place in MK Stalin's cabinet. After the results, however, it quickly moved to TVK's side and helped Vijay form the government.The alliance therefore contains a built-in contradiction: the party that needs Vijay's government to survive does not want Vijay to emerge as the leader of the national opposition.
Congress leader on TVK's 'Vijay-for-PM' pitch.
The 'agnipath' of Vijay's path
Vijay's route to Delhi runs into a problem that no amount of success in Tamil Nadu can entirely solve: numbers.Tamil Nadu sends 39 MPs to the Lok Sabha. Even a TVK sweep in 2029 would leave Vijay nowhere close to the 272 seats needed for a majority in the 543-member House.History, however, offers a little hope.In the past, India has had PMs whose parties did not come close to a Lok Sabha majority. HD Deve Gowda became PM in 1996 after the Janata Dal won just 46 seats, emerging as the consensus choice of the United Front with Congress support. IK Gujral followed a year later under much the same arrangement, with the Janata Dal holding only around 45 seats. Chandra Shekhar became prime minister in 1990 after breaking away from the Janata Dal with just 64 MPs, relying on outside support from Congress.This may give Vijay some hope.But it is also where the historical comparison begins to fray. The coalition politics that made these leaders PMs belonged to a different national landscape where coalition governments were a norm. The BJP, however, has changed that equation, building the NDA into a durable national coalition rather than the loose, post-election arrangements that defined much of the 1990s.The opposition, meanwhile, has come together in the form of the INDIA bloc which Vijay's TVK is not part of yet.And yet, paradoxically, being outside the INDIA bloc may give Vijay an advantage over Rahul Gandhi.Rahul comes with the weight of the Congress's history: its national footprint, its alliances and rivalries, the Nehru-Gandhi legacy and the political resistance that the party can provoke among regional leaders. Vijay comes with much less baggage. He would enter a coalition conversation not as the leader of a decades-old national party, but as a new political force with a mass following built before he entered politics.
Rahul Gandhi's political journey.
That distinction could matter if the next Lok Sabha produces another fractured mandate. But that is a big if, and one that looks unlikely in the present circumstances.Congress MP Karti Chidambaram has already put the arithmetic bluntly: "Every party has dreams, ambitions, and desires ... but we know what the political reality is. There are 543 constituencies."Thus, for Vijay, even if his party manages to sweep all 39 Tamil Nadu seats, the real test would be in finding enough allies to make Delhi possible.
Can Tamil Nadu be Vijay’s launchpad?
There is, however, one route Vijay could attempt that would give his national project a distinct political identity.He could build around Tamil Nadu's distinctive relationship with the Centre and a broader southern assertion in national politics — the argument that Delhi needs a stronger voice from a region that has historically resisted political and cultural centralisation.That could give TVK's national project a political argument beyond Vijay's celebrity and the anti-incumbency against established parties.But it comes with its own problem.
BJP has used the opportunity to question TVK-Congress alliance.
A political identity rooted in Tamil pride and southern assertion may work strongly in Tamil Nadu, but it does not automatically translate into votes in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, West Bengal or other states.Vijay would therefore have to balance two identities: the Tamil leader whose legitimacy comes from Tamil Nadu and the national leader who must persuade voters elsewhere that his politics is not confined to the state.
Why Congress cannot simply step aside
For Congress, the dispute is not simply about Rahul Gandhi's personal ambitions or the future of the Gandhi family. It is about whether the party can retain its position as the principal national pole of the opposition after years of organisational and electoral decline.Rahul has spent years positioning himself as the principal challenger to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP. Congress's improved performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha election and Rahul's emergence as leader of opposition strengthened that claim.The subsequent assembly elections, however, have weakened the party's position against the BJP.A recent survey placing Rahul as the second-most preferred PM choice and Vijay next is nevertheless significant. Vijay's position is remarkable for a leader whose party has contested only one assembly election, even though such surveys are hardly a substitute for actual elections.For Congress, conceding the national leadership question to Vijay now would risk allowing another regional leader to occupy the political space the party is trying to reclaim, especially after the weakened positioning of Mamata Banerjee, MK Stalin and Kejriwal.
The Kejriwal test
Kejriwal also began with an extraordinary political breakthrough in a single territory before attempting to turn his party into a national alternative.When he launched the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) in November 2012, his political project was built around challenging established parties, particularly Congress, which had governed Delhi for 15 years under Sheila Dikshit.AAP's breakthrough came almost immediately. Kejriwal became CM in December 2013, resigned after 49 days and returned in February 2015 with one of the most emphatic mandates in Indian electoral politics: AAP won 67 of Delhi's 70 assembly seats, reducing Congress to zero.But Kejriwal did not intend to stop at Delhi.The 2014 Lok Sabha election was his first major attempt to build a national footprint. AAP contested 432 seats and won four, all in Punjab. Kejriwal himself challenged Narendra Modi in Varanasi, while Kumar Vishwas contested Amethi against Rahul Gandhi. Neither challenge produced the national breakthrough AAP was seeking.The party then entered the Punjab and Goa assembly elections in 2017. Punjab became a second political laboratory, with AAP winning 20 of 117 seats and emerging as the principal opposition force behind Congress. Goa, however, exposed the limits of the expansion strategy, with AAP failing to win a single assembly seat.Punjab eventually provided the big breakthrough. In the 2022 election, AAP won 92 of 117 seats and formed a government under Bhagwant Mann.Kejriwal had therefore achieved something genuinely difficult: he had built governments in two states and turned AAP into a recognisable political force beyond Delhi.Yet the national leap remained elusive.AAP's electoral strength outside its core states never matched the scale of its Delhi and Punjab victories. In Gujarat, where it tried to establish itself as a third force, the party won five assembly seats in 2022, while Goa remained marginal. Its Lok Sabha presence also remained modest.
Vijay's one-point lead on Kejriwal
The Tamil Nadu CM has one advantage over Kejriwal though that their starting points are different.Kejriwal had to build a mass political identity almost from scratch. Vijay, however, spent decades building one through cinema before entering politics. He then converted that popularity into 108 assembly seats in his very first election, which was dubbed as an extraordinary political conversion.But it can also become a weakness.The question is no longer whether millions of people know Vijay. They do.The question is whether voters who know him as an actor and Tamil Nadu CM will vote for TVK in states where the party has no political history, local leadership or cadre network.To go national, Vijay would need candidates, local leaders, a cadre network and alliances. Most importantly, he would need a political proposition that resonates with voters who do not know him primarily as a Tamil film star.This is where Kejriwal's experience matters most.AAP's success in Delhi could not simply be reproduced across the country. Punjab offered a favourable political opening, but Goa and Gujarat demonstrated that national visibility and electoral organisation are very different things.Vijay's task could be even harder because many of the states he would need to enter already have powerful regional leaders with their own political ambitions.For now, the 2029 PM debate may therefore be premature, but the political conflict it has exposed is not. Vijay may need Congress to consolidate the power he has won in Tamil Nadu even as he seeks to challenge Congress's claim to national opposition leadership.
That is the paradox at the heart of his political project.If Vijay can use the Congress alliance to build a durable organisation without becoming politically dependent on it, he may have found a route Kejriwal could not. But if TVK's national ambitions remain ahead of its organisational reach, the 2029 debate could end up looking less like the beginning of a national challenge and more like the first sign of a regional party reaching beyond its electoral weight.
