Nepal rescuers try to reach dozens trapped in tunnel after two found alive
- Published
Rescuers in Nepal are stepping up efforts to find scores of workers believed to be trapped in tunnels, nine days after the devastating flash floods which hit the area on the border with Tibet in China.
Hopes have risen after two people were pulled out alive on Friday. The body of a third person was also found in one of the tunnels used to supply hydropower stations.
The massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out entire villages.
There are now 1,311 confirmed dead and 5,330 still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of foreign citizens are believed to be among those missing, from at least 34 countries.
The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.
In Nepal, however, rescue operations are taking place at seven hydropower tunnels in which more than 150 people are feared trapped - as well as in 19 other areas.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices at the Trishuli 3A hydropower site.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".
Crews clambered in to find Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan - both had injuries on their hands and legs, "possibly" from crawling through the tunnel. Both were airlifted to the Army Hospital in the capital, Kathmandu.
Maharjan, who was rescued second, is in a critical condition, the prime minister's office said. Shah was also undergoing medical tests.
The body of a third person was found in the same tunnel later. A local official said it was swollen and could not be immediately identified.
Officials believe another 39 people are in the Trishuli 3A tunnel, although it is not clear if all are alive.
Col Jhabindra Reshmi said that his teams had rescued more than 400 Nepali nationals and 270 foreign citizens following the flash flooding on 26 August.
He has said mud and rocks have made entering tunnels difficult and rescuers were having to dig access holes to get underground.
Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels.
Last week's floodwaters washed away a lot of heavy machinery, making it harder for rescuers to unblock tunnels, says a representative for Nepalese power companies.
Uttam Bhlon Lama, vice president at Independent Power Producers of Nepal, told the BBC's Newsday programme that the rescue of the two men on Friday would "motivate the rescuers to do more".
"The flood level is still very high," Lama added.
Nepalese authorities have warned that rainfall may cause additional flooding in the region.
At least 1,287 people are known to have died in Nepal, with 5,083 still missing.
On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.
Emergency teams in Tibet appear to be focusing on helping the living rather than holding out hope for more survivors.
Scientists are still studying the exact cause, but it is believed to have been caused by a glacial collapse and climate change may have been a factor.
Moments after the seismic event, which was initially thought to have been an earthquake, a massive wall of water and debris crashed downstream, taking buildings, roads and vehicles with it.
Experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment said there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the collapse and better early-warning systems could have saved lives.

SaaS startup Meritto’s parent NoPaperForms has filed its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP) with Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its initial public issue (IPO). The startup’s proposed public offering will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹375 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 3.8 Cr equity shares. As reported earlier, only investor Info Edge will participate in the OFS. As per the UDRHP, the venture capital giant, via Startup Investments (Holding) Ltd, will offload 3.8 Cr shares. The startup also enables educational organisations to deploy AI agents across student-facing and institutional workflows with its Mio AI suite. The startup claimed to have catered to 1,183 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, including 104 overseas clients. India accounted for 91.2% of its total revenue in FY26, while international operations contributed the remaining 8.8%. NoPaperForms processed invoices worth ₹124.6 Cr in FY26 and ₹39.9 Cr in Q1 FY27. Meanwhile, the startup’s profits surged 534% to ₹11.9 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹1.9 Cr in FY25. The startup also posted an operating revenue of ₹44.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 against a net profit of ₹6 Cr in the quarter under review.

In late August 2026, a rumor spread online that claimed Canadian officials were refusing to grant passage through the Welland Canal — which connects lakes Erie and Ontario — to ships that had "Lake America" listed in their documentation, as opposed to "Lake Ontario."
The rumor circulated after U.S. President Donald Trump renamed Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in the United States.
Posts on X, Threads, Facebook (screenshott) and Reddit claimed Fox News had reported on the alleged Canadian blockade. Snopes readers contacted us to investigate the claim's legitimacy.
(X user @MykhailoRohoza)
This claim originated as satire. A search of Fox News' archives via its website found no evidence the news outlet had reported on such a claim.
Searches on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo also found no relevant and credible news articles reporting on this claim as fact. If Canadian officials really were preventing ships using the term "Lake America" in their documentation from crossing the Welland Canal, it would certainly have made news, and search inquiries would have uncovered evidence of it.
The St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corp. oversees ship traffic on the Canadian side of the Welland Canal, which is part of the St. Lawrence Seaway. The Canadian Press reported that Serge Auclair, vice-president of commercial and external relations at the corporation, said vessels are traveling the canal as usual.
"Seaway operations are continuing normally and have done so throughout the weekend. Vessels are transiting the Welland Canal as usual," Nicole Giroux, a spokesperson for the St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corp., told Snopes.
The earliest version of the claim we found came from an Aug. 28 X post (archived) from a Russian X user listed as "Comedian" on the account's profile (archived). We reached out to the X user to confirm the account originated the claim and will update this story if we hear back.
Many of the earlier versions of the claim shared in English also labeled it as satire, or at least acknowledged its satirical origins.
Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before. For example, in May, we alerted readers to a fake story about Canadian officials denying Trump a $573 billion railway bailout.
For more on Lake Ontario, we previously confirmed it was named by Indigenous people, not after the Canadian province of Ontario.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Reckoning looms for golf carts that zip through Rome's crowded historic center
Rome's historic center is facing a golf cart controversy
ROME -- Beneath the splendor of its monuments and ruins, Rome is taking aim at a modern-day chariot: the golf cart.
Hundreds of them have started carrying tourists through the historic center. Even rolling along at a moderate speed, these golf carts have so far outpaced regulation. But the city is mounting a crackdown.
For critics, the carts are running amok, parking illegally, worsening congestion and unlocking another level of overtourism. Some local media invoke sensational language, calling it an “invasion” and saying Rome is being “held hostage by golf carts.”
Advocates argue carts are silent, occupy less space than tourist vans and buses, and don’t choke the air with exhaust that also stains historic monuments.
The Associated Press got a taste of the enmity during a late August ride when a black, eight-seater van pulled up alongside.
“You’re in the middle of the road!” its driver barked. “Move it!”
“Always the same! The road isn’t yours!” the golf cart driver shouted back. Both gesticulated angrily with their free hands, following a time-honored Roman traffic tradition.
Carts like this zip through Rome’s cobblestone alleys, past tourists eating spaghetti carbonara from checkered tablecloths and shops hawking hot priest calendars and tote bags stamped with cliches (Ciao Bella!). But there’s no time to buy anything except a cappuccino or gelato; these tours are targeted blitzes on Rome’s hot spots — at least until they collide with authorities.
Best buckle up.
Ruth Sanderson from Manchester, England, surprised her husband with the tour for his birthday during their first trip to Rome. They could see the major sights in three hours and “just potter around” for the rest of their short stay, said Sanderson, 50.
Their guide swung around the basilica where Pope Francis is buried then headed to the Spanish Steps, where he parked in an area exclusively for car-sharing — the first of several illegal spots he snagged.
“We don’t have a proper stop for golf carts, so we park where we can — as legal as possible,” driver Martin Halili explained to them.
Even before the golf cart boom, parking was a pain. Cars, vans, Vespas and motorcycles are stationed atop curbs, crosswalks and medians. Trucks double-park while unloading.
Any spare cranny is claimed in Rome's historic center, because there are only 4,300 regular on-street spots available, about one-quarter the number of cars owned by the area's residents, according to the city's transport chief, citing a field survey conducted last year. Plus, an average 50,000 vehicles enter daily. Unsurprisingly, some residents are unhappy.
“This was the last straw because, unfortunately, there has already been traffic here for a long time, since there are too many categories of vehicles authorized,” Luigi la Licata, head of the Monti neighborhood association, told the AP. “The golf cart is the most obvious one — and the latest — but there are many others.”
Golf cart bookings this summer grew 147% from 2024, according to TripAdvisor, whose subsidiary Viator is the biggest source of passengers. Rome has as many as 500 carts, with one-fifth belonging to the Metur association of tour operators, established last December to seek common ground with locals and the city.
“Overtourism is a real problem, and we’re not denying it. And maybe we’re also part of it in a way. But if we’re part of it, then at least be part of it in a smart way,” Pascal van Duijnhoven, the association’s president, said. “We believe, especially for Rome, that it’s a solution. And we really hope that people start looking at it like this. But we need a hand. We need some help from the authorities.”
Rome’s deputy mayor for sustainable mobility and transport, Eugenio Patanè, is striving to restore order and reduce traffic — and not just golf carts.
In July, electric vehicles started paying for admission to the historic center, as gasoline-powered cars had been — a strategic shift from cutting emissions to tackling congestion. The number of authorized vehicles is down about one-quarter, to 350,000, and Patanè aims to halve the number of daily entrants.
But it hasn't been so simple to put the brakes on golf carts. First, not all carts are created equal; technical specifications mean some fall under existing rules while others can roam freely. Second, passenger transport and tourism businesses are regulated regionally, Patanè said.
So he requested the region transfer that power to Rome, and anticipates that will occur this month. Then he can present his regulation that would establish fixed tour routes, cap the number of carts of all types and create a system to select operators.
“Cities where this golf cart phenomenon is expanding truly have very few weapons,” he said. “We will be able to regulate this phenomenon that has now become rampant and, in some cases, even worrisome.”
Operators say such proposals would kneecap their nascent industry. Meantime, their carts are already getting curbed.
Authorities stopped vehicles owned by Metur associates 14 times in the back half of August, with reviews of drivers' documents that lasted up to an hour, van Duijnhoven said, and punishments that were inconsistent and severe. Carts allegedly operating as black-market, private-hire vehicles can be banned from the streets for over a month, or drivers slapped with 4,000-euro ($4,600) fines for unlicensed tour guiding.
One block from the Pantheon, the AP saw an officer from Italy's financial police inspecting the documents from a cart carrying a family from Florida. During the half-hour stop, he took their IDs and copied down their information. Three nearby private-hire vans — also parked illegally — were receiving no such scrutiny.
Halili, who guided the couple from Manchester and owns Wheel Tours, says private-hire and taxi drivers are bristling at the new kid on the block taking a bite out of their business.
“They have waged a war against us, filing complaints and appeal after appeal, because they are a powerful lobby,” he said. “This is the problem: They have it in for golf carts.”

Matthew Floca, the Kennedy Center's vice president of facilities, said in April 2026 sworn testimony that the center felled its weeping willows "because they were falling down." He also confirmed Trump was not involved in the decision.
In late August and early September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the removal of weeping willow trees outside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C.
"The iconic weeping willow trees outside the Kennedy Center have been cut down by Trump," Adam Parkhomenko, a former Hillary Clinton adviser, wrote on X.
The iconic weeping willow trees outside the Kennedy Center have been cut down by Trump. pic.twitter.com/5bZ0AnaPDx
— Adam Parkhomenko (@AdamParkhomenko) September 1, 2026
Similar claims also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify them. One reader asked, "Did Trump have the willow trees at the JFK center cut down?"
That was not the case. 
Floca said in his testimony that the center felled the trees because of a "maintenance need" (Page 28) and that it was "contemplating" their replacements. Floca added that he had not spoken to Trump, who is the chair of the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees, about the weeping willows or what should replace them (Page 28).
Given the above, we rate the claim that Trump ordered the removal of the Kennedy Center's weeping willow trees false. Rather, the center's management said it felled the trees because of a maintenance need and confirmed Trump was not involved in the decision.
We contacted the Kennedy Center to ask when it cut down the weeping willows and whether it had any plans to replace the trees, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. A White House spokesperson referred our request for comment to the Kennedy Center.
Citing a spokesperson for the Kennedy Center, Newsweek reported that the center removed its weeping willow trees in October 2025. Snopes found one image published by Reuters that showed weeping willows at the Kennedy Center in September 2025 and a geo-tagged image from Google that showed at least one such tree cut down in October, supporting this reported timeline.
The neighborhood blog PoPville, which covers Washington, D.C., reported on the removal of the weeping willows on October 14, 2025. Snopes could not view metadata for the images in order to establish their authenticity, but had no reason to believe they were inauthentic.
What we know about the trees
Floca told a Washington, D.C. district court on April 29, 2026, that the weeping willows at the Kennedy Center had to be removed because they were in poor health. He said (Page 28):
Ninety percent of the trees were decaying and every time there was a heavy wind or rain a tree would fall down. If you walk around the center at that time, you would see limbs falling and trees falling down.
When asked whether he discussed what tree would replace the weeping willows with the Kennedy Center chairman (meaning Trump), Floca said (Page 28):
We haven't specifically talked about the weeping willows or the replacement. I think that a weeping cherry tree would be perfect. But we are going to come up with a complete landscape — a comprehensive landscape plan that doesn't only talk to the planters and the willow trees, and that will be part of the plan, the replacement.
As of this writing, it was unclear what tree would replace the weeping willows, which lawyer Abbe David Lowell claimed were meant to represent "the grief of the nation" for the death of former U.S. President John F. Kennedy (Page 27).
Trump posted digital renderings of his suggested "new, highly improved" Kennedy Center in March 2026 that replaced the weeping willows with either pink or orange-leafed trees. Though weeping willows change color in the fall, their leaves turn yellow or gold, not orange, red or pink like the trees in Trump's renderings, which appeared to suggest the president wanted to replace the weeping willows with a different kind of tree.
Floca's testimony was part of a lawsuit brought by several conservation groups that sought to stop Trump and the Kennedy Center's board from carrying out proposed renovations without third-party review. On May 29, a federal judge denied the conservation groups' request for a preliminary injunction that would stop the renovations while the court case was ongoing.
Nonetheless, the center remained open at the time of this writing, despite Trump initially saying it would close on July 4, 2026, for renovations.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump cut down dozens of cherry trees in Washington, D.C., to make way for a golf course.

Volkswagen to cut up to 50,000 jobs amid growing Chinese competition
Volkswagen has been under unprecedented pressure to restructure the business model that underpinned its success for decades
Volkswagen Group is preparing to trim its vehicle range substantially while removing 50,000 roles under newly introduced corporate restructuring plans.
The company's Supervisory Board has ‘unanimously approved’ the new ‘Future Plan 2030’ strategy as it seeks to reduce expenditure in response to rising market rivalry from China.
Consequently, Volkswagen intends to contract its car model lineup by roughly 50 per cent. It also intends to ‘reduce its offering complexity’ – decreasing trim options and specifications – by about 75 per cent.
The carmaker will downsize its workforce by approximately 50,000 positions. As this step is ‘beyond existing programs’, previously planned job cuts will continue to be rolled out as they were scheduled.
Plants in Emden, Zwickau, Hannover and Neckarsulm in Germany will be phased out of auto production in 2031-34, although alternative uses will be explored. The board statement said there would be an “adjustment of the employee numbers of around 50,000 positions,” including management jobs.
Oliver Blume, Volkswagen Group CEO, said: “The Supervisory Board has unanimously approved the Executive Board’s Future Plan presented today. This is a strong sign for the future of the Volkswagen Group. We are taking responsibility for our entire team, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide.
“Over the coming years, we will invest a three-figure billion sum to make our iconic brands even more attractive, stronger and more competitive.”
The Group is also looking to develop both its North American and Chinese areas of business, with the former being one of its “most profitable segments”.
Hans Dieter Pötsch, chairman of the supervisory board, said: “With the Future Plan now approved, the Supervisory Board and Executive Board of Volkswagen AG have shown that the company’s transformation is being driven forward with full force.”
Thursday’s news release was accompanied by a statement from chief employee representative Daniela Cavallo that the plan was “a necessity for our company to move successfully into the next decade without the associated undertakings coming only on the side of the employees.” Cavallo had been strongly critical of the plan when it was presented over the summer.
Grappling with high costs and excess capacity at home, rising Chinese competition, and US import tariffs, Volkswagen has been under unprecedented pressure to restructure the business model that underpinned its success for decades.
Volkswagen, which has around 650,000 employees, reported a 30 per cent drop in after-tax earnings for the first half of the year as sales took a hit in China.

Donald Trump's oil arrangement in Venezuela will prove the US a direct stake in the country’s vast crude resources while reshaping the arrangements around who controls the revenues generated from them. A deal involves a new Venezuelan oil venture covering 17 fields with around 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The US government will hold a 35% stake in the company and it will also have the right to buy 20% of its production at cost. The arrangement gives US buyers access to Venezuelan crude, but without paying a market-based premium. One of the most controversial aspects is the involvement of Alejandro Betancourt, Venezuelan businessman who heads the country’s second-largest private oil company – North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Betancourt has previously accused of involvement in a corruption scheme at Venezuela's state-run PDVSA oil company. The Trump administration has nevertheless defended his role. a US official said Betancourt was a "proven operator," while acknowledging that geopolitics sometimes involved dealing with "imperfect" characters. "I'm not nominating anyone for sainthood here. What I am telling you is that this is a person that, in the past, has been helpful to the United States government," the official added. This arrangement is also part US's broader effort to control Venezuela’s economic relationships with China and Russia. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has asserted on Wednesday Beijing won’t have any claims to revenue from Venezuela’s oil production, disrupting Caracas’ existing mechanism for repaying billions of dollars owed to Chinese creditors. The step seems quite severe because China became Venezuela’s largest crude customer and most important foreign creditor after years of US sanctions. In fact, Chinese state banks had extended more than $60 billion in oil-backed lending to Venezuela by 2015. By 2025, however, the outstanding debt was believed to have fallen to at least $10 billion. The deal therefore serves two purposes for Washington. First, securing access to Venezuela’s oil and second, reducing Beijing’s economic influence over the country’s energy sector. For China, the immediate economic impact may be limited because its exposure to Venezuela has already declined. Crude from the country accounted for only 4% of the country’s total oil imports in 2025. No Venezuelan cargoes have been recorded arriving in China since the Trump administration assumed control of the assets following the capture earlier this year of then President Nicolás Maduro. China’s reaction so far has been relatively muted. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China’s legitimate rights and interests in Venezuela “must be protected,” at a regular briefing in Beijing on Thursday. “Cooperation between China and Venezuela is protected by international law,” he added. “It doesn’t concern any third party.” However, the geopolitical significance of the action could be much larger. Analysts say the arrangement could establish a precedent for Washington to use its influence to exclude Chinese interests from strategically important assets in Latin America. “South America has long been a geopolitical crossroads where the interests of China and the US intersect and, at times, collide,” said Liao Na, founder of energy research focused firm GL Consulting. “Given the importance both powers attach to Venezuela, friction is almost inevitable whenever their interests overlap.” In that sense, Venezuela’s oil deal is about more than crude. It is becoming a test of how far the Trump administration is prepared to go to reassert US economic and geopolitical dominance in the Western Hemisphere. Taiwanese boxer Lin Yu-ting told AFP she considered retiring after winning gold at the Paris Olympics but wanted to carry on fighting in part to defy those who questioned her eligibility.
Lin and Imane Khelif of Algeria found themselves in the middle of a major gender row at the 2024 Games, with Donald Trump, Elon Musk and author J.K. Rowling among those wading in.
The two boxers had been disqualified from the 2023 world championships by the International Boxing Association (IBA) after the organisation said they failed unspecified gender eligibility tests.
However, the IOC allowed them to compete in Paris, saying they were victims of “a sudden and arbitrary decision” by the widely discredited IBA. Both went on to win gold.
Hailed as a star in Taiwan, Lin wondered at the time whether it was the right moment to bow out of the sport she loves.
“I achieved everything I had worked for. It seemed like a good moment to make a graceful exit,” the 30-year-old told AFP in a rare interview.
Initially the choice was taken out of her hands and her career forced on hold.
Then in March this year World Boxing -- which has taken over the running of the sport -- cleared her to return after 19 months in limbo following a one-off sex test.
Lin, a two-time world champion who will compete at the Asian Games in Japan starting on September 19, said quitting would have let down the people close to her.
“I couldn’t leave the people on my team behind,” Lin said. “And I also wanted to see how far my own abilities could go.”
Lin is keen to put the darker moments of Paris and its aftermath behind her. Dwelling on negatives will get her trapped in a “pessimistic mindset”, she said.
“I’m able to continue competing now,” Lin added. “In a way that’s a rebuttal to many of the things people were saying before.”
‘Falling into place’
Lin has stepped up a weight class as she pursues a second Asian Games gold in a row. She won last time at 57kg, the same weight as her Paris triumph, but will box in the 60kg category in Nagoya-Aichi this month.
“Right now I feel like things are gradually falling into place for me,” she said. “This year I started competing again and I’ve gradually regained my reactions and form. It really does feel like I’m getting back into my rhythm.”
On her return to international competition Lin won bronze at 60kg at the Asian Elite Championships in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, then silver at the World Boxing Cup in China.
“Moving up a weight class means everything is new for me,” Lin said. “It’s a new goal, a new challenge and a new milestone.”
‘Clarity and determination’
Lin was 13 when she first pulled on a pair of boxing gloves at her junior high school gym in Yingge district near Taipei. She was “a small-stature student without an obvious physical edge”, said her coach Tseng Tzu-chiang, who has been her trainer ever since.
Lin worked hard and captured a string of titles including world crowns in 2018 and 2022. “Once she set her eyes on something, she would commit to it wholeheartedly,” Tseng told AFP.
She meets setbacks head-on, resetting her goals and achieving them with “absolute clarity and determination”, he said.
Lin admits to “very high standards” and a “rigorous attitude” towards training. But there is a fun side too, unwinding from the physically taxing sessions with Tseng by playing Pokemon Go.
She dabbles in the stock market.
“I manage risk very strictly,” Lin said, likening trading stocks to throwing punches. “The best risk management in the ring is making sure I’ve done my own part well. That’s something I can control.”
Prized possession
Winning the gold in Paris was the culmination of years of devotion. She failed to secure a spot at the 2016 Rio Games and was eliminated in the early stages in Tokyo in 2021.
Two years after her Paris win, Lin’s gold medal remains carefully wrapped and stored in her bedroom, rarely making public appearances.
“I haven’t displayed it yet because I haven’t found a good way,” Lin said, adding she might one day show it alongside her other medals. “I’m worried about damaging it, getting it dirty, or accidentally scratching it.”

Out in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms. Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.
Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.
One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.

Bengal’s new anti-graft body inspects factories of TMC veteran Firhad Hakim
A West Bengal anti-corruption commission inspected two factories owned by former minister Firhad Hakim, who called the move “character assassination”.
Officials of the newly formed West Bengal Commission on Institutional Corruption on Thursday inspected two factories owned by former cabinet minister and rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MLA Firhad Hakim in Kolkata, triggering a political row.
“We came here to conduct an inquiry based on a complaint,” one of the commission officials told the media outside the plastic goods factories in Kolkata’s New Alipore area, refusing to share details.
Hakim, once one of TMC founder Mamata Banerjee’s closest aides but who joined the Ritabrata Banerjee-led rebel camp in June, said the inspection’s real intention was character assassination.
“This is character assassination. I set up the factory in 1985 when I was unemployed. I took a loan from a bank. I expanded the factory in phases over the years. The land belongs to someone else; I have taken it on rent,” Hakim, the MLA from the Kolkata Port assembly seat, told the media.
People living around the factory, however, claimed that the original unit was a small unit and the major expansion took place two years ago when Hakim was state urban development and municipal affairs minister and also Kolkata’s mayor.
Hakim did not comment on this allegation but claimed the land was not disputed.
“The inspection was held because someone lodged a complaint. The complaint letter was shown to me. I pay rent for the land to the landlord every month. There is nothing illegitimate in this business. If people are harassed in this manner then nobody will set up businesses,” Hakim said.
TMC Lok Sabha member Saugata Roy from the Mamata Banerjee camp targeted Hakim and the Bharatiya Janata Party government.
“The inspection is an eyewash. We were told that Firhad Hakim was behind all big corruptions in Bengal but there has been no investigation,” Roy said.
Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari formed the Commission on Institutional Corruption in May, days after the BJP ousted the TMC government.
Retired Calcutta high court judge Biswajit Basu is the chairman of the commission, and senior IPS officer K Jayaraman is the member secretary.

I drink the blood of my fourth rat tonight. It’s only got so much life to give, so as soon as I drain it, I know I'll need to feed again. My hunger is not fulfilled. My health bar is only half full. I need more blood. Now.
I toss the rat away as my glowing eyes flicker to another, just across the street. I bare my sharp, bloody teeth, turn into a cloud of shadow and bats, and teleport to my unsuspecting prey. I bite down hard. It’s too late to realize my target has changed. As I swarmed, a human city guard happened to walk right in front of me. My teeth sink into his throat instead. I could let go, but I do not. I drink, drink, drink. Then he falls to the ground. Dead. I wipe my mouth as the last rat scurries away into the dark.
“Well, I guess I’m going to Hell anyway,” my character quips.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a vampire simulator and role-playing video game that launches today. It’s a dark adventure where you play as the titular Dawnwalker—human by day, monstrous vampire at night.
You can’t talk about The Blood of Dawnwalker without talking about The Witcher 3. They’re both third-person monster-slasher video games starring handsome protagonists with cool scars on their faces, both made by some of the same people.
Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, a former director at the Polish game studio and Witcher developer CD Projekt Red, was one of three directors of the very popular The Witcher 3. His new studio, Rebel Wolves, even feels like a cheeky nod to Geralt, the main character of The Witcher series who is often called the White Wolf. The gameplay and graphics feel very similar. Combat involves swinging your sword and blasting magic abilities, while cutscenes and dialog have familiar dialog trees and quick-time events. You have a special sense that makes important items glow so you can find footprints and track down monsters.
The music also sounds almost identical to The Witcher 3 soundtrack—think somber swelling violin strings plucking away while you wander a gloomy open world. I was almost ready to allege copyright infringement before realizing that Dawnwalker features the work of fellow Witcher composer Mikolai Stroinski.
Ah, so, “We have The Witcher at home,” is that it? Well, not exactly. The sameness might feel derivative at first, but give it a minute. Once you get through the prologue, the world opens up in a way that invites exploration of its very pretty, blood-soaked world. There’s no way to beat The Witcher 3 in depth, breadth, or sheer volume, but The Blood of Dawnwalker doesn’t try to replicate or surpass that scale. Instead, it gives you a simple goal and a limited time to pull it off. That sounds restrictive at first, but it plays out in a way that's more freeing than you’d expect.
Dawnwalker takes place in a fictional plague-era medieval world. You play as Coen (I call him Young Geralt), a poor peasant who lives with his family in a town controlled by evil vampires. After some inciting events, the Draculean boss vampire kidnaps Coen’s family and turns him into the Dawnwalker—a vampire hybrid that manifests as a human in the daytime and a bloodthirsty vampire at night. You’ve got 30 in-game days to save Coen’s family. You’re already running out of time.
Gameplay is split into day and night cycles, each with eight time segments. Completing a quest or doing anything of consequence will pass one or a few time segments. Otherwise, time does not pass idly. If you’re running around and exploring, you have all the time to fart around in the world that you need. The game warns you when something you're about to do will pass the time, so you can choose to keep going or leave and find something else to do.
I worried this system would feel constricting, like being forced on a set path in an open-world game. Turns out, it was exactly what I needed to stay motivated and keep exploring.
My problem with The Witcher 3 and open-world games like it is that there is so much of it. You’re tasked with some time-sensitive mission—rescue your daughter before the world ends, etc.—but then you while away hours and hours on side quests. Games like this can punish you if you rush the main storyline, cutting off quests, choices, and even characters that those smaller efforts would have unlocked. When I play, I feel obligated to do all the small stuff first, then build to the main quests. When a narrative and world gets that dense, it can start to feel like a chore.
Dawnwalker gives you many activities across the world. Some are clearly story quests; many are treasure hunts or things that feel much smaller-scale. Knowing I can’t do everything lets me prioritize what needs doing. A ticking clock always counting down on the screen usually would make me anxious in games, since failing to do the right things at the right time means you lose. Weirdly, Dawnwalker’s countdown feels less punishing and more like motivation to do the very best you can with the limited resources you have. If you know you can’t see everything in a single playthrough, it’s easier to let go of the things you miss.
It’s by no means a perfect game. The Blood of Dawnwalker is a clunky name. It really should be Blood of the Dawnwalker or just Blood of Dawnwalker. (Dawnwalker is your character’s title after all, not his name.) There is also undeniable jank throughout, like when you sheathe your sword, it floats directly behind the center of Coen’s butt. When you run with your heightened vampiric sense, the sword bounces around and spanks Coen’s behind as he runs. It is very funny, and I hope the devs don’t change it.
It is particularly unfortunate for Dawnwalker that the game is launching in the shadow of news that The Witcher 3 is getting a free remastered update later this month and a whole new expansion pack in 2027, 11 years after its original release.
Despite all the blood, gore, and sorrow, Dawnwalker has charm and a lightness to it. Combat is bloody, wet, and satisfying. At night, Coen’s vampiric abilities are a hoot, letting you teleport around across the rooftops, drink the blood of any crawly creature you like, and sprint across the map as a wolf. Most of the vampires, aside from smokeshow Coen, are the truly monstrous kinds, all claws and teeth and gory bloodsucking. But the world slowly reveals some real beauty. The other characters develop and become much more interesting than they first appeared. The voice acting that carries some pretty wrenching story beats and character moments is stellar.
Above all, it does something remarkable: It takes an established game formula and really infuses it with its own personality and quirks. It takes a bite out of the Witcher formula and makes it its own. And has a bloody good time doing it.

This rugged smartphone's camera is a removable action cam
It’s waterproof and can record up to 40 minutes of video.
Few companies are pushing back against the black, oblong smartphone design hegemony in 2026, but RugOne is one of them. It's part of Ulefon, which has been pumping out ruggedized phones for a few years, and its newest phone, the Xsnap 7 Pro, is very rugged but has a magnetic removable camera unit that can work like an action cam.
Yeah, it made me go "ooh" when I heard about it. (Unfortunately, my sample landed while we report on IFA 2026 here in Berlin. I'll update this story when I get to see the device in person later this week. The almost cube-shaped camera weighs 39 grams and can record video up to 2.7K resolution at 30fps — it's not coming for the latest GoPro quite yet.
RugOne says the module can run for up to 40 minutes on a full charge, with 64GB of built-in storage. It'll broadcast a preview feed to RugOne's companion app, up to 50 meters away. It also includes a handful of software features, including distortion correction, horizon lock and a Freeframe shooting mode that captures the full sensor area, so you can crop to vertical or horizontal footage as needed.
The camera is waterproof up to five meters (without any additional protective cases), and the company will also include a companion magnet pendant so you can wear it on your body for capture; it will also work with third-party accessories that support a universal mount.
The Xsnap 7 Pro also has a 50-megapixel "AI main camera" with optical image stabilization, plus a 64MP infrared night-vision camera with IR LEDs for "crisp black-and-white detail" during nighttime wildlife shooting — RugOne's suggestion, not mine.
And let's not forget: still a phone. The Xsnap 7 Pro has a 6.67-inch display with 1,700-nit peak brightness and up to 120Hz refresh rates. It packs a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, and the device has strong durability credentials. It's rated IP68 and IP69K and can handle water submersion up to two meters deep for 30 minutes as well as 1.5-meter drops onto concrete.
While a prototype was teased at MWC 2026 a few months ago, the Xsnap 7 Pro is officially debuting at IFA, with early-bird sales opening on Kickstarter on September 7 at a discounted preorder price of 799 euros (roughly $930). The phone will then go on sale globally sometime next month on Amazon and RugOne's online store, priced at $999, in Sand Dune and Classic Black.

Apple’s September 9th launch event could be one of its biggest in years. It will be Apple’s first event since John Ternus took over as CEO on September 1st, stepping in for Tim Cook, and will likely feature the first models in Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup. That could include the long-rumored foldable “iPhone Ultra,” coming just a couple months after Samsung debuted its own passport-style foldable, the Galaxy Z Fold 8.
What to expect at Apple’s September 9th launch event
Apple’s expected to announce a new lineup of iPhones, which could include its first foldable phone.
Here’s how you can watch the event live, and a few possible highlights to keep an eye out for.
How to watch Apple’s September launch event
Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event kicks off on Wednesday, September 9th, at 1PM ET / 10AM PT at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. It will be livestreamed on Apple’s website, Apple TV, and YouTube.
The iPhone 18 might be a no-show
Apple usually announces new iPhones at its September event, but the base iPhone 18 might not make the cut this year. It’s reportedly being held until early next year, and it might end up launching alongside the iPhone 18E and an updated iPhone Air. So, if you’re looking to upgrade to one of Apple’s less expensive phones, you’ll likely need to wait a while longer.
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max could launch with a price hike
While we might not get a new base iPhone, Apple is still expected to launch its new lineup of phones on September 9th with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Both models are rumored to have larger batteries than their predecessors, and possibly a smaller Dynamic Island. They might even get a variable aperture camera upgrade that’s been rumored for years now. Leaked photos supposedly showing dummy models of the phone also hint at this year’s slate of colors, which could include black, silver, light blue, and a dark cherry purple.
Unfortunately, there’s also a good chance the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will get a price bump over last year’s models. Apple raised prices on nearly all of its products earlier this year, and those price hikes might finally reach the iPhone during the September 9th event.
Apple might announce its first foldable phone
One of the premium phones Apple launches on September 9th could be the rumored foldable “iPhone Ultra.” Images of an apparent dummy model of the folding phone leaked earlier this year, showing a passport-style design similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 has been well received so far, with The Verge’s Dominic Preston saying it “feels like the future.” Will Apple’s first foldable be able to compete, despite being fashionably late?
The ceramic Apple Watch may finally return
Last year’s September Apple event included the Apple Watch Series 11 and Ultra 3, and there’s a good chance both watches will get an update again this year. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the Series 12 could bring back the premium ceramic case option. Gurman also says the Series 12 will have new band colors and configurations, but most likely won’t have any big redesign. Aside from new cases and colors, Apple might also announce new health features for its wearables, like always-on heart rate sensing.
Apple could launch new AirPods, but probably not with cameras
It’s been a couple of years since Apple released the AirPods 4, so they’re due for an upgrade and could make an appearance at Apple’s September 9th event. However, Gurman says the camera-equipped AirPods that leaked last month won’t be released until 2027. So, if Apple announces the AirPods 5 at its upcoming event, they’ll likely be an iterative upgrade, potentially including a new chip and some new health sensors.

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.
According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.
The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.
The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.
The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.
The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

What does Norris deal mean for Piastri? F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli will try to tighten his grip on the drivers' championship on home ground at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
However, the 20-year-old can expect to face a challenge from a resurgent McLaren and in particular Lando Norris, who has won the past two grands prix.
And Monza is of course also home territory for Ferrari, although the long straights of the historic circuit may not suit the characteristics of their car.
BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 13 of the 2026 season.
What does Lando Norris' new contract extension mean for Oscar Piastri? There clearly is some tension behind the scenes and this season his development performance-wise has clearly dipped. - Juha
There is no question that Oscar Piastri has not started this season as well as he did last.
In 2025, the Australian for a large part of the year appeared on course for a first world title, until his season unravelled somewhat in the final third.
This season, team-mate Lando Norris has won two races - and should have won a third in Miami.
Piastri has only looked in contention for a victory in Hungary, when Norris took his first win of the year.
After taking the lead when Norris made an error on the first lap, there was some bad luck involved in Piastri losing the lead to Norris, when he was delayed lapping Carlos Sainz's Williams.
But Piastri acknowledged it would have been difficult to hold Norris back if he had retained the lead because his pace on the hard tyres was weak. It became academic when he retired with a broken gearbox.
Although the qualifying head-to-head statistics between them do not make pleasant reading for Piastri - Norris is 12-4 ahead - on actual pace, there is not a lot to choose between them over one lap. Norris is only faster by 0.071 seconds on average.
It's fair to say, though, that Norris has been comfortably the more convincing race performer - hence the 55-point and three-place gap between them in the championship
There seem to be a few things at issue here.
One might be that Piastri has always been strong in high-speed corners. But the numbers of these that are grip-limited has reduced this year because the engines are often using them to charge the battery, something about which all drivers have complained. So that reduces a point of potential advantage for Piastri.
Second, the cars have less downforce than last year, and Piastri is less comfortable than Norris in low-grip conditions.
Finally, there is no question that Norris upped his game consistently over the course of the second half of last season to win the world title, and has continued to raise his level through this year. Without question, he is one of the drivers of the season so far.
Team principal Andrea Stella said at the last race in the Netherlands: "Last year, we had seen already with Oscar that, from a technical driving point of view, when the car has this low level of grip, like we saw last year for instance in Mexico or in Austin, he needs to adapt the way he drives, the way he thinks, the driving, his expectations.
"This requires a bit of mental effort, which gets him to lose a couple of tenths of a second because you sort of have to process rather than drive through pure instinct because what happens is what you expect.
"So it's one of those cases in which you have to adapt your natural driving style to the demand of the car. So it stays in the space of driving and in the space of the technical side of things. I don't think it has anything to do with any psychological kind of opportunity. This is purely technical."
Stella points out that the top three teams are very close in terms of performance, which means, as he puts it, "as soon as things are not optimised, then you may have a very significant positional loss - it's very brutal from this point of view".
Both McLaren and Piastri reject any suggestion that there might be tension in their relationship.
It's a fact, though, that McLaren wanted to sign Max Verstappen this summer, and that if they had it's virtually certain it would have been Piastri who was replaced.
That possibility has receded for now, with Verstappen's new contract with Red Bull. But that contract has performance clauses, and if Red Bull are still struggling next year, it may well be that McLaren have another go for Verstappen.
For now, Piastri is under contract to the end of 2027 at least, and will be focusing only on getting back to where he knows he can be.

Why are Mercedes choosing to take a grid penalty for Kimi Antonelli at the next race in Italy? Why not take it at a future grand prix to give Kimi a better chance for a home win or is this not a concern for Mercedes? - Michael
Mercedes have been quite open about the fact that Kimi Antonelli will take a new engine for the Italian Grand Prix, and with it a significant grid penalty that is likely to mean him starting at the back.
The reality is that early season reliability meant this penalty - for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts - was inevitable, and Mercedes have calculated that Monza is the best place to take it for Antonelli.
They have tried to make the decision on facts, and not let the emotion of it being his home grand prix enter into the equation.
This decision will be based partly on the fact that Monza has long straights, and so is one of the tracks where a new engine and it's slight performance increase will translate most effectively into lap time.
But also important is Mercedes' analysis of how the engines in his 'pool' can be used most effectively over the remainder of the season
Team principal Toto Wolff said: "With Kimi, we are taking the full thing. In theory, our calculations say that it's the best track to take it. Obviously, algorithms don't take the nationality into consideration. I'm not ready to fight for a championship and get the best PR. That's what we're going to do."
Antonelli's championship lead is still very comfortable, at 59 points. So he can afford to be phlegmatic about this.
He says: "Of course, it's my home race and all that kind of stuff, but, you know, I think it's the best race to do so. So, I think it still will give me a chance to do a great result and bring home good points."
George Russell will have to take a penalty soon, too. This is most likely to be at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, for similar reasons to Antonelli's being at Monza.
Are Ferrari allowing emotion to get in their way? It's perhaps a stretch to say Ferrari can go on to win the title, but surely their best chance is backing the nearest challenger? Are they allowing the emotion of their attachment to Charles Leclerc, and his history with the team, to get in the way of making the clinical, ruthless decisions needed? - Alex
Presumably this question is a reference to the brief dispute between Charles Leclerc and the team at the Dutch Grand Prix, when Lewis Hamilton was coming up behind him on fresher tyres mid-race.
We dealt with what happened there in detail in last week's Q&A.
But in the context of the question, it's worth pointing out that they actually did ask Leclerc to move out of the way to optimise Hamilton's race in Zandvoort.
Ferrari operate a policy of equality between their drivers and only favour one over the other if it is obviously in the interests of the team.
That could work either way, and the most obvious time it would be employed is if a race victory was at stake.
Hamilton is their closest driver to the championship lead, at 59 points behind Antonelli. Leclerc is 28 points behind the seven-time champion - only four points further back than Lando Norris.
Hamilton and Leclerc have won one race each, and the qualifying battle between them is incredibly close.
Hamilton is ahead 9-7 on the head-to-head in races where a fair comparison can be made, but Leclerc is actually slightly quicker on average by 0.053secs.
Beyond that, the question seems to presume that the team would favour Leclerc emotionally. But why make that presumption?
Team principal Frederic Vasseur was instrumental in getting Hamilton to join Ferrari for 2025, but he has a long and close relationship going back many years with both drivers.
Why would he be emotionally connected to one more than the other, or consciously allow emotions to rule his management decisions?

Zandvoort is a great circuit and it's disappointing that they have pulled out of hosting the F1 grand prix for a second time. Is there any chance the circuit might return to the schedule some time in the future? - Lynne
In F1, one quickly learns to never say never, but the chances of the Dutch Grand Prix returning to the calendar seem remote for the foreseeable future.
The race was unique in that it owed its existence to the popularity of one driver - Max Verstappen.
The organisers did an impressive job to host a grand prix at a track that has many logistical challenges, in terms of both its location and its facilities, and to make it work financially for as long as they did.
It was highly popular with Dutch fans. But the event was privately run with no government financial support, and organisers decided that, as race fees went up, the risks that the event would not turn a profit were becoming too high.
This decision was influenced by the fact that there had been a slight decrease in interest in the last couple of years. Understandable, as the novelty wore off.
So organisers decided to end the event after a good run before any decline became more significant and they made a loss.
F1 has no shortage of events with which to replace it. Portugal and Turkey are both coming back to the calendar next year, for example.

The story so far: India’s food regulator has proposed a red, hexagonal warning label on the front of packaged foods high in added sugar, saturated fat or salt, in a move aimed at giving consumers a simple, at-a-glance signal about unhealthy products.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), in an affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on August 28, has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages.
The proposal comes after years of debate over front-of-pack labelling and intervention by the Supreme Court. The Court is scheduled to consider the affidavit on September 10.
Also Read | FSSAI’s proposed warning labels could let unhealthy foods escape scrutiny, says expert
How the proposed system is expected to work?
FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages.
In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase.
The thresholds are proposed to be based on the Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024. However, the FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat.
Single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey, are also proposed to be exempt.
Also Read | Supreme Court slams FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products
What do critics say about the proposed change?
Nutrition advocates say the biggest concern is the decision to initially require a product to be high in two nutrients before it attracts a warning. A product that is high in sugar but low in salt and fat, for instance, could escape a warning altogether.
“This defeats the purpose of a warning label,” Arun Gupta, convenor of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPI), told The Hindu. He has argued for a simpler principle: if a product is high in sugar, salt or saturated fat, it should carry a warning.
Also Read | Why the FSSAI is also putting liquor under the scanner
The distinction could matter particularly for products such as sugary beverages, which may be high in added sugar but contain little or no fat or salt and could therefore fall outside the warning requirement in Phase I.
Dr. Gupta has also raised concerns over the use of “added” rather than total sugar and fat, the size of the proposed warning and the absence of a firm deadline for Phase II. He has called for the warnings to be available in Hindi and English, arguing that language and visibility are essential if the labels are to reach consumers across the country.
He has urged the Court to examine the proposed nutrient thresholds, definition of high-fat/sugar/salt foods, warning size, language requirements and exemptions to ensure that the system remains visible and scientifically robust.
Also Read | From Bournvita to ‘100% Pure’: Why is FSSAI tightening the rules on food claims?
Why is this significant?
Front-of-pack warning labels have been under discussion in India since at least 2018. Draft regulations on high fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods were proposed in 2022, but did not become law.
The issue returned to the centre of the public-health debate in 2026 after the Supreme Court directed FSSAI to move towards interpretive warning labels for unhealthy packaged foods.
The regulator’s approach has also evolved rapidly in recent weeks. An earlier proposal placed before the Court in August relied on displaying nutritional information against recommended daily limits. Following the Court’s intervention, FSSAI returned with the red-hexagon warning framework in its August 28 affidavit.
Also Read | FSSAI proposes front-of-pack red pictorial warnings for foods high in fat, sugar, salt
For consumers, the proposed red hexagon is intended to make it harder for marketing claims such as “natural” or “multigrain” to obscure the nutritional profile of a product.
For the food industry, mandatory warnings could increase pressure to reformulate products by reducing sugar, salt and saturated fat. FSSAI has said the phased approach would give industry time to reformulate.
But the proposal is not yet a notified regulation. The immediate question before the Supreme Court is whether the framework provides a clear and meaningful warning or leaves products high in a single nutrient outside the net for an unspecified period.

The anger was impossible to miss.
As television reporters walked into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and adjoining protest sites to cover the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, many were greeted with chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’. Several journalists carrying microphones or wearing lanyards bearing the logos of prominent television channels — including NDTV, News X, ABP News, and Times Now — found themselves surrounded by protesters questioning their coverage of the movement. In some instances, reporters were heckled. In some instances, the confrontation turned physical: Times Now reporter Dev Kotak was roughed up by the crowd at Jantar Mantar, and video of the aftermath circulated widely. A Zee News reporter was filmed in Mumbai standing in the rain as youth protesters around him jeered.
The mood was most poignantly captured, perhaps, by a banner at the protest site. It contained the mugshots of six senior mainstream media journalist-cum-anchors: Arnab Goswami of Republic, Sudhir Chaudhary of DD, Chitra Tripathi of ABP, Anjan Om Kashyap of Aaj Tak, Amish Devgan then of News 18, and Rubika Liyaquat of Times Now Navbharat. Above their photos, the banner said, “India’s worst enemies — More dangerous that terrorists or anti-nationals”.
Taken together, the scenes that unfolded in Delhi raise the important question: Why did a large section of young protesters reserve some of their sharpest criticism not for politicians or police, but for television news channels?
Television Crew Faces Public Anger
The protests that erupted in Delhi in June-July brought together thousands of students and young people from across the country, turning a satirical political collective called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) into the nucleus of a wider youth-led movement. What began as a mobilisation around the NEET-UG paper leak and concerns over the examination system expanded into a broader expression of anger against the government, with protesters demanding accountability from those in charge. The demonstrations grew in scale over weeks, drawing sustained public and media attention and eventually contributing to Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.
As the protests grew, major television networks deployed reporters to cover the events. Instead of the routine interactions that often accompany live reporting, many ground reporters encountered open hostility from sections of the crowd.
Slogans of “Godi Media” were raised during a gathering in the national capital Delhi. pic.twitter.com/oyZpCVz0EY
— The Nawakadal (@thenawakadal) July 20, 2026
Videos shared widely on social media show protesters chanting ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ — a phrase originally coined by journalist Ravish Kumar, roughly translating to ‘lapdog media’ — as reporters prepared to go live. In one video, a protester says he stopped a News18 vehicle from being damaged despite his own anger towards the channel. “I am a Muslim myself. I protected their vehicle from being damaged. Though I know this evening, they will again do a Hindu-Muslim debate,” he said.
GODI MEDIA IS DEAD!
Yesterday’s Massive Student Protest Delivered The Final Verdict:
Traditional Mainstream Media has COMPLETELY LOST Gen Z’s Trust!
Lakhs of Students who hit the streets got EVERY piece of Real Information from Social Media — not your Biased Propaganda Boxes.… pic.twitter.com/zLIOM5GXP1
— তন্ময় l T͞anmoy l (@tanmoyofc) July 21, 2026
As reporters started being identified by the brands they represented, some began using unbranded microphones instead. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor and Vishnu Som, and India Today’s Preeti Choudhry were among those.
The outbursts were not confined to a handful of isolated incidents. Numerous videos from different locations captured similar confrontations, while comments beneath those videos echoed the protesters’ criticism of mainstream television news. Smaller outlets perceived as pro-government were heckled as well, suggesting the hostility was directed at a type of coverage rather than at legacy television alone.
At the same time, several incidents crossed the line from protest into intimidation. Videos also emerged showing journalists being pushed, chased or physically heckled by sections of the crowd.
This andhbhakti of CJP is now crossing all limits. You can tell godi media to walk away, raise slogans, but you can’t physically push, grope or beat them.
Wonder whether these are genuine protestors or lumpen elements.https://t.co/Xo4bTJ1DgX
— 🍉 (@DelhiIsNotFar) July 21, 2026
In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.
You are the most vile, most pathetic, most disgusting person @sudhirchaudhary
I always agree to disagree, never hate anyone but you are really a bad person.
You are now labelling innocent students for your propaganda.
Shame on you! pic.twitter.com/lYj5cNlURk
— Arpit Sharma (@iArpitSpeaks) July 21, 2026
Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.
ALSO READ: Op Sindoor: As Indian media made false, outrageous claims, PIB looked the other way
Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.

A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.

The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
