— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

In May 2026, amid the raging US-Iran war, PM Narendra Modi urged citizens to reduce gold buying, travel abroad and fuel consumption to preserve India’s foreign exchange reserves which had come under pressure due to rupee’s depreciation exacerbated by the Middle East conflict.
Before the start of the war at the end of February, India’s forex reserves had hit a record high, but the 
Reserve Bank of India
’s (RBI) steps to curb rupee’s slide and the drain due to rising fuel costs and gold import values strained the forex reserves.
Now, months after the start of the conflict, India has reported its highest ever foreign exchange reserves of over $740 billion! Forex reserves hit a record high last week itself at $729 billion, and this week has seen a further rise. In fact, reserves have for 9 weeks now!.
How has the RBI managed to secure high forex reserves in times of global economic uncertainty? What’s worked for India and why does the rise in forex cover matter? And, importantly, is it sustainable?
RBI’s FCNR(B) window bonanza
What the RBI did was simple, but with better-than-expected results: The central incentivised Indian banks to attract foreign-currency deposits from overseas Indians. This was done by absorbing the currency-hedging costs on FCNR deposits. 
This helped banks by reducing the exchange-rate risk and allowed them to offer more attractive returns to depositors.
FCNR(B) deposits are essentially foreign-currency deposits that non-resident Indians can hold with Indian banks, with the principal and interest maintained in a foreign currency.
The arrangement also allowed banks to leverage the foreign-currency deposits, with some lenders offering loans several times the original deposit. The initiative helped bring fresh dollar inflows.
What was the FCNR(B) scheme?
And the scheme has resulted in bumper inflows!
RBI has garnered $136.38 billion through the special dollar swap scheme which it launched in June to replenish foreign currency supplies and strengthen its reserves war chest.
The inflows have far exceeded the RBI's initial estimate of about $80 billion. In fact, nearly half the mobilisation came in the final 10 days before the scheme closed on August 31.
FCNR(B) deposits accounted for $127.23 billion, while overseas foreign-currency bonds contributed $5.3 billion and external commercial borrowings $3.9 billion. The programme tapped India's 35-million-strong diaspora and was designed to help support the rupee as it came under pressure.
Forex reserves at record high
Not only that, the structure also allowed NRIs to borrow substantially more than the amount deposited. In some cases, borrowing could be as much as 19 times the deposit, with the borrowed funds placed as FCNR(B) deposits.
This has led to India’s forex reserves touching new records even amid the conflict.
The scheme revived a strategy used during the 2013 taper tantrum, when a similar window attracted about $26 billion and helped fuel a sharp rupee rally. The latest scheme was so successful that RBI ended the FCNR window a month earlier than announced.
What it means for India
Experts attribute a large part of the increase in forex reserves to RBI’s swap window. The added cover works well in the current economic situation, providing an important buffer from external shocks.
Experts also note that while inflows from the swap facility were higher, forex reserves have not seen a commensurate increase due to possible central bank interventions to step rupee’s fall.
“The swap facility has been responsible for the bulk of the recent reserve rebuilding, though the extent of lift is lower than the scale of inflows, implying some offset through intervention and balance-sheet adjustments,” says Radhika Rao, Senior Economist and Executive Director at DBS Bank.
According to Rao, the rise in reserves strengthens India's capacity to manage an oil shock, even if it does not fundamentally alter the economy's dependence on imported energy.
How India mopped up dollars
“FCNR deposits are usually medium-term liabilities and thereby a more durable form of financing. Further out, authorities will be focused on generating more resilient sources, including current-account-generated support, capital inflows, FDI, and remittances to backstop the reserves' stock,” she tells TOI.
Importantly, the increased forex reserves amid global turmoil provide confidence to investors and also keeps the speculators at bay knowing the RBI has the firepower to intervene if there is excessive speculative trade.
Ranen Banerjee, Partner and Leader, Economic Advisory, PwC India says that with forex reserves covering over 10 months of imports, India is in a comfortable position.
“The export margins on refined petroleum products have increased significantly and we are getting some cushion from the exports of these products given the hit on foreign refining capacity. Hence, we have a partial cushion on oil price shocks from these exports,” he explains.
“The FII outflows have ebbed, FDI is improving, investments are growing and given markets have been subdued for almost 2 years, the valuations are normalising. Hence, the forex reserves are unlikely to face any immediate outflow concerns,” he adds.
Madan Sabnavis, Chief Economist, Bank of Baroda is of the view that India’s forex position was strong entering into the crisis, and has now strengthened further.
“Forex reserves were already quite strong covering 10-11 months of imports and hence were resilient. Adding these dollars just makes the position much stronger. At a different level given the rather high forward position of around $100 billion, these incremental deposits would in a way balance them,” he tells TOI.
He adds that the current cushion is durable for at least a year, helping greatly in cushioning the blow. “We have been having a negative balance of payments in the last couple of years. This will make it positive,” he said.
Rupee on upward curve
With record inflows reported, the rupee has appreciated to hit a two-month high. Experts believe that had the window not existed, rupee’s depreciation would have been more rapid.
On Thursday, the rupee strengthened by 49 paise, or 0.5%, to end at 94.48 against the dollar, marking its highest level in two months.
The rupee’s appreciation followed the RBI’s disclosure on Wednesday that its special initiative to attract foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians had generated several billion dollars of inflows.
DK Srivastava, Chief Policy Advisor at EY India says that in the absence of FCNR contribution, it is likely that the rupee would have depreciated further.
“It may be noted that the pressure on the rupee is driven by market forces, the balance between imports and exports of goods and services, net flow of capital and global crude prices. RBI does not aim to intervene in correcting the direction of change of the exchange rate which is determined by these broader forces. At best, it tries to contain the volatility of the INR/$. This became possible by the FCNR contribution,” he tells TOI.
Rupee vs Dollar: Up upward curve
Caution ahead?
The US-Iran war is far from over and India is still importing energy needs such as crude oil, LPG, and LNG at high prices. Foreign investors are still pulling out money and the global economic headwinds continue.
India’s forex cover has grown, which provides the economy with a credible external sector shield. But, the road ahead may continue to be bumpy in lieu of continued external pressures.
DK Srivastava strikes a cautious stance.
The previous peak of India’s forex reserves was $728.5 billion at the end February 2026 which was almost equal to the $729.3 billion post FCNR scheme, he notes.
“Thus, the present level of forex reserves was already achieved earlier when the balance of trade was more favourable. It is important for India’s forex reserve profile to achieve a more positive balance of trade rather than depend on one time schemes which help to minimize depletion in the forex reserves,” he tells TOI.
Some experts have also flagged the eventual hedging cost for RBI. But reports suggest that the government expects the central bank to face limited material costs from the swap facility.
While economists have estimated that hedging could cost the RBI around 3% of roughly Rs 12 lakh crore, or Rs 36,000 crore, policymakers believe the returns from investing the dollars in US Treasuries could offset these costs.
Even as the reserves touch record high, PM Modi has urged Indians to continue preserving forex. He has asked people not to go for foreign holidays, host weddings abroad, or buy gold unless necessary. And that itself is indicative of the government’s measured approach despite economic resilience.

Union minister Chirag Paswan’s party seeks FIR against ‘influencer’ Swatantra Bhardwaj, calls for strict action
Union minister Chirag Paswan’s party filed a complaint at Parliament Police Station against Swatantra Bhardwaj, alleging that he had falsely used Paswan’s name.
Union minister Chirag Paswan’s party, Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), on Friday sought registration of an FIR against self-styled influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj, accusing him of using Paswan’s name publicly to falsely suggest he had political backing.
Notably, a clip that went viral purportedly showed Bhardwaj admitting to a violent attack on the father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Nishu Aazad.
In the same video, Bhardwaj allegedly bragged about Delhi Police refusing to take action over the incident, citing his political connections.
Chirag Paswan seeks FIR against Bhardwaj
The Union minister’s party filed a complaint at Parliament Police Station against Bhardwaj, alleging that he had falsely used Paswan’s name and publicly claimed an association with the LJP(RV) president, reported news agency ANI.
The party has urged the police to register an FIR against Bhardwaj and formally record that he has no association with the party or the matter in question.
It has also called for strict action against the accused.
Will ensure justice for Aazad's father: Paswan
The complaint comes after Paswan earlier said he was "taking full responsibility" for ensuring justice for CJP activist Nishu Aazad's father, who was attacked and seriously injured during protests at Jantar Mantar.
"In public life, many people come to meet us. But if somebody claims, on this very basis to be a personal acquaintance of ours, then that is a misuse of our name. The attacker has sought to give the impression that action has not been taken against him because of me and my party. I have lodged a formal complaint against this misuse of my name," Paswan was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.
He added, "It is indeed a serious matter that the student activist's father was beaten so severely that he could have died. The attacker has the temerity to brag about the incident on TV, and he roams scot-free. I take full responsibility to ensure justice to the aggrieved family by pursuing the matter with Delhi police."
Swatantra Bhardwaj detained
Bhardwaj was taken into custody in Uttar Pradesh’s Bulandshahr on Friday, just hours after Delhi Police allegedly assured CJP protesters that he would be arrested within 72 hours.
Police said Bhardwaj had tried to flee but was caught, HT has learnt.

WhatsApp launches bill payments in India: How to pay electricity, gas, water bills on messaging app
WhatsApp users can tap the ₹ icon at the top of the home screen to access bill payments, said a press release
WhatsApp has launched bill payments in India to make it easier for users to find, manage and pay their everyday household and utility bills on the app. WhatsApp, in a statement on Thursday, said the bill payment service will be powered by the Bharat Connect (BBPS) network, allowing people to pay bills to more than 22,700 billers across 30 categories, including electricity, gas, water, FASTag, insurance, credit cards and loan repayments.
Users can tap the ₹ icon at the top of the home screen to access bill payments, view past payments, and upcoming bills, manage multiple accounts under a single provider, and pay with the payment mode of their choice, said the release.

Steps to access and use bill Payments
- Open WhatsApp and tap the ₹ icon at the top of the home screen.
- Select the bill category and biller.
- Add and confirm your account details.
- Review the fetched bill amount and other required details.
- Select your payment mode (UPI, debit card or credit card).
- Confirm the payment.
Arun Srinivas, Managing Director and Country Head of Meta India, said, “For millions of Indians, WhatsApp is already the simplest way to stay close to family and friends, talk to businesses, access citizen services, and buy everything from metro tickets to insurance — all without leaving the app. With bill payments, we're bringing that same simplicity to one of the most routine tasks in every household. No more juggling apps or tracking multiple due dates. We want to make paying a bill on WhatsApp as effortless as sending a message, and help bring the convenience of digital payments to people across the remotest parts of the country.”
This is the second major announcement from WhatsApp since Kunal Shah joined as the CEO of the messaging app. WhatsApp had earlier launched browser calling, allowing users to make and receive one-on-one and group audio and video calls directly through WhatsApp Web, without downloading any desktop application.

Swiss star Audrey Werro and Olympic champion Letsile Tebogo, along with newly minted world record holders Masai Russell and Alison dos Santos, headline the second half of the two-day Diamond League finals in Brussels on Saturday.
The final night in the Belgian capital gives the Diamond League winners in events contested at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship automatic qualification to the $10 million showdown next week.
AFP Sport looks at four stand-out events to watch in Brussels:
Women’s 800m
Britain’s Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson is not competing in Brussels, but Werro will face stiff competition from Femke Broeders-Bol.
The Dutch athlete is steadily improving as she transitions from the 400m hurdles, an event in which she was twice a world champion.
“I never expected to go this fast in the first season,” Broeders-Bol said.
The 26-year-old expressed hope that she and her rivals “can push the event further together”.
“We are in an era where there are so many amazing girls to run against.”
Werro has been the form athlete at the distance, going third in the all-time list with victory in Zurich pushing her to within 0.42sec of Jarmila Kratochvilova’s 43-year-old world record — the oldest in track and field.
Men’s 200m
Tebogo heads to Brussels with a best time this season of 19.84sec, some way shy of his personal best of 19.46sec.
American Kenny Bednarek is the fastest this year in what looks like a rapid field.
Bednarek leads the rankings with a time of 19.62sec, while other threats come from South Africa’s Sinesipho Dambile and Makanakaishe Charamba from neighbouring Zimbabwe.
Tebogo has won two Diamond League 200m races, including the most recent in Lausanne, and finished second in two others in what has been a long season for the Botswanan.
“Now it’s about enjoying every race in this final part of the season so that it doesn’t take a toll on my mental health,” he said.
Men’s 400m hurdles
Brazil’s Dos Santos, like Russell, set a new world record, running 45.80sec in Zurich, smashing Karsten Warholm’s previous best mark in some style.
Warholm is absent from Brussels, leaving Dos Santos a potential procession.
His teammate Matheus Lima, with a season’s best of 47.26sec, is the closest to Dos Santos, more than a second-and-a-half off the pace.
“I have been showing a great form throughout the season - that I am fast, I am strong,” said Dos Santos.
“We changed a lot of aspects of my training and racing in the preparation for this. I’m starting faster, I’m finishing stronger, and that is what I have to do to be able to break a world record.”
Women’s 100m hurdles
Russell touches down in Belgium fresh from setting a world record in Zurich where she clocked 12.09sec to better Nigerian Tobi Amusan’s previous best by 0.03.
She almost immediately turned her attention to becoming the first woman in history to break 12 seconds.
“I knew that the field was going to be pretty hot,” she said of Zurich. “I felt the temperature outside. It was perfect sprinting weather.
“I didn’t really have any expectations. I guess everyone else around me did. They were like, ‘Tonight’s the night’. They didn’t tell me that!”
Russell added: “When I heard that Alison broke the world record, in the back of my mind, I was trying to focus and lock in, but I knew the track was hot. I got a lot of motivation from him for sure.”
Among those aiming to stop her on Saturday are the woman she usurped as world record holder, Amusan, world indoor champion Devynne Charlton of the Bahamas and Nadine Visser of the Netherlands.

Hello there from STAT’s Andrew Joseph, writing to you from London and filling in for Mr. Pharmalot for the day. We just picked up a new bag of coffee beans that boasts notes of cola, cherry, and grape, so we’ll have to see if we pick up on any of that when we grind them up for tomorrow’s cup of stimulation. For now, though, perhaps some headlines will suffice …
An experimental gene therapy for Angelman syndrome from Ultragenyx failed in a Phase 3 study, STAT reports. The medicine showed no benefit compared to a sham treatment in the rare disease, which causes severe intellectual disability and developmental delays. The drug, called GTX-102, had shown powerful results in early trials, raising the hopes of families affected by the devastating condition. The trial failure is also a significant blow to Ultragenyx’s business, and the company said it’s now planning “significant expense reductions.”
Just a week after the landmark U.S. approval of a game-changing drug for advanced pancreatic cancer, the same therapy is showing promise against the world’s biggest cancer killer, Nature tells us. In a small trial in non-small cell lung cancer, the drug, Revolutions Medicines’ Rasonque, shrank tumors in more than 30% of participants. Each patient had tumor-promoting mutations in a member of the RAS family of proteins, and had previously tried other therapies. A larger study in which participants with non-small cell lung cancer are randomly assigned to receive either the drug, also called daraxonrasib, or standard chemotherapy is underway.

Having An air quality monitor for your home is more important than you may think. As climate change speeds up and wildfires increasingly engulf large swaths of land, leaving behind smoke that makes air potentially hazardous to breathe, it's more important than ever to ensure you're breathing clean air. An at-home air quality monitor is a simple way to ensure that, whether it be car exhaust, wildfire smoke, pollutants from seasonal changes, or simply fumes from your gas stove, the air around you is safe to breathe.
These air quality monitors test the air quality both indoors and outdoors, and on top of measuring PM2.5 (particulate matter) in the air and AQI (air quality index), they can also give insights into the air you're breathing, including measuring temperature, humidity, CO2, VOCs, and more.
Our top pick, IQAir's Air Visual Pro ($330), measures for several factors and has an easy-to-read display, while our more basic budget pick, Temptop S1 PM2.5 Air Quality Monitor & Indoor Thermometer ($28), has been solid throughout prolonged testing.
For more ways to keep your air quality in check for a healthier environment, take a look at our guides to the Best Outdoor Air Quality Monitors, Best Air Purifiers, and Best Multiuse Air Purifiers. Plus, check out how we test them and how to pick the right air purifier for your home.

The AirVisual air quality monitor has an easy-read 5-inch LCD display screen and a graphic of a boy’s face along with the AQI color scale that lets me know my indoor air quality from across the room. As the air quality gets poorer, the little boy will stop smiling with a green background and become solemn with a yellow background; finally, if the air is truly dangerous, he’ll put on a gas mask and the color turns dark purple. I like that I don’t have to log on to the internet or open an app to know if I have clean air. Plus, the AirVisual has the added feature of giving both indoor and outdoor air quality data. This saves me the extra step of checking the outdoor air quality on my phone. And it cycles through various displays—it has the time, then it will show both indoor and outdoor readings, along with congratulating me for achieving excellent indoor air quality or it will recommend that I open a window. The AirVisual air quality monitor measures PM2.5 and CO2 and displays the temperature and humidity. It has an easy-to-read dashboard on the app and keeps data for a year, but its biggest strength is its display, especially when I burn a pizza and the boy gets sad and dons a gas mask. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

How I Tested
In the past, I've relied on my phone's weather app to measure the air quality around me, and the government’s free AirNow website, where you can plug in your zip code and see its easy-to-read air quality meter. Now, as I test air purifiers, I always make sure to corroborate the purifiers' built-in PM2.5 or AQI measurements with an independent outside source—a separate air quality monitor—to test both the accuracy of the machine and the purifier's efficacy in filtering pollutants and getting the air quality back to a healthy level.
These air quality monitors were tested in various locations around my house, when cooking on my unventilated gas stove, under my living room window that draws in a lot of building and exhaust fumes, and outside my cat's litter box. Plus, I did additional testing outdoors, where I measured the monitors’ readings against local weather apps. And when field testing air purifiers with a sealed tent and smoke pellets as mentioned above, I always use an air quality monitor to check pollutant levels and the purifiers' efficacy when timed to get back to healthy levels.
Why Do I Need an Air Quality Monitor?
Like I mentioned above, I think it's especially important to have an air quality monitor to test whether your air both inside and outside the home is healthy if you don't have an air purifier. But it's also important to have one to measure the efficacy of the air purifier(s) in your home to ensure they are doing their job as efficiently as claimed. Especially since after prolonged use (and time), the built-in sensors can clog and give inaccurate readings.
When placing or installing an air quality monitor, try to measure at the breathing zone height, around 3 to 6 feet off the floor. An air quality monitor is especially helpful against some of the more harmful effects of things like wildfire smog, which can't always be smelled or seen. But an air quality monitor can sense that there is too much bad air, and then you can adjust the air purifier fan(s) accordingly.
It can also help to instill healthy habits, as WIRED Reviews contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro notes, using air quality monitors taught her to turn on the kitchen exhaust fan and crank up an air purifier before she turns on her gas stove. In the past, she didn’t think much of a little smoke from cooking. Now she takes proactive steps to avoid inhaling harmful pollutants.
Once you start noticing bad air and take steps to correct it, you'll notice fewer allergy symptoms and, often, fewer upper respiratory sicknesses and improved sleep. Even innocuous household things like lit candles, cooking on a stovetop without an exhaust fan (guilty), or aerosol air fresheners can negatively impact indoor air in real time. Get yourself an air quality monitor and see for yourself.
What to Consider Before Buying
Even though many current air purifier models have built-in air quality sensors, having a designated air quality monitor is a great way to independently corroborate or monitor air quality and pollutants. Plus, these handheld monitors are also portable and able to more accurately test air quality outdoors.
Before you purchase your own indoor air quality monitor, here are some things to know: Sensors on the WIRED-tested AirVisual Pro and PurpleAir all performed well in an independent study. Low-cost consumer air quality monitors are much cheaper (in the $200 or less range) than what's used by the professionals, but are also less accurate and not as easily calibrated. When testing multiple air quality monitors, they will not usually give the exact same AQI, but they are usually very close.
Consumer air quality monitors use sensors to detect tiny invisible particles in the air and other contaminants, with some sensors using light scattering to detect fine particulate matter known as PM10, like the dust visible in light, and invisible health hazards like PM2.5, which can reach the deepest parts of the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

Fire erupts during demolition of quake-damaged chimney at paper factory in Japan
A fire has broken out during the demolition of a chimney at a paper factory in Japan's Kumamoto prefecture
TOKYO -- A fire broke out Thursday during the demolition of an earthquake-damaged chimney at a paper factory in Japan’s southwestern prefecture of Kumamoto.
Footage on NHK national television showed an orange blaze coming from one of the broken chimneys at the factory, with billowing black smoke rising into the sky.
The municipal fire department in Yatsushiro City said it received an emergency call Thursday evening from an employee at the Nippon Paper Industries' factory saying the fire erupted during demolition work.
Three of five chimneys at the factory were severely damaged when the magnitude 7.1 quake struck on July 28, killing 38 people. An 80-meter (262-foot) high chimney collapsed, killing nine factory employees.
Some 36,000 houses and buildings were destroyed or damaged, and more than 2,000 people are still living in evacuation centers, including school gymnasiums and community centers.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Nick Kyrgios accepted a one-month suspension from the International Tennis Integrity Association (ITIA) for testing positive for cocaine at a tournament in Spain in June, the organisation announced Thursday.
The 31-year-old from Australia had been provisionally suspended since August 4, which was revealed just over two weeks later.
The ITIA in its announcement said Kyrgios told investigators that he socially used cocaine during a night out before he was due to play in Mallorca, and after consulting with an expert from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), accepted that it was outside of competition.
WADA’s default three-month ban can be reduced to one by completing a treatment program. The ITIA said Kyrgios’ suspension is over Thursday pending the completion of that program.
Kyrgios’ prize money and ranking points from the Mallorca event are forfeited. He lost his only match to countryman Adam Walton.
A finalist at Wimbledon in 2022 when he lost to Novak Djokovic, Kyrgios has played only four ATP singles matches this year and is ranked 918th in the world.

On Feb. 24, 2025, the Food and Drug Administration did something it arguably should have done long ago: It removed the elaborate monitoring program that has governed one of psychiatry’s most important drugs, clozapine, for more than 30 years. For anyone who treats serious mental illness, this is welcome news.
But I want to say something more complicated about it, because I have spent a large part of my career prescribing this drug (or trying to) to the most vulnerable population there is: children with psychosis. The paperwork was never really the problem.
Very few things in all of medicine have struck me as close to miraculous. Vaccines. Antibiotics. And, in children with childhood-onset schizophrenia, clozapine. That will not surprise anyone who has worked with it in schizophrenia.
Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic we have for the sickest patients: the roughly 1 in 3 people with schizophrenia whose illness does not yield to other medicines. It is the only drug approved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, the only one shown to reduce suicide, and it is associated with lower death rates than the alternatives. When nothing else has worked, clozapine can, sometimes, give a person back to themselves. I have watched it happen in children, in the carefully controlled trials my colleagues and I ran, where young people who had been lost to relentless psychosis began, within days, to return to their families.
And yet it is one of the most underused drugs in all of medicine. In the United States, only about 4% of people with schizophrenia receive clozapine, though perhaps a third could benefit, and the figure should probably be higher still in childhood-onset schizophrenia, which tends to be even more treatment-resistant. There is, in plain terms, a proven, lifesaving, sometimes life-restoring treatment that American medicine mostly declines to give.
For years, simply to prescribe clozapine, a clinician had to enroll in an FDA-mandated registry. Patients submitted to regular blood draws, which are weekly at the start, with each result logged into a national database before a pharmacy could release the next supply. The goal was to catch the small number of patients in whom clozapine can sharply reduce the white cells that fight infection.
Whatever caution it began in, there is good evidence it also kept the drug from people who needed it. That is the very program the FDA has now retired, perhaps influenced by advocacy efforts, including those by parents.
But the deeper barrier was fear. Clozapine carries a fearsome reputation: the blood tests, the long list of side effects, the rare but genuine danger. This has scared clinicians; they just don’t want to take the risk. And the FDA can remove the registry, but cannot make the fear go away.
This is especially true when dealing with children, in whom neutropenia tends to be more common than in adults. I have watched capable, caring clinicians steer around clozapine for years, reaching for a fourth or fifth less-effective medication rather than the one most likely to work, because avoiding it simply felt safer. Recently I could not find a single child psychiatrist across four academic centers willing to start clozapine in a child with childhood-onset schizophrenia.
When I first started using clozapine, I was afraid as well. But it soon became clear that it was not a particularly difficult medicine to work with. Yes, you have to monitor the side effects carefully, but the benefits simply made the risk worth taking. And as I started seeing the benefits of clozapine, the fear quickly went away.
After all, in other areas of medicine, we treat children with many risky medications (such as chemotherapeutic drugs) because we know they are lifelines for those illnesses. We need to approach clozapine the same way when it comes to schizophrenia.
In my experience, parents were rarely the problem. They understood, they were desperate, had often done the work of getting over their fear, and were ahead of the curve. They typically had already heard and read about clozapine and were ready to be on board as soon as we were ready, partly because they had tried everything and nothing had worked. I used to say, after seeing what I saw at the National Institute of Mental Health, “If someone in my family was diagnosed with schizophrenia, I would want them on clozapine yesterday.”
The cost of our avoidance of clozapine is invisible but enormous, measured in people who stay sick, and in lives that end early, for want of a drug already sitting on the shelf.
I do not mean to minimize the side effects of clozapine. The risks are very real. My colleagues and I ran into them at the NIMH every now and then. We went on to study how often it happened in our children, and who was most at risk. The problem is concentrated in the first months of treatment, and it never quite reaches zero.
But we found ways through: We showed, for instance, that adding lithium could lift the neutrophil count enough to keep a child safely on clozapine, and we published it. Its other side effects, too, can be managed, and there is ample literature, including from our own group, on how to do that in children. In fact, as we published more, we began to notice something new: Some of the children referred to our study arrived already on clozapine, something we had never seen in the study’s earlier years.
Those of us who worked closely with clozapine had argued for years that its monitoring was stricter than the evidence justified; that a rigid, uniform schedule, largely unchanged for decades, treated every patient as though the danger were constant and equal, when in truth it was concentrated in the early months, foreseeable, and, in most cases, manageable. The FDA’s recent decision, in that sense, is less a reversal than an overdue acknowledgment of what the people closest to the drug had been saying all along.
Notably, the FDA still recommends the blood tests; it has simply stopped forcing them. This is a welcome change, and it means the responsibility that used to live inside a federal registry now lives where it probably always should have: in the judgment of the clinician and the informed choice of the patient.
That is the real opportunity in this decision, and the real test of it. Lifting the program is not permission to be careless; it is an invitation to be wise, and better informed.
Ideally it will empower clinicians to reach for clozapine sooner, for the people most likely to be saved by it, including the young. The worst outcome would be to lose the bureaucratic barrier and go on avoiding the drug anyway, only now without even a rule to blame.
And perhaps, and this is my real hope, it will move us to reach for clozapine earlier, rather than only as a last resort. To my colleagues who care for the youngest and sickest patients, I would put it as plainly as I can: Do not let fear make this decision for you. We have spent three decades treating clozapine as the door you open only after every other has failed. The science has never justified waiting that long. The government has now removed one of our excuses. Whether we use this moment to actually reach the patients who need it, or simply find a new reason to look away, is up to us. It always was.
Nitin Gogtay, M.D., is a psychiatrist, physician-scientist, and author of “The Vanishing Children” (HarperCollins, January 2027). He spent almost two decades studying and conducting blinded clinical trials of clozapine on childhood-onset schizophrenia at the National Institute of Mental Health.

In Summary
- The CMF Buds Neo are the latest TWS from Nothing’s sub-brand, CMF.
- The new buds come in attractive colors, in true CMF tradition, and punch above their price point in terms of specs and features.
- At Rs 1999, the CMF Buds Neo are the most affordable TWS in CMF’s audio portfolio, and have also been called the most accessible entry point to the CMF ecosystem. They do face a lot of competition, though.
While it is hard being a new smartphone in this tech climate, we believe it is harder being a new pair of TWS. The number of new TWS, as well as increasingly competitive prices and features across a wide range of price brackets, make it quite a task for a new pair to make its mark in the tech world. The latest addition in this lineup comes from Nothing’s sub-brand CMF, the CMF Buds Neo. Priced at Rs. 1,999, the Buds Neo are positioned as the most accessible entry to the CMF ecosystem. They come with an impressive feature list and a quirky design. But is that enough to help the CMF Buds Neo make space for itself in the TWS market?
CMF Buds Neo Appearance and Design: Typically CMF, Geometry with some flair
CMF, like its parent company Nothing, speaks a very distinct design language. A language no one else in the industry has adopted (yet) – a very smooth blend of Nothing’s industrial design combined with CMF’s bright colored flair. The CMF Buds Neo speak this language. Their square-shaped case comes with soft, rounded edges that make it sit very comfortably in one’s hands. The top left corner has a tactile, round dial. This is not just a design touch but also has some utility – it can be used to attach a lanyard that will keep your Buds Neo from getting lost.
The buds come in three different colors: Black, White, and Dark Blue. The Dark Blue and White color options bring very vibrant color contrasts with green and orange ear tips and tactile dials, respectively, while the Black is all black. The white variant, whose white case comes with a super bright orange tactile dial, is perhaps the most distinct. There is a small ‘CMF by Nothing’ badge in orange on the front as well. The cases have a matte finish while the dials are glossy.
The case has a very tiny LED light on the front and a USB Type-C port on the back. Flip the case open, and you find the buds resting nicely inside, with a ‘Buds Neo’ branding slightly above the earbuds. The buds come with a typical TWS design – a bulbous head attached to a long pill-shaped stem. The eartips bring the pop of orange to the white buds, while the texture of the overall buds is a mix of glossy and matte.
There is a small glossy dot on the head of the stem of the right bud and a thick, slightly raised circle on the stem of the left bud. The buds are comfortable to wear and come with one set of eartips attached and two others in the box. We used the medium-sized eartips, and they fit snugly. Speaking of snug fits, the buds also attach magnetically to the case.
The CMF Buds Neo case itself is quite compact – it is square, with length and breadth both at 54.3 mm, and is a little thick at 23 mm. It weighs 50.3 grams, while the buds weigh just a little over 4 grams each. The case is very pocket-friendly, and the buds are light on the ear. The buds come with an IP55 rating, making them good enough for sweaty gym sessions, while the case has an IPX rating, making it splash-proof, which is handy (most TWS cases still do not have splash resistance).
The white case does get dirty very easily (it caught dirt marks in our bag), but all in all, the design of the CMF Buds Neo is very eye-catching and definitely something not-so-usual. If you are not into pops of color, you can choose the black variant. Those who want to be right between these two extremes can go for the blue variant, with its flash of green eartips and disk.
CMF Buds Neo Specs and Controls: Very impressive at this price point
The CMF Buds Neo come with impressive specs for their price. They have 12.4 mm dynamic drivers with a 20 Hz- 20 kHz frequency response, two mics per earbud (for a total of four), Bluetooth 6.0, support for AAC and SBC codecs, and ANC of up to 35 dB. There is also support for spatial audio, and you get six EQ presets. All of these features are accessible through the NothingX App. The case comes with a 460 mAh battery with support for fast charging, and each earbud has a 45 mAh battery in it as well. The buds support Google Fast Pair, Microsoft Swift Pair, and also Dual-Device connectivity.
Pairing the CMF Buds Neo is simple: you flip the case open, wait for the buds to appear in your device’s Bluetooth list, and select them. To get the buds in pairing mode to connect with other devices, you can simply tap and hold the stem of the buds for five seconds, then select them from your device’s Bluetooth list. The controls on the buds are basically a series of taps- double-tapping on either bud will take you to the next track or reject a call; triple-tapping will take you to the previous song, while tapping and holding will let you switch between ANC and transparency mode.
No action is assigned to the double-tap-and-hold, but one can assign it to increasing or decreasing the volume or summoning the voice assistant. Apart from the call functionality, these controls can be customized using the Nothing X app. Interestingly, there is no option to map a control to a single tap, perhaps out of concern for accidental touches.
CMF Buds Neo Performance: Good audio, decent ANC and very good calling
The 12.4 mm dynamic drivers on the CMF Buds Neo come with a titanium-coated PET dome and a flexible PEEK and PU surround. This, as per Nothing, adds a bass-ful punch to the audio while ensuring vocals do not get muddied. The buds certainly deliver on both these fronts. The audio is full-bodied, and while it does focus a bit on bass, it does not drown out the treble or vocals. It is not balanced in a way that would give an audiophile an eargasm, but we seldom see that at this price anyway. On the other hand, they will impress casual listeners in a heartbeat, delivering a thoroughly enjoyable experience in pop, Bollywood, R&B, and hip-hop, and similar genres.
The Nothing X app comes with six EQ presets, and each one offers a distinct sound profile, which sometimes is not the case in this price segment. There is also the option to create an EQ based on one’s own preferences. The buds provide a reasonably spacious sound, which is usually not very easy for TWS to achieve, especially at this price point. The sound obviously does not feel as immersive as some of the high-end audio gear available on the market, but for the price, it is a hit in our books. The vocals are sharp enough to listen to hour-long podcasts or watch content.
The CMF Buds Neo also come with ANC. There are four options – low, medium, high, and adaptive. We mostly stuck to the ‘high’ setting. It will not cancel out very loud noises, but the snug fit of the buds combined with effective ANC does kill environmental noise with ease. It managed to drown out noise in a crowded cafe very effectively. We could not hear our friend sitting across from us with ANC on. The transparency mode brings back awareness to what would otherwise be a very isolating experience – the conversation we were not able to hear earlier became clear with transparency mode.
The call quality of the buds is very good as well – a pleasant surprise at this price point. We did not have any issues hearing the caller and did not get any complaints about our voice quality either. There is a low latency mode for games, but we had to turn it on manually, which was a bit of a pain.
The controls of the CMF Buds Neo are easy to remember but take some serious getting used to. We often found we had to tap harder than we are used to in order to register a command. The buds also lack wear detection, which means the audio does not automatically pause when one takes the buds (one or both) out. While this is a feature not often found at this price point, its absence was inconvenient.
Battery is another strong suit of the CMF Buds Neo. The buds promise 11 hours of listening time with ANC off, with 52 hours of total playback with ANC off, including the case. With ANC on, the numbers become 5 hours for the buds, and 30 hours with the case. We found the buds’ actual performance to be close to these numbers. With mixed use (ANC/ transparency mode on and off) at 70 percent volume, the buds easily lasted for around 9 hours. The buds also have a fast charging feature in which 10 minutes of charging gives one 5.5 hours of play time with ANC off . However, there is no cable in the box, which is a bit of a letdown.
CMF Buds Neo App: NothingX remains as clean and easy to use as ever
The NothingX app is the perfect accompaniment to the CMF Buds Neo – simple, clean and easy to use. We did have some trouble adding our Buds Neo to the app, but after a little struggle, the buds were added to the list of our other CMF devices. There is one main page, and you can scroll down to access all the functions and features. ANC, Spatial Audio, controls, bass enhancement, equalizer settings, low lag mode, dual connection, and firmware updates can all be accessed through the app. One also gets the exact charge percentage left in each earbud, although rather oddly, not that of the case. The app is easy to use and remains one of our favorites.
CMF Buds Neo Review Verdict: Superb value for the price
The CMF Buds Neo come with a price tag of Rs. 1,999, which is quite competitive for the performance and specs they offer. The similarly priced OnePlus Nord Buds 3r bring a comparable spec sheet, as do the Realme Buds T200 Lite, but both come with Bluetooth 5.4, marginally less playtime, and are not even close to the Buds Neo in the design department.
The CMF Buds Neo are near-perfect entry-level TWS options. Their audio, ANC, and battery performance give them an edge over the competition, and the distinct design is the cherry on this TWS cake. If you do not want to burn a hole in your pocket and still want a good pair of feature-packed TWS, the CMF Buds Neo are the perfect pick.
- Distinct design
- Enjoyable audio
- Good ANC
- Super call quality
- Very good companion app
- Good battery life
- Controls take some getting used to
- No charging cable in the box
- The white coloured case attracts scratches and smudges easily

As the curtain closes on an upbeat summer box office, the team behind The Invite has reason to cheer. The indie comedy is a breakout, grossing over $55 million worldwide as of last weekend amid behemoths like The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Unusually, it’s a pretty even split between U.S. and international coin.
A24, which nabbed domestic rights in a days-long bidding war at Sundance for a sum north of $10 million, has taken the film — directed by and starring Olivia Wilde with Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Ed Norton — to $25.6 million. International totaled $29.7 million from 50 territories including Canada, according to FilmNation, and that’s without Italy and France (both opening September 16) and Spain, where The Invite originated (launching October 16).
“It’s incredible to see a comedy become an international hit, and with major territories still to release, the global momentum behind The Invite is just getting started,” says Glen Basner, founder and CEO of FilmNation, which handled international sales and produced the film alongside Permut Presentations and Megan Ellison’s Annapurna. Annapurna financed it.
Watch on Deadline
Producer David Permut sees The Invite is connecting with moviegoers for a few reasons: “It’s hysterically funny — and it’s wonderful to hear audiences laugh out loud like they have all over the world. It’s also got emotion and heart. It takes a mirror to all of our relationships, past and present, even though you may not identify specifically with the characters and what they’re going through.”
In a summer dominated by blockbusters and franchises, this one-room set piece is proof adult comedies can still break out on the big screen, says a source close to A24, which opened The Invite Stateside in late June 26 to $380,000 at seven theaters in New York and L.A. — one of the top limited debuts of the year. It expanded to 1,600 screens by week 3 with consecutive berths in the top 10 and great reviews. (Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh at 96%), see Deadline’s.
Wilde and Rogen star as struggling married couple Angela and Joe, raising their young daughter in a bespoke San Franciso apartment inherited from Joe’s parents. He’s a frustrated musician, she’s a fraying stay-at-home mom who’s invited upstairs neighbors Piña and Hawk (Cruz and Norton) for dinner. She preps desperately. Joe protests, the nightly racket from the bedroom upstairs has been ticking him off. The doorbell rings, The Invite is off and running.
“It’s combustible. You’re wondering what is going to happen with these four individuals, these couples getting together,” says Permut, who’s been making films of all sizes for the last four decades with credits ranging from Hacksaw Ridge to Face/Off to The Polka King. He hits TIFF on September 10 with the fest’s opening-night selection Being Heumann, from Apple and directed by Siân Heder.
The Invite, available on streaming since mid-August, is winding down in theaters, on about 60 screens through the end of next week.
Fans may get another crack at it — live — as Permut says he hopes to take the play to Broadway next year. He declined to elaborate. “I can’t right now, but I can tell you that we’re going to be doing it. That was always my intention. First to cut the umbilical cord with our movie, get that out the world. And now we’re starting to focus on the Broadway production. Nothing specific yet.”
That would take the story full circle as The Invite was born as a Spanish stage play called The Neighbors Upstairs (Los vecinos de arriba) by playwright, director and filmmaker Cesc Gay. “A woman who lived above him in Barcelona was making a lot of noise at three in the morning,” says Permut. “And they weren’t moving furniture. The passion is coming through the ceiling to Cesc and his mate downstairs. That’s where the seed of the idea was born.”
Gay followed the play with Goya Award-winning film Sentimental, which premiered at TIFF in 2020 titled The People Upstairs. Permut watched it (at home, it was Covid and the fest was virtual) and says he immediately jumped on the phone with a distributor in Spain and with Gay, acquiring English-language rights to both film and play.
He brought aboard Jonathan Dayton and Valerie Faris, directors of 2006 hit Little Miss Sunshine. He asked Rashida Jones and Will McCormack, who wrote and starred in Celeste and Jesse Forever (2012), to adapt the screenplay. The cast came together with Amy Adams and Paul Rudd downstairs, Tessa Thompson and Pedro Pascal above. Then the Hollywood strikes hit and “by the time things got going again, everybody’s schedule had changed. So we reinvented it.”
Permut loved Wilde’s first feature, the Annapurna-produced Booksmart (2019), and they’d met once and hit it off. “I never forgot it because she was so incredibly perceptive,” he says. He reached out to her about directing and “she was the perfect fit… with the reshuffled deck, with the great script that Rashida and Will had written.”
“Olivia is such a rare talent. Making Booksmart together, we saw it right away in her creative instincts and in her humanity. There was never a doubt she’d take it even further on The Invite,” says Annapurna’s co-head of film Chelsea Barnard.
Casting Wilde as Angela wasn’t intended but Permut says he’d just come off a great experience working with James Sweeney wearing multiple hats on Twinless. “I’ve done 40 movies, but never with an actor, director and writer on the same one until [Sweeney], who delivered a home run for us … I thought the part fit her perfectly, so I advocated very strongly that Olivia step into that role.”
The Invite was the first movie to shoot in L.A. after the devastating wildfires and, at the time, the only stage in operation at Hollywood’s Sunset Las Palmas Studios. Post was in London. The budget was under $15 million. “We wanted to make it for a price,” says Permut. “Everybody took the haircut. We all shared the same passion.”

‘Buying or not buying Russian oil won’t solve Ukraine crisis’: Jaishankar says India needs to take care of energy needs
S Jaishankar said India also needs to address the energy needs of its 1.4 billion people, and that this is something other countries should also respect.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Thursday said that whether India buys Russian oil or not, it will not solve the ongoing crisis between Russia and Ukraine. Jaishankar made the remarks after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv.
Addressing a question from the media about Ukraine’s concerns over India buying Russian oil, Jaishankar said India also needs to address the energy needs of its 1.4 billion people, and that this is something other countries should also respect.

“You know, the reason for your question, I get that, but I think it’s also important that all of you get the challenges of providing for energy for 1.4 billion people at a time when the world energy situation is very, very difficult. So, I would say, this is something where clearly the Ukraine side has its perspective, which we respect, and we have ours, which I would expect others to also respect,” Jaishankar said.
The EAM also said that India buying energy from Russia or not buying it would not solve the crisis that has been ongoing between the two countries for five years.

“This conflict, which is today in its fifth year, will not be solved because somebody is buying or not buying oil or minerals or metals or fertiliser. This conflict will be solved by dialogue, by diplomacy, by negotiation. And that is why it is something we would encourage,” Jaishankar said.
Jaishankar says India ready to help end war in Ukraine
Jaishankar also said that India is ready to help end the Ukraine war. Speaking to reporters on Thursday during his visit to Kyiv, the External Affairs Minister said that, if needed, India stands ready to mediate.
“If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there,” Jaishankar said alongside Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, as per news agency Reuters.
He also added that attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea were discussed during his meeting with Sybiha.
Zelensky, meanwhile, thanked India for its support to end the “unjust war” that Russia started against Ukraine.
“Held a meeting with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of India, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar. We discussed important issues. We are grateful to India for its desire to end this unjust war—the war of Russia against Ukraine. This time must certainly not be a time of war. Peace is needed. This is India's clear position,” Zelensky wrote in a post on X.

Google's new AI weather model uses live satellite data for higher-resolution forecasts
WeatherNext 3 is also supposed to be much better at predicting precipitation.
Google DeepMind has released the WeatherNext 3, an updated version of its last AI-powered weather model that it claims offers even more detailed forecasts across key variables like temperature, moisture and wind speed. DeepMind notes the new model should be particularly useful to companies working in renewable energy production, because of its ability to forecast "100-meter wind speeds (roughly at turbine-height) for precise wind-energy output, alongside high-resolution cloud cover and sun radiation levels to help solar farms."
WeatherNext 3's ability to offer hourly and higher-resolution forecasts (in a 5-kilometer square grid rather than the 25-kilometer square grid of WeatherNext 2) is all due to the new data it's trained on, DeepMind says. Rather than primarily relying on data from numerical weather prediction models, which include a six-hour lag, WeatherNext 3 incorporates live satellite data, which gives the model "a rich, continuously updating view of the atmosphere." The model's ingestion of sparse weather station data means it can also offer more detailed forecasts of variables like humidity, which can usually change dramatically from one kilometer to the next.
Combining precipitation data from NASA and Google's own satellite analysis also means WeatherNext 3 is better at predicting things like rain and snow. DeepMind says the model produces "up to 50 percent more accurate precipitation forecasts — with the greatest improvements in regions where forecasts have historically been less reliable."
WeatherNext 3 will power weather experiences in Google Search, the Gemini app and Google Maps, along with the Google Maps Weather API and the Google Earth Engine. If you're curious about experimenting with the model yourself, you can give it a spin right now in the Google Weather Lab. If you want to take the next step and build something with Google's model, the original WeatherNext model is also open-source as of August 2026.

Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets.
The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.
Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident.
The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said.
Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads.
While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency.
The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said.
Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h.
“We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

We’ll start this conference looking back on 2026 Washington Architecture by being honest: We have no idea what happened here. The snapshot of this planet that my comrades and I managed to obtain on our brief visit left us, if anything, more confused about Earth than we had been before. What follows are theories only.
All we know of 21st-century human political figure Donald J. Trump is what we can guess from the architectural record and a few bits of digital evidence. (Due to a misunderstanding, we ate most of the written records of this planet before figuring out that they contained information.) Was he a builder or a destroyer? There are also ruins of an arch—commemorating a triumph, but over what? Perhaps the successful defeat of 250 years of democracy, a system of rule that he despised?
Did he have access to the internet (a human technology that seems to have been primarily used for the sharing of pornography and misinformation)? Impossible to say. Some records suggest that a female of his species accessed the internet on his behalf. We don’t know his exact relation to this female, but we can observe that she was swift of foot and skilled at concealment in small enclosures, probably a trait admired by others. Were such relationships common? Did many human leaders consider it an honor to be chased by another human carrying a printer? (Did George Washington have a “Human Printer” of his own? Perhaps Benjamin Franklin fulfilled this role?)
Although other human figures enjoyed construction, Trump seemed to prefer the wrecking ball (what we would refer to as Grogon’s Tail) as a mode of expression. From a forensic analysis of these structures, we know that the Smashing of the Residence was first to take place, followed by the Desecration of the Pool.
Donald Trump seems to have smashed the Residence deliberately, as a warning to rivals. As his nestlings were at that time all mature and dwelling independently, such a gesture posed no danger to his young. Some papers we found suggested that there were plans to put something in the enormous hole, but these drawings are on an unlikely scale, and their suggested purpose is inconsistent. Ballroom? Bunker? No one can seem to agree, not even the plans themselves.
The situation of the pool is puzzling. We may never know why Donald Trump hated the pool (pond?) so much, but his action to strip it of its water, paint over its interior with a humiliating sealant, and fill it with a thick green algae speaks of immense disrespect. Had the pool or pond offended him? We know from the many banners he left bearing his visage around the city that he seems to have been incapable of smiling; a golden idol located in Florida represents him as having a slightly melted appearance. Perhaps glimpsing his reflection in the pond reminded him unpleasantly of these facts? Or were its ducks hostile to him? Some records show that even when the pool was drained of water, it was patrolled by an armed guard; what danger lurked in its shallows?
The structure with the giant head in it puzzles us most. We think this site on the Potomac may once have been used for entertainment and functioned as a kind of temple to the performing arts. Others suggest that it was an oversize dwelling place for mice. Some scholars believe that people really went inside the building and sat in red chairs while someone stood and bellowed in Italian. Perhaps this hall was used for punishment? Were wrongdoers subjected to the “tuba”?
Letters found near the site marking it “The Donald J. Trump and the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts” suggest that the enormous bronze head may represent either Donald J. Trump or John F. Kennedy, in whose joint memory the center seems to have been erected. Who were these men? They must have loved the arts. Perhaps an American Harmodius and Aristogeiton? Curiously, we do not see them commemorated jointly in other locations.
Some scholars argue that Donald J. Trump was in fact alive at the time of the center’s commemoration, but other scholars reply that this claim is ludicrous—where else is there evidence of a Memorial Center constructed while its subject was still living? The same theory suggests that he added his name to the center decades after its construction, halted all the shows, removed the public artworks, and threatened to demolish it if his name was not kept on, but other scholars reply that smashing things unless you can write your name on them is hardly the behavior of a full-fledged adult. We truly don’t know what to make of this place. (Just for the record, though, we didn’t do the pyramids.)

Audacity 4 has been in the works for some time, and had its own mini controversy last year when an unfortunate redesigned logo started making the rounds. The final version of the new icon isn’t nearly as bad as the early rendition that was circulating last October. But more importantly, all the promised improvements to the self-proclaimed “world’s most popular audio editing and recording app” are here, turning Audacity from a free and capable but extremely clunky audio editor into a powerful modern tool.
Audacity 4 is a complete revamp of the ‘world’s most popular’ audio editor
Non-destructive editing, better clip management, and a new look bring the app into the modern age.
The biggest change is the move to a non-destructive editing workflow. That means you can trim a clip down, then recover the audio simply by dragging the edge of the clip back out if you change your mind. Clips can now overlap too, which means you can still paste in audio even if there isn’t enough space and adjust after, or just freely drag audio around the timeline. Previously, if you tried to drag a clip past another one in the timeline, it would just stop dead in its tracks. You’d instead have to cut and paste it to move it past any existing audio.
You can also split clips now to easily chop up and rearrange audio. The developers refreshed clip envelopes and the built-in effects, and added a home screen with revamped project organization. Audacity also got a dramatic facelift that brings it more in line with Muse’s other products like Muse Score and Audio.com, complete with customizable themes.
While Audacity has been a staple of many people’s toolkits since it debuted way back in 2000, it’s stayed stubbornly consistent in its design and layout as new features have been bolted on, sometimes clumsily. This big refresh to Audacity 4 brings it much closer to a modern digital audio workstation (DAW).

US job market rebounds as employers add 162,000 jobs and unemployment rate holds steady
The jobs report, released Friday by the Labor Department, may offer a welcome signal for President Donald Trump just two months prior to midterm elections
The U.S. employment landscape experienced a rebound in August, with business owners adding an unexpected 162,000 positions while the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1 percent.
The employment figures, released Friday by the Labor Department, may offer a welcome signal for President Donald Trump just two months prior to midterm elections where economic performance is a central issue for voters.
The monthly expansion comfortably beat expectations of 65,000 additions predicted in a FactSet survey. Upward revisions by the Labor Department also painted a stronger picture, raising June and July employment figures by a combined 55,000. Companies actually added 21,000 jobs in July, reversing an initial government calculation of a 23,000 loss.
Meanwhile, the overall size of the American workforce—representing individuals currently working or seeking employment—rose by 683,000 last month after shrinking throughout June and July.
Enterprises continue to navigate a restricted supply of labor, driven by President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown along with an ongoing wave of retiring baby boomers. In response, some firms are turning toward digital technology to perform roles previously managed by human staff.
However, organizations remain hesitant to trim existing headcounts, granting the majority of American workers exceptional job stability while keeping overall jobless numbers depressed.
"It’s a very strange labor market,’’ David Kelly, chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, wrote in a commentary Monday.
The primary paradox facing analysts is that while new recruitment remains sluggish, job reductions remain exceptionally sparse.
Firms show little inclination to rapidly expand staff levels. Data from the Labor Department published Tuesday indicated that total gross recruitment—before factoring in departures or layoffs—dropped 5 percent to just under 5.1 million positions.
The U.S. economy no longer requires the same volume of monthly job creation as in previous years to prevent unemployment from escalating. President Donald Trump's immigration restrictions combined with baby boomer retirements mean fewer active job seekers are competing for openings, with over 1.3 million individuals leaving the active labor supply in the past 12 months.
Consequently, the monthly "break-even" target for new job creation—previously set at 155,000 over the 2023-2024 period—has fallen to near zero, according to research conducted by the Federal Reserve.
Rather than competing to recruit from a reduced pool of potential hires, "businesses are increasingly focused on boosting efficiency through technology and AI and increasingly seek to do more with their existing workforce,’’ EY-Parthenon economists Gregory Daco and Lydia Boussour wrote in a commentary this week.
Even without active recruitment initiatives, executive leadership remains unwilling to dismiss current employees, remembering the severe personnel deficits experienced after COVID-19 restrictions were lifted.
Thus, jobless figures stay low. Over the last year, initial applications for unemployment compensation—a key indicator of job cuts—have consistently hovered within a historically subdued bracket of 200,000 to 230,000.
This dynamic has created what financial analysts describe as a "no-hire, no-fire" economic environment, offering solid job security to existing staff while presenting substantial hurdles for younger applicants pursuing entry-level positions or out-of-work individuals trying to re-enter the labor market.

A pregnant soldier mourns her 21-year-old husband at his funeral in Ukraine
A pregnant woman in Kyiv mourns her 21-year-old husband, who was killed in action
KYIV, Ukraine -- A pregnant woman in a black dress stood at the head of her 21-year-old husband’s casket Tuesday in Kyiv, mourning the man she met when they were both soldiers fighting Russia's full-scale invasion of their country.
Yeva Smyrnova and Danyil Smyrnov both joined the army in 2023, at 18, and married two years later, in July 2025. Young as they were, decided they needed to hurry and start a family.
“We dreamed of this child, but because we were both always at war, it was very difficult,” said Smyrnova, who serves as a drone pilot under the call sign “Yunha.”
Danyil Smyrnov was killed in action on Aug. 28, 2026, on the Sumy front in northeastern Ukraine, one of a group of four soldiers killed in action serving with military intelligence. He held the rank of junior sergeant, served as a reconnaissance operator, and helped train recruits.
“This month our son is due to be born — the son Dania dreamed about so much. He dreamed of being the best father," Smyrnova told The Associated Press.
But instead of choosing a name for her firstborn child, she and hundreds of others came to say goodbye to her husband at St. Michael’s Golden-Domed Monastery.
In the days after Smyrnov's death, his wife wrote online that their son would be “his continuation.”
The monastery, where Ukraine typically holds funeral services for soldiers killed in the war, was packed. Mourners of all ages came to pay their respects, including fellow soldiers holding bouquets of roses.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Smyrnov was 16 and finishing high school. He went on to study psychology at a university in Lithuania but did not stay long — fighting had intensified around Bakhmut, where his uncle was serving at the time, and the young man left his studies. As soon as he turned 18, he signed a military contract.
“He … called me that evening, very happy, and said, ‘Sorry, Dad, I signed the contract. I forged your signature. Forgive me,’” recalled his father, Oleksandr Smyrnov, his voice shaking. He struggled to speak about his son, but embraced his daughter-in-law, saying he also found some comfort in the grandson soon to arrive.
Danyil Smyrnov went on to command an assault group in the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade. He was wounded by shrapnel in both legs and underwent rehabilitation, then returned to service, later transferring to Ukrainian military intelligence. Many knew him by his call sign, “Surfer” — from the age of 6, he had flown to visit his mother in Bali every summer, where he became a skilled surfer.
“Despite all the horrors of war, Dania managed to find his treasure — his girlfriend, and later his wife, Yeva,” read a passage from the eulogy at the monastery, as explosions echoed through the city. “Their relationship changed them both. They were both fighting for life, for a shared future.”
Now his wife is left alone, widowed at 21.
“He wanted all of us to be able to live in peace,” she said. “And in the end, he paid for that with his life.”
Smyrnov often wrote about the war on his Instagram, an account that holds mostly photos from his military life — himself in uniform, at different positions — with his most recent photos showing him with his wife, who is also pictured in military fatigues.
In an earlier post, written around his 20th birthday, he wrote: “In my 20 years, I’ve understood one thing: people don’t value life until they feel its edge. … War is not romance. It’s an experience that strips you down to what’s real,” the message said. “The choice is simple: who will you be — a victim, or someone who takes responsibility?”
