Israel’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, with the intention of sending them abroad.
Speaking in the run-up to close-fought Israeli elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of its population of roughly 2 million over the next six years.
“It’s realistic,” Ben-Gvir said, claiming there were countries that were “ready” to take in Palestinians from Gaza, without naming which ones.
While the forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, Israeli political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for Gaza, rebuffing efforts by the US president, Donald Trump, to advance a half-baked and largely moribund ceasefire deal that has been marked by continuing Israeli attacks.
Ben-Gvir said the far-right Jewish Power party would demand “a ministry in charge of emigration” during the formation of the next government, adding that his plan was “the result of a year and a half of work and … is concrete”.
The proposal is contained in a 20-page document with the euphemistic title of “National Work Plan for Voluntary Emigration from the Gaza Strip”.
Despite the use of the word “voluntary”, the plan will be seen as coercive by the international community because of the dire conditions imposed on Gaza’s population by Israel and because of Ben-Gvir’s explicit intention: to remove Gaza’s Palestinian population.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
Ben-Gvir’s comments follow hard on the heels of comments by Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the approval of the Trump administration to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he claimed was still under discussion after being “frozen” by Trump.
Katz, at a conference hosted by the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion.
Trump himself provoked international outrage at the beginning of his second term with a suggestion that all 2 million Palestinians leave Gaza and that the US redevelop the territory, a proposal he later walked back.
With elections in Israel in October, Ben-Gvir has made a series of inflammatory interventions aimed at his far-right base, including sharing footage from a site where Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks by Israeli military courts – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – are to be executed. In another video, he revelled in the mistreatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli custody.
Polling suggests that Jewish Power, the party led by Ben-Gvir – who has convictions for incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organisation, and who has been put under sanctions by various countries – would gain about seven seats.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part staged a visit to a military outpost in Gaza on Wednesday to insist that Israel would not withdraw from the areas of Gaza that it occupies.
“We are not withdrawing. We are staying on this line. We control 60% of the strip. And there is still more to come, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us – we do this day in and day out,” he said.
According to Israel’s deputy chief of general staff, Maj Gen Tamir Yadai, the country now controls 65% of Gaza. This is far beyond the 53% agreed under the ceasefire brokered last year by Trump.
As well as pushing for the expulsion of Gaza’s population, Ben-Gvir has called for the deportation of two MPs and others “who are disloyal to the state of Israel” – including Jews – saying he would promote such a policy if he is included in the next government.

US-based fintech company PayPal has handed the pink slip to about 220 of its employees based out of India as part of its global layoff exercise. Nearly 4% of its India workforce has been impacted by the exercise, a company spokesperson confirmed to Inc42. “The recent staffing changes are part of our previously announced multi-year transformation to simplify our global operations, strengthen execution, and position the company for long-term growth,” the spokesperson said. The layoffs likely impacted roles in tech, engineering, operations, payments and finance across the company’s offices in Chennai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. Moneycontrol, which reported the development first, said around 600 employees across PayPal’s India operations were impacted. Reported earlier this year, PayPal is said to be eyeing trimming its global workforce by about 20%, about 4,760 jobs, over multiple years. The overhaul is also intended to generate at least $1.5 Bn in savings. An impacted employee told the publication that employees were asked to join a call on August 31, where they were informed about the layoffs. Their access to company systems was revoked shortly after. The job cuts in India come as PayPal undertakes a broader organisational overhaul to simplify operations, lower costs and focus investment on areas it believes can deliver stronger long-term growth. The exercise is being rolled out in phases, beginning in the Asia-Pacific region, including India, before moving to the US, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, according to media reports. "We are simplifying our organisation and reducing our cost structure to increase investment for long-term growth. Over time, we will shift from stabilisation to targeted growth investment and accelerate our momentum with next-generation innovations," CEO Enrique Lores said earlier while disclosing PayPal's Q2 performance. Layoffs Becomes A Recurring Theme In The Tech Sector PayPal’s layoffs come amid a broader wave of job cuts across the technology and startup ecosystem. Multiple reports of mass layoffs undertaken by tech giants have surfaced within this week itself. While it was reported that tech giant Oracle could cut about 3,000 jobs in India earlier this week, Uber is axing 200-250 Indian jobs as part of a broader global restructuring that would see it cut 3,300 roles. The developments are not an isolated event within this week. Multiple mass firings have happened within this year. Earlier this year, Amazon announced 16,000 job cuts globally, while Meta downsized its metaverse division by around 1,500 employees as it shifted its focus towards AI. Atlassian, the parent company of Jira, also announced 1,600 job cuts, with India-based employees accounting for around 16% of the impacted workforce. In India, ecommerce enabler GoKwik laid off around 100-120 employees as part of a restructuring exercise, while Livspace cut around 1,000 jobs as part of an AI push. AI-focused healthcare technology company Innovaccer also reportedly reduced its workforce by around 350 employees, while IPO-bound Acko trimmed approximately 5% of its workforce as part of an AI-led restructuring.

I flossed fake teeth with Dyson's tech-riddled CameraJet toothbrush
No, I didn't share a $500 toothbrush at a trade show.
Dyson's biggest product announcement was its latest step into a new product category: a tech-loaded toothbrush and water flosser. The CameraJet doesn't sound like the name of something involved in oral hygiene, but here we are.
While I was hoping to test the toothbrush (and maintain my British teeth), a trade show, understandably, isn't the place for sharing a toothbrush with hundreds. For now, tech demos with fake teeth will have to suffice. It was very clear at the event that it was Dyson's new toothbrush was still the highlight of the show — although I want that giant air purifier in my tiny apartment, thank you)
After Dyson's big unveiling in just outside of IFA, it had all the robot vacuums, haircare devices and air purifiers assembled for media and industry to poke and prod, including the new CameraJet. In a chaotic demo area, I got a brief walkthrough on how to control what is definitively the most complicated toothbrush I've ever handled.
You can switch between brushing and flossing modes, or have both engaged at once. The device's "Gap Optical Targeting" system processes 28 images per second from the built-in camera, firing controlled jets of water at the gumline and crevices between teeth, so it doesn't use as much water as existing water flossers. I was wary that the water tank was so small on the CameraJet, but I was more than able to do at least two passes on Dyson's demo dentures without needing to refill. As a toothbrush, the CameraJet feels a little unwieldy compared to existing devices, but as a water flosser, it's frankly portable.
It also offered better insight into how the flossing function works and how much more advanced it is than my limescale-coated, battle-worn Waterpik at home. Aside from the reduced water volume (no more dribbling out of your mouth), it only triggers when the CameraJet detects gaps between teeth, so it won't start spraying the instant you turn it on. The demo units, however, managed to blast me in the eyes when I inadvertently switched the CameraJet to manual jetting. My mistake led to a minty shock to the face.
I also got to see the live feed in action, broadcasting from the tiny 100k-pixel camera to a nearby iPhone running Dyson's companion app. It looks like, well, a feed from a medical camera, but it's surprisingly clear when you consider all the movement, vibration and water involved. How will it fare with toothpaste (non-foaming or otherwise)? We'll have to see.
Some other concerns remain, like privacy issues. It's got a camera; it connects to the app; therefore, panic? I'm less concerned about that. Dyson has stressed several times that the video feed isn't processed anywhere beyond the stream on your smartphone. The feed remains entirely private to the user.
There is also, of course, a classic concern with Dyson: the price. The CameraJet is roughly a couple of hundred bucks above the most premium Philips Sonicare or Oral-B IO toothbrush, even if it is a water flosser too. Then there is the economics of replacement heads from Dyson, non-foaming toothpaste from Dyson and special mouthwash from Dyson, although other brands can be used for the latter two.
However, Dyson's attention to detail before the device has even shipped keeps me intrigued. The company has already barraged its YouTube channel with how-tos and deep-dives for all of the CameraJet's features, even including troubleshooting like how to factory reset the brush and how to put the brush into 'travel mode,' which stops the device from turning on in your baggage and draining the battery. Sadly, Dyson didn't hand me a sample to test that feature on my way back from Berlin.

Karnataka sets up DNA profiling centre for missing Nepal victims
Karnataka has named Bowring and Lady Curzon Hospital in Bengaluru as the nodal centre to collect DNA samples from first-degree relatives of people from the state reported missing in Nepal. The process is meant to help identify mortal remains and support their repatriation to families.
The Karnataka government has designated Bowring and Lady Curzon Hospital in Bengaluru as the nodal centre for collecting DNA samples from first-degree relatives of people from the state who have been reported missing in Nepal.
The move comes after the Embassy of India in Kathmandu issued a note regarding the identification and repatriation of mortal remains of foreign nationals.
According to an order issued by the Karnataka State Disaster Management Authority on September 4, Dr Nagesh Kuppast, Professor and Head of the Department of Forensic Medicine, has been appointed as the Nodal Officer.
Dr Kuppast will be responsible for verifying the relationship between relatives and missing persons, collecting DNA samples and coordinating their profiling and further processing.
First-degree relatives of those reported missing have been advised to approach the designated officers at Bowring and Lady Curzon Hospital.
They have been asked to carry a recent passport-size photograph, Aadhaar or another government-issued identity document, along with documents establishing their relationship with the missing person.
The DNA profiling process is aimed at assisting authorities in identifying mortal remains and facilitating their repatriation to the families.

Bartesian is the Keurig of cocktails. After trying several automatic cocktail makers on the market, it was the only cocktail maker I could see fitting into my normal routine. It works like any capsule-style device, but with booze. You fill the Bartesian’s glass bottles with your liquor of choice, make sure there’s water in the reservoir, plop in a cocktail capsule (these typically cost $2-3), choose your drink strength, press “mix,” and then a drink comes out. (If you’ve got kids, the Bartesian Professional version comes with a lock that will stymie curious fingers.)
Do you need a Bartesian to make cocktails? Of course you don’t. You can dump tequila into sour mix anytime and call it a margarita. But perhaps you’d like to make an espresso martini, a blackberry margarita, and also a Long Island Iced Tea? The Bartesian is a sort of shortcut to a home bar, without having to store all the mixers—and a bit of a novelty. It will be fun, and silly, and the drinks are kind of fine in a Spring Break way: strong and sweet and with sometimes fun flavors. Don’t expect sophistication. Expect a bit of a party trick, the sort of thing that makes a summer a little more fun.
You’ll, of course, want a Bartesian coupon to make that fun more accessible. Luckily, the current Bartesian discount codes are good for up to 35% off.
Save up to 35% With a Bartesian Cocktail Subscription
Standard pods on the Bartesian come in packs of 8, for $20 to $25. But if you know you plan to use the cocktail machine often—garden parties, art gallery openings, a really cool barber shop, an interesting home life, Friday afternoon margaritaville—the easiest way to save on the Bartesian pods is to sign up for a cocktail subscription. No Bartesian subscription discount codes are required. Subscription boxes always cost $20, so get the ones that’d be otherwise expensive for a 20% discount—then get additional tiered discounts of Bartesian depending on volume and frequency. If you order often or in large quatnities, this can add up to 35% off the regular price.
Save 15% (Or More) When You Purchase a Cocktail Bundle
I can’t tell you what to do. But at current discounts on Bartesian cocktail bundles and add-ons, only a sucker buys a Bartesian as a standalone item. If you flip to the Bartesian bundles page, you can find multiple bundles that offer glassware and cocktail variety packs for about the same price as the machine by itself. The Mom Bundle in particular costs less than the Bartesian Pro machine by itself, but includes 8 margarita capsules and two glasses. As of April 2026, Bartesian is also offering a Mother’s Day deal, offering $100 off the Bartesian Pro or the Bartesian Duet as long as you add a cocktail capsule pack to your order. Presumably, if you are buying the machine, you’ll want the cocktail capsules anyway.
Bartesian Rewards Club: Get More for Your Buck
Bartesian also has a loyalty program that they’re calling, alternately, the Bartesian Club, the Bartesian Rewards Club, or Bartesian Mixologist Rewards. US Vice President JD Vance has said the United States is investigating an airstrike that Iran says struck a wedding party in Iran, news agency Reuters reported "We're investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know," Vance told reporters during a White House press briefing on 3 September (Local Time). A US missile hit a home in Sirik of southern Iran where dozens were gathered to celebrate the wedding of a fisherman's daughter, according to a rights group and Iranian media as reported by news agency AP. "If we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran, when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them," Vance added. Iranian officials say four people died and nearly 70 were wounded by a strike that hit a home during a wedding. Iranian state TV reported on Thursday that a fifth person, a 22-year-old woman, had since died in hospital. The US military had earlier said it was aware of the Iranian reports but that it "never targets civilians". Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, was quoted by Al Jazeera saying that the “brutal” attack that hit the residence in the city of Kuhestak early on 2 September was a “war crime”. “The truth of this unlawful war of choice – and the true face of the war crime – is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America’s desperate struggle to conceal its failure,” Baghaei wrote on X. Videos shared by the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) showed a building with walls and windows blown out, and debris scattered on the ground. The rights group also published pictures of several children receiving treatment at a hospital. Baghaei also shared visuals. The IRCS sent a letter to the International Criminal Court calling for legal action following the US missile attack in southern Sirik. “Given the reported civilian character of the location as the venue of a family wedding ceremony, as well as the presence of civilians at the site, the incident raises serious concerns under international humanitarian law and warrants an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation,” the IRCS letter was quoted Al Jazeera. The injured were taken to a hospital in the nearby city of Minab and were “in stable condition”, Reza Shahidiyan, the governor of Sirik county, told the IRIB state broadcaster. Earlier, US Central Command (Centcom)spokesperson was quoted by BBC saying it "never targets civilians", adding that it was aware of the reports. Centcom spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins told the BBC it was aware of reports from Iranian state media of the attack in Sirik. “The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” he added. Centcom said strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks" by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against American forces and commercial shipping in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway, through which around 20% of global oil and gas shipments usually pass. Iranian authorities said another 14 people were killed elsewhere. In response, Iran launched missiles and drones at US targets in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Bahrain. Iranian media also reported explosions across the southern provinces of Hormozgan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Kerman and Khuzestan. Anthony Joshua's driver attempted overtake before fatal crash, trial hears
- Published
The driver of a car carrying Anthony Joshua was attempting to overtake another vehicle when it crashed, killing two of the boxer's friends, a court in Nigeria has heard.
Adeniyi Mobolaji Kayode, 46, faces charges including causing death by dangerous driving and driving without a valid national driver's licence. He denies the charges.
The court was told that the group - who had been travelling to visit Joshua's father in Ogun State, near Lagos in Nigeria, last December - were asleep when Kayode lost control of his Lexus SUV while he overtook a moving truck and collided with a parked lorry.
Joshua's personal trainer, Latif Ayodele, and strength coach, Sina Ghami, died in the crash.

  - Published16 January
A second defendant Abubakar Adamu, 35, the driver of the stationary lorry the car collided with, denies a charge against him of obstructing the free flow of traffic.
Inspector Christopher Ajayi Taiwo of the Ogun State Motor Traffic Division told the court that by the time he arrived at the scene, both the damaged Lexus and the stationary lorry had been removed.
But debris from the crash and soya beans scattered on the road from the lorry's load were found by officers, he added.
The only items recovered from the Lexus were a logbook, painkillers and an energy drink, which were found near the driver's side, Ajayi said.
The court heard police has yet to take a statement from Joshua following the crash.
During cross-examination, Kayode's lawyer questioned Ajayi over the lack of statement, to which he replied that "efforts are ongoing" and that he had not contacted Joshua because he "didn't have his number".
The trial was adjourned until 10 September.
Joshua, who was born in Watford, has family roots in Sagamu - a town in Ogun state, near the crash site.

Dozens missing, 5 dead after migrant boat is found drifting near Spanish islands
At least five people have died after a boat carrying West African migrants ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean
BARCELONA, Spain -- At least five people died and dozens more were feared dead after a boat carrying West African migrants ran into trouble in the Atlantic Ocean. Forty-four people were brought to safety in the Canary Islands.
Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said Thursday that one of its planes had spotted a “precarious” boat drifting some 120 km (74 miles) south of the island of Gran Canaria on Wednesday afternoon.
Three survivors were immediately evacuated by helicopter to a hospital on the island. The remaining 41 migrants were brought to safety by boat and disembarked early Thursday in the port of Arguineguín, where they were cared for by the Red Cross. All survivors were men, some underage, and came from Mali or Senegal, said José Antonio Rodríguez Verona, a spokesperson for the Red Cross in the Canaries.
In a phone interview with The Associated Press, Rodríguez Verona said survivors were disoriented and dehydrated, with many collapsing or vomiting upon reaching land. While it was difficult to get precise information given their fragile state of health, migrants reported leaving Gambia and being stranded at sea for “many, many days.” Some estimated they had been at sea for nearly a month. Running out of provisions, they fell ill from drinking seawater.
Survivors also told the Red Cross that more than 100 people were originally on board, including women and a baby. As people died on the journey, their bodies were tossed in the ocean until they had no more strength to do so.
In an emailed statement, Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said that it was not able to retrieve the remains of the five dead found inside the boat due to strong winds and waves that were 2.5 metres (8 feet) high.
Separately, Helena Maleno, founder of the migrant rights group Walking Borders, which monitors deaths and disappearances on migration routes to Spain, reported that 83 people had died on the voyage, including three women and a baby. In a post on X, Maleno said the boat had departed Gambia 27 days ago.
Maleno and her NGO are frequently contacted by relatives of missing migrants and often relay calls for help and rescue to Spanish authorities. The AP reached out to Maleno and Walking Borders seeking further details but has not yet received a response.
The West African Atlantic route to Spain’s Canary Islands is one of the deadliest crossings to Europe. While arrivals to the Spanish archipelago have fallen significantly in the past year, tens of thousands of people have died or gone missing in recent years, with several migrant boats getting lost and drifting all the way across the Atlantic to the Americas.

Kathmandu, Sep 04: Around 600 children remain unaccounted for in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts after the devastating flash floods, as the death toll rose to 1,282 on Friday with more than 4,700 missing.
The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal, leaving a trail of destruction.
So far, 359 bodies have been recovered in Chitwan, 218 in Nawalparasi East, 208 in Nawalparasi West, 185 in Nuwakot, 72 in Gorkha, 60 in Dhading, 140 in Rasuwa and 38 in Tanahu, according to Nepal Police.
With two people dying while undergoing treatment in two hospitals in Kathmandu, the death toll has reached 1,282.
The joint command of security forces is searching for 4,798 people missing from different areas.
An estimated 280 children are missing in Rasuwa, and between 300 and 350 others remain unaccounted for in the neighbouring Nuwakot in central Nepal, the Kathmandu Post newspaper reported, citing figures compiled by local Education Development and Coordination Units (EDCUs), local governments, and educational institutions.
Surya Bahadur Khatri, head of the Nuwakot Education Development and Coordination Unit, said, “We are actively liaising with headmasters to collect verified data on missing students, though school heads are struggling to provide exact figures due to broken communications.”
“Although a few missing students have been located, new reports of unaccounted-for children continue to arrive from various schools. We estimate that at least 300 pupils are missing in our district.”
In Bidur Municipality of Nuwakot alone, roughly 250 children are missing since the floods hit, according to Navaraj Sapkota, school inspector of the municipality's education unit.
“The situation on the ground is deeply distressing. In some cases, we have located surviving parents who cannot find their children, while in other instances, surviving students are searching for missing parents,” said Sapkota.
Bidur houses 170 educational institutions—142 community schools and 28 private schools.
In Rasuwa, Durga Prasad Silwal, chief of the local education unit, said that official verification is ongoing but preliminary records indicate that 280 students are currently missing across the district.
The disaster has also taken a toll on teachers and school staff. Education units confirmed that 22 teachers and school staff members remain missing across both districts.
Additionally, several teachers from Dhading and Gorkha who had travelled to Rasuwa for pilgrimage were caught in the deluge and remain missing.
Rasuwa reported 16 missing teachers—15 from community schools and one from a private institution—while Nuwakot confirmed six missing teachers, according to Kathmandu Post.
Although several bodies of victims have been recovered in downstream districts, authorities have yet to verify the exact number of identified students or teachers.
According to the Ministry of Education data, the floods affected 22 schools across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, with 12 institutions completely destroyed, the report said.

The 2026 Kailash Manasarovar Yatra has officially ended with all Indian pilgrims having left Chinese territory bordering Nepal, following the flash floods in the Bhote Koshi River on August 26, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Friday (September 4, 2026).
MEA official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed that 275 Indian nationals remain missing till now and 169 Indians have been rescued. He further indicated that the total number of missing persons may fluctuate a bit in the days to come as some survivors are still being discovered in various areas of the vast stretch of the disaster-hit region.
The Kailash Manasarovar Yatra 2026 was announced by the MEA on April 30 and the pilgrimage was to take place between June to August. This year 10 batches, each consisting of 50 pilgrims and travellers, were scheduled to travel through Lipulekh pass and Nathu La pass.
Apart from the Government of India-assisted tour of Mt. Kailash, travellers who chose private travel agencies used the Nepali route through Gyirong border crossing of China. On August 26, significant number of pilgrims and travellers went missing from the Gyirong border port, which was hit by the flash floods.
Official sources said that with the evacuation of the private Indian travellers, all Indians have left the Tibetan region bordering Nepal that hosts travellers during the season when Chinese authorities allow the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra. During the Chinese official season for tour of Kailash, some international travellers also travel to the mountain through major Chinese cities like Beijing and Shanghai.

The proposal to link the Godavari and Cauvery rivers faces complex political and legal hurdles among southern states. Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has advocated linking the Godavari with the Cauvery by tapping surplus river water flowing into the Bay of Bengal and diverting it to drought-prone regions, proposing a route starting at Polavaram and seeking national project status. Under the Central government's National River Linking Project blueprint, the route begins at Inchampally in Telangana and passes through Nagarjuna Sagar and Somasila before reaching the Grand Anicut in Tamil Nadu. However, interstate disagreements persist. Telangana questions how surplus water is calculated, raising concerns over downstream diversions impacting its needs. Karnataka insists any extra Cauvery inflows cannot solely benefit Tamil Nadu and demands its own share be protected. Tamil Nadu seeks additional water without compromising existing river entitlements. Upstream states including Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Maharashtra also hold stakes, leaving a consensus among stakeholders elusive.

100 influencers invited to US Open spark debate on 'tennis etiquette'
- Published
Lights. Camera. Quiet please...
When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.
Apologising after winning a point from a net cord. Honesty around line calls, double bounces and double-hits. Post-match handshakes.
As for the spectators, it is common courtesy not to disturb the players during points.
Around 100 influencers and content creators have been granted accreditation for the tournament in New York - double the amount from last year.
Their presence has led to debate over how to balance bringing tennis to a new, different audience while respecting the game's etiquette.
"I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," world number four Coco Gauff said.
"But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans.
"I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."
During two-time champion Naomi Osaka's first-round match on Arthur Ashe Stadium, one group held a photo shoot in their hospitality suite while play was going on.
The group turned on a portable ring light while Osaka was serving, leading to a reprimand from the umpire.
When Osaka returned on Thursday, the umpire had to remind the crowd several times to be quiet.
"Today the umpire told everyone to be quiet more than I've ever heard an umpire tell a crowd to be quiet," Osaka said.
"I tell people I normally just focus on the match and the court, but there was a moment where there was people shouting and you could hear it quite clearly.
"I think it bothered my opponent, too."
In one video, which has gone viral, a group can be seen speaking loudly as they film themselves during Osaka's first-round match on Tuesday, which led to the chair umpire calling for them to stop.
"I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport," Osaka said.
"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette.
"It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like my first-round match.
"Overall, I think there are huge positives. You want people to continue to grow the sport.
"I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."
- No Britons left in US Open singles as Dart & Jones lose 
  - Published7 hours ago
'More upside than downside' or 'a little too much'?
Arthur Ashe is the biggest tennis stadium in the world, and matches are often accompanied by a buzz of noise from conversations around the arena.
Some players love it. Some do not.
Men's seventh seed Daniil Medvedev, who has had a tricky relationship with the New York crowds in the past, believes whatever brings more eyes to tennis can only be a good thing.
"I think the more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is," the Russian said.
"The more the sport grows, the better it is. I trust USTA [tournament organisers the United States Tennis Association] with what they are doing.
"I think [there is] a lot more upside than downside, so go for it."
American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe praised the diversity of the crowd in New York.
"I think the Open is great because you get all types of people that want to come and watch tennis," he said.
"All different walks of life, different types of people, different type of occupations. Personally, I love that.
"I have no problem with anybody doing anything, coming to watch the tennis."
American world number three Jessica Pegula, however, said some of the behaviour had been "disrespectful".
"I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said.
"But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.
"People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful.
"I think it's become a little too much this year.
"I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."
The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning fans no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.
A year later, the tournament was expanded to 15 days. The week before the singles draw is now marketed as a 'Fan Week', showcasing the revamped mixed doubles competition and exhibition matches between players past and present.
It is all part of what tournament chief executive Craig Tiley hopes will become "the tennis Disneyland".
Tiley, asked about influencers being accredited in a pre-tournament news conference, said: "We need to find ways of reaching new audiences, reaching people in a way that they connect with media today.
"The creation of the creator credential has been a key part of that because it's enabled us to talk to people in a way that they're listening. That's been a big focus."
Since the incident in Osaka's first match, there has been increased messaging on screens around the ground reminding people to "refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights".
The USTA said in a statement it "is always striving to grow tennis in this country and bring new audiences into the sport".
"We want all of our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend, but we also need to ensure they do not interfere with the action and competition on the court," it added.
"We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited."

OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Astra, its latest frontier model, in a bid to push into AI systems that can use computers and execute tasks more autonomously. OpenAI says that GPT-6 Astra is its most capable model yet. The model supports reasoning efforts ranging from low to maximum and comes with a 1.05 Mn-token context window and a maximum output of 1.28 Lakh tokens. As per the ChatGPT parent, Astra can autonomously navigate websites, interact with software, work with documents and spreadsheets, write and test code, and handle other multi-step workflows. The model is pitched as a significant upgrade for AI interface. "Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helped solve long-standing open problems in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment," the company said. Initially, GPT‑6 Astra will be rolled out to a limited set of organisations and will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, soon. GPT-6 Astra has an April 30, 2026 knowledge cutoff and supports tools including web search, file search, computer use, code execution and image generation. It is priced at $10 per Mn input tokens and $50 per Mn output tokens, with discounted cached-input pricing of $1 per Mn tokens. The company also doubles down on agentic AI with its new model, a segment where it is competing with companies including Anthropic and Google. Instead of requiring users to break down a task into a series of prompts, these systems are designed to perform several steps on their own. OpenAI claimed state-of-the-art results for Astra on benchmarks including Agents’ Last Exam, AutomationBench and ScreenSpot Pro, which measure an AI model’s ability to handle computer-based workflows. “We believe it is the best model in the world for computer use, professional work, science, coding, cybersecurity, and more,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a social media post on X. GPT-6 Astra Steps Up Coding, Science Capabilities ChatGPT parent has also positioned GPT-6 Astra as its strongest model yet for software engineering. There is a rapid growth in modifying AI to perform coding tasks with less to no human intervention, where models like Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3 Pro, Grok Build and Cursor agents have been operating well in recent times. In Codex, OpenAI has introduced a new mechanism that allows Astra to preserve and retrieve information across context windows instead of relying solely on compressed summaries. Beyond coding, Astra has been trained for scientific and mathematical applications. Cybersecurity is another key area of focus for the new model. OpenAI claimed that GPT-6 Astra has reached the "critical" level of cybersecurity capability under its preparedness framework, making it the company's first model to cross this threshold. The launch comes as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and other AI players race to develop increasingly capable AI agents that can move beyond generating text and instead execute tasks on behalf of users. Last year, OpenAI rolled out GPT-5 for users of ChatGPT as well as enterprises leveraging its APIs for artificial intelligence (AI) products, with enhanced features across coding, math, writing, health, visual perception, and others.

A summer of hostilities in the Black Sea proved deadly for seafarers, as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other’s ships and port infrastructure, preventing vital grain exports and prompting concerns that the conflict will push global food prices even higher.
More crew were killed in the Black Sea in July than during the entirety of the war before that month as the conflict has intensified, making the body of water the most dangerous in the world for commercial shipping. This is despite the conflict between the US and Iran, with vessels still being targeted in the strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
As many as 23 people died in July as a result of attacks on 35 ships in the Black Sea, according to estimates from the Turkish seafarers’ union Türkiye Denizciler Sendikası.
Attacks on vessels continued into August and escalation in the Ukraine war has prompted the head of the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization, to condemn the “deterioration of maritime security around the globe”.
Russia first launched waves of attacks on port infrastructure and vessels anchored in Ukrainian Black Sea ports in the months after its invasion in 2022, preventing Kyiv from exporting grain. In July, Russia again struck Ukraine’s main grain export hubs of Odesa and Chornomorsk.
However, the recent escalation in the Black Sea and neighbouring Sea of Azov – connected by the Kerch strait – has also resulted from Ukrainian retaliatory attacks. Drones have hit Russian vessels, including tankers Kyiv says belong to a shadow fleet of hundreds of ships used by Russia to evade sanctions on its oil exports. Ukraine has targeted ships and port buildings at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, vital for oil and grain exports.
In a grim illustration of the danger to vessels and their crew, an abandoned Russian-flagged cargo ship – with a burned-out command deck – recently ran aground on Turkey’s Black Sea coast as startled holidaymakers looked on.
The Omskiy-107’s crew abandoned ship after it was hit by a Ukrainian drone near Novorossiysk, leaving the unmanned vessel to drift hundreds of miles and end up close to the Bosphorus, the narrow strait straddled by Istanbul that is one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes.
Shipping in the region is under increased threat, according to analysts at the maritime risk intelligence firm Vanguard. “Merchant vessels are now more likely to be affected because of the ports they visit, their trading activity and the cargoes they carry. Attacks have also extended beyond ports and their immediate approaches, increasing the risk to vessels across a wider area of the Black Sea,” they said.
The precarious maritime situation has already significantly reduced Russian and Ukrainian grain exports, raising concerns the disruption will worsen the impact of other food price shocks and hurt countries reliant on imported wheat, barley and maize.
Russia is the world’s largest grain exporter, with its produce mostly going to the Middle East and north Africa, particularly Turkey and Egypt, while Ukraine is the fifth-largest.
In July, Russia suspended shipping in the Sea of Azov after a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks, before deciding to redirect some grain exports to alternative routes such as via the Caspian and Baltic seas and the Pacific. However, more than 70% of Russia’s seaborne grain exports are shipped from Black Sea ports, and a further 20% from the Sea of Azov, according to analysis from Oxford Economics.
“I have seen estimates that Russian grain exports were down to 40% of normal export capacity in August,” said Tatiana Orlova, the lead emerging markets economist at Oxford Economics.
Ukraine, which had a bumper and early grain harvest this year, has also found itself unable to export large volumes through its Black Sea ports. Kyiv exported only a third – about 1.4m tonnes – of the grain it could have exported, using sea, rail, river and road, according to recent comments from Ukraine’s food minister.
Global wheat prices have been trading higher in recent weeks, but remain below levels at the beginning of the Ukraine war in 2022.
However, analysts say the latest disruption to seaborne grain exports is likely to push prices higher and exacerbate other food supply shocks, including the Iran war and lower European grain yields after extreme summer heat and the rapidly developing El Niño weather system.
Global food prices are forecast by Oxford Economics to rise by nearly 12% this year and a further 4.8% in 2027.
Unlike in 2022, when many big food importing countries were caught napping by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, “a lot of countries have grain stocks, which should help, so there is better preparedness for this kind of shock”, said Orlova. “But it is pretty clear the food price is going to be affected.”

For decades, India’s relationship with West Asia operated under a doctrine of deliberate ambiguity and even of some strategic distance. Delhi treated the “Middle East” primarily as an economic hinterland: a critical source of crude oil, a reliable destination for outbound labour, and a vital conduit for remittances. When regional crises flared, Indian foreign policy defaulted to hedging, balancing relations between competing power centres such as Riyadh, Tehran, Tel Aviv, and Abu Dhabi without tying itself to the security obligations of any single capital. Of late, we called that approach “multi-alignment”.
What worked until now
But while India was careful to be friendly to all, it was not too friendly to any, in an effort not to offend any of the various capitals in the mix. The logic was clear: there was much to be gained from all parties in what was widely seen to be a likely West Asian economic renaissance. The region was seen through a macroeconomic vision that highlighted its convenient geographic features, its immense natural resources of oil and gas, massive capital accumulation, and its receptivity to imported labour and skills, of which India has a surplus. In this framing, the global economic centre of gravity was seen as inexorably shifting away from an aging, debt-burdened West toward a highly dynamic Asia, positioning West Asia as the ultimate maritime and terrestrial bridge between a declining West and a rising East.
This defensive and essentially transactional posture served India well in an era when the United States stood as the undisputed guarantor of West Asian security, keeping sea lines of communication open and maintaining regional stability. However, the geopolitical bedrock of West Asia is undergoing a violent structural shift. As Washington recalibrates its global commitments and retreats into an unpredictable “selective engagement” posture, a profound security vacuum has emerged, sparking a scramble among regional states for durable security guarantees. Here, has India been caught napping, continuing a business-as-usual approach that risks early obsolescence?
West Asian capitals no longer view distancing, whether called non-alignment or multi-alignment, as a virtue. They are actively seeking alternative, dependable security partners who can offer more than diplomatic platitudes and routine economic cooperation. This structural reality was highlighted by the signing of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, bringing together Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan into a collective defence arrangement. While framed as a defensive effort to manage shared vulnerabilities, the pact signals a broader security realignment. By linking Gulf capital with Turkish defence technology and Pakistani military manpower and skill, the agreement creates a powerful new security architecture right at India’s western maritime doorstep.
A clear signal of change
For New Delhi, the Mecca Agreement is not an isolated diplomatic transaction; it is a clear structural signal that West Asia’s security framework is being fundamentally rewritten, often by actors whose strategic interests directly run counter to India’s own long-term objectives. While India’s strategic silence on this development is understandable, it still begs the question: what next? The growing influence of external powers and hostile regional pacts directly threatens India’s trade routes, energy security, and the welfare of millions of Indian citizens living in the Gulf. Is India going to build its own partnerships, or become irrelevant to the region’s security?
If India continues to rely on legacy diplomatic processes and transactional commerce, it risks being marginalised in a region essential to its national survival. The challenges are formidable. The eruption of hostilities involving Iran demonstrated that modern, highly integrated economic infrastructure remains profoundly fragile when subjected to grey-zone, asymmetric warfare. State-of-the-art port facilities, energy networks, and logistics corridors proved highly vulnerable to low-cost drones, showing that capital-intensive infrastructure cannot fully compensate for localised security vacuums. Hyper-secure economic enclaves will remain perpetually exposed to the spillover effects of surrounding instability in the region. Since the modern Gulf model relies heavily on foreign corporations and expatriate labour, regional stability is intimately tied to global perception. If security risks cross a certain psychological threshold, the talent and capital that flowed in seamlessly can exit just as rapidly. And when narrow naval chokepoints or overland trade routes face active disruption, global supply chains inevitably stall, revealing that these ambitious trade corridors are only as strong as their most unstable geographic link.
Against this critical background, the assumption that trade ties and diaspora diplomacy alone can preserve Indian influence is rapidly unravelling. A region grappling with maritime threats in the Red Sea, drone strikes on critical infrastructure, involvement in conflicts in Iran, Yemen, Sudan, the Strait of Hormuz and now the Bab el-Mandab, requires partners capable of providing tangible security assets. West Asian powers are hungry for hard-power options such as naval patrols, intelligence sharing, defence-industrial collaboration, and credible counter-terrorism capabilities. If India Delhi-dallies over stepping into such a role, others will fill the void, as Türkiye has already demonstrated in Mecca.
The hard moves India must make
To protect its strategic space, New Delhi must contemplate a decisive doctrine change, evolving from a passive beneficiary of regional stability into an active guarantor of it. This requires moving beyond high-level bilateral visits and economic summits to actively project hard power into the western Indian Ocean and the broader West Asian region. India’s immediate focus must be the rapid expansion of naval and maritime security partnerships across key choke points, including the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf of Aden, the waters off the Somali coast and the Bab-el-Mandeb. By embedding its naval footprint more deeply through joint maritime patrols, permanent logistics access arrangements, and interoperable surveillance networks with friendly Gulf states, India can establish itself as a, if not the, premier net security provider in its immediate neighbourhood.
Furthermore, India must leverage its growing defence manufacturing ecosystem to offer West Asian states a reliable alternative for hardware and technology. Collaborative defence ventures, joint military exercises with real operational teeth, and deep intelligence-sharing mechanisms must replace mere procurement discussions. Developing robust bilateral and “minilateral” security frameworks with partners such as the United Arab Emirates or Israel, and separately even with Saudi Arabia, will allow Delhi to build a counterweight against hostile axes without succumbing to rigid Cold-War style alliances. The goal is not to entangle India in foreign quagmires, but to build a strategic deterrence web that safeguards Indian interests and reassures regional allies.
The era of passive presence in West Asia has reached its natural end. The Mecca Agreement serves as a stark reminder that regional security arrangements will coalesce with or without Indian participation. If Delhi wishes to secure its economic destiny, safeguard its energy arteries, and claim its rightful place as a leading global power, it must act with urgency and ambition. Moving decisively beyond routine diplomatic engagement to construct real, hard-power security partnerships in West Asia is no longer just a strategic choice for India. It is an imperative for its national security.
Shashi Tharoor is a fourth-term Member of Parliament (Congress) for Thiruvananthapuram, who served nearly three decades at the United Nations, where he rose to the position of Under Secretary-General. He has also been a Minister of State for External Affairs in the Government of India and is the bestselling author, of 29 books, including Pax Indica: India and the World of the 21st century. He currently chairs the Parliamentary Standing Committee on External Affairs

Abdul El-Sayed is trying to win over undecided Jewish voters in Michigan — without compromising his substantive positions on Israel or disavowing his most radical allies.
The Jewish Democrats trying to get to “yes” on Abdul El-Sayed
A Democratic fundraiser on how the candidate’s charm offensive is going.
During both his primary and general election campaigns, El-Sayed’s opponents have portrayed him as insensitive to Jewish concerns, if not outright antisemitic. These charges have often rested on falsely equating El-Sayed’s opposition to Zionism (he is not committed to Israel’s existence as a majority Jewish state) with a hostility for Jewish people.
But in recent weeks, two other concerns came to the forefront. One was El-Sayed’s response to an antisemitic attack on a Michigan synagogue. In March, a 41-year-old named Ayman Mohamed Ghazali drove a truck into Temple Israel’s Jewish preschool. Days later, El-Sayed condemned the attack, while also noting that Ghazali had recently lost family members to an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon. El-Sayed suggested that these events illustrated how “hurt people hurt people” and that “violence is a cycle,” one that had led Ghazali to perpetrate “an evil act of displaced rage.”
Separately, El-Sayed had campaigned with the far-left streamer Hasan Piker during his primary campaign. This had always sat poorly with many Jewish and centrist Democrats in Michigan. But Piker made his association with the Democratic Senate candidate more conspicuous in late August. During a broadcast, Piker lambasted Jeremy Moss, a pro-Israel Jewish Democrat running for Congress in Michigan who had not endorsed El-Sayed but was in active conversations with the candidate about how to bridge lingering divides with Jewish voters. More explosively, Piker said, among other things, that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually somebody is going to come around and take action, not against the State of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” He subsequently insisted he was merely spotlighting the hazards of portraying all Jews as ardent Israel supporters, not making some kind of veiled threat, as his detractors alleged.
Nonetheless, this triggered a new round of calls for El-Sayed to both disavow Piker, and to take other measures to reassure Michigan Jews that he cares about their safety.
These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally.
El-Sayed declined to disown the streamer. But he did defend the right of all Americans “to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” saying this was “particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.”
Some Jewish Democrats found this insufficient. In an open letter Wednesday, 400 Democratic Jewish Michiganders — including donor Rob Orley — announced that they would be supporting Republican Mike Rogers in their state’s Senate race.
Days earlier, El-Sayed had sought to mend fences with such voters at a summit held by the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus. During his appearance there, he apologized for his remarks following the Temple Israel attack, saying “I should have issued a statement, of course condemning it, and it just should have been the full stop.”
Among those in attendance was Charles Gaba, a healthcare analyst and major Democratic fundraiser; Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow has called him “the biggest powerhouse democratic donor wrangler that nobody has ever heard of.”
Gaba was a strong supporter of Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. And he has expressed serious reservations about El-Sayed, even while committing to voting for him and raising money for his candidacy.
These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally: over how far Democrats can and should go in criticizing Israel, whether the left takes antisemitism seriously, and if centrists are using allegations of anti-Jewish bigotry to stigmatize legitimate dissent.
To explore these debates — and clarify the concerns of “Sayed-skeptical” Jews in Michigan — I spoke with Gaba this week.
Our conversation has been edited for clarity and concision.
From your vantage point, what are undecided Jewish Michiganders’ biggest reservations about El-Sayed — and how many are actually addressable by his campaign?
I’d say that there’s probably four main ones. Two are connected to his comments about the Temple Israel attack. And he definitely addressed one of those complaints with his statement: that it was awfully timed. In other words, that days after the attack was not a good moment to raise other issues instead of simply condemning the violence full stop.
But the larger issue to me — and to a lot of other folks I’ve spoken with — is he seemed to be under the impression that timing was the only problem. That it was just too soon and if he’d waited a month and then made the exact same comments about “context,” that would have been fine. He doesn’t seem to get that trying to put it in context at all is the larger problem. Because a bunch of preschoolers at a synagogue in Michigan have absolutely nothing to do with a military conflict overseas, just nothing. If a family member of someone who died in the September 11th attacks had gone and attempted to kill Muslim children, their loss wouldn’t be relevant context. You couldn’t say, “Oh well, but he was upset about that attack.”
I think an El-Sayed supporter might say: There’s a difference between explaining an abominable act and excusing it. In his original statement, El-Sayed did say explicitly that “there is never a justification for attacking innocent people or houses of worship” and described the violence as “heinous” and “evil.” Taken literally, he was arguing that the strike that had killed Ghazali’s family members led to his act of antisemitic terrorism, even as nothing could possibly justify it.
There was just no reason to try to put it in context at all. Pretty much everyone understands that the Israel-Hamas war has brought emotions to a fever pitch for a lot of people.
I don’t think we needed someone to say, “Hey, that whole mess in the Mideast might have inspired this!” Yeah, no shit. Who was the audience for this? Who was he trying to give context to? Certainly the Jewish community understands the situation. I think the Muslim community understands the situation. And so does everyone else. I don’t think it served any purpose other than to upset and offend a bunch of people. So he was lecturing to no one essentially, in my view. Which I get; I have a tendency to do that myself sometimes in other ways. But it isn’t helpful. And shifting the timing wouldn’t have made it helpful.
So, what are the other two big sticking points for Jewish Democrats not sold on El-Sayed?
The third is this Hasan Piker guy. The media certainly seems to be pretty focused on that. If memory serves, El-Sayed seemed to be trailing Mallory McMorrow and Haley Stevens in the primaries up until around March. And then it was announced that he was going to be rallying with Piker at Michigan State and the University of Michigan.
A combination of that and the reaction to it — namely the McMorrow campaign heavily criticizing him for the rally — generated a bunch of attention and certainly raised Abdul’s profile tremendously. I don’t know how much credit to give Piker, but it made some difference. And next thing you know, he’s kind of running in the lead.
So, it’s pretty clear that Piker was brought in specifically to help him win the primary with a very young, progressive crowd. To that effect, it worked. But that doesn’t mean he’s helpful for winning a general election.
So, why do you think El-Sayed refuses to distance himself more explicitly from Piker, if the influencer’s support is not helpful in the general election?
I don’t know. Maybe he thinks that he’s being noble or something by not throwing him under the bus. But the guy just seems to be kind of an asshole, and I would not want to be associated with him in either the primary or the general. And so associating himself with Hasan Piker makes me think less of Abdul.
And I have a lot of respect for Abdul. I’ve met him about a half-dozen times or so, back when he ran for governor and then several times during this campaign. And we’ve also been in contact a few times in between to discuss healthcare policy. And I know he’s a very intelligent guy, very thoughtful guy, and very passionate about universal healthcare. I respect him for all of that. But I think less of him for associating with Piker. And I think a lot of Jewish Michiganders feel that way.
So, what’s the fourth issue?
Well, this is not so much about Abdul specifically as it is about the left. A lot of progressives get that you should condemn antisemitism, or bigotry against the Jewish religion. But many don’t seem to grasp that Judaism is not just a religion; it is also a people. And we do have a several thousand-year connection with the land of Israel — not the leadership, not the current government — but with the land itself. And so that makes the distinction between antisemitism and anti-Zionism complicated. You know, to try to say, “Well, as long as you give up Israel, then Judaism is fine” — many of us can’t do that because it’s an intrinsic part of who we are.
Is there not a distinction between recognizing Jews’ historical and religious connection to Israel — and being committed to the maintenance of a majority Jewish state in the Middle East?
In other words, there are anti-Zionists who deny Jews’ roots in Israel — or the right of Jewish Israelis to live in the region. But I think most progressive anti-Zionists would dispute neither of those things. Rather, they’d argue that Israeli Jews have a right to live in their land — but that maintaining a majority Jewish Israel should not take precedence over allowing Palestinian refugees and their descendants to return to their ancestral territories.
It’s definitely true that there’s more than one type of anti-Zionism. I think there’s several groupings and different shades between them. And that also holds true on the Zionist side. There are right-wing extremists like [Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar] Ben-Gvir who say, “We should annex both the West Bank and Gaza.” And then there’s others that go even more extreme and say that Israel should dominate the entire region, including Lebanon and Egypt.
And then, at the other end, there’s Hamas and other extremists who literally want to either kick out or slaughter every Jew in the region.
And those extremes have led people to think that Zionism means “Jews get to take over the region” and that anti-Zionism means “Jews have to be kicked out.”
I think for most people, it’s somewhere in between. I’ve started calling myself a “small-z Zionist,” which is basically a more mainstream, two-state solution type. I don’t know how feasible that solution is. There’s only a slim chance these days. But the odds of a two-state solution are still better than those of creating a single “kumbaya, let’s all live together in peace” nation, in my view.
How were El-Sayed’s remarks to Michigan’s Jewish Caucus received, from your vantage point?
They were better received than I expected, to be honest. Although, I suspect that those most opposed to him probably didn’t show up at the event at all, since they’ve made up their minds.
Having said that, I did have discussions with several people afterwards, and there was definitely still concern about the whole “context” thing. People were polite and it was a reasonably warm reception. And to his credit, he did stick around afterwards and had one-on-one personal conversations. He was there for quite a while, so I give him credit for that.
From a purely electoral perspective, how much does El-Sayed actually have to lose, if he fails to consolidate the Jewish vote? In demographic terms, the bloc of Jewish voters who are open to voting for El-Sayed — but still need to be persuaded — would seem to be tiny. After all, we’re talking about a small minority of small minority; Jews account for only about 1.4 percent of Michigan’s electorate. So, what’s at stake here politically?
In terms of activism, organizing, and donations, the Jewish community punches far above our weight.
But yeah, we’re a fraction of a fraction. I think the biggest thing is just reassuring moderate Democratic voters in general. Basically, if the headlines start to read, “Jewish leaders seem reassured by Abdul apology,” then some non-Jewish folks — who aren’t sure about El-Sayed — might say, “Oh, well, if the Jews signed off on this guy, I guess he’s okay.”

U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday (September 4, 2026) said the conflict in Iran is “small potatoes” as he defended Vice President JD Vance for asserting that months of on-and-off attacks in West Asia are not a “war.”
Asked during an Oval Office exchange about Mr. Vance's comments made a day earlier, Mr. Trump noted that U.S. strikes on Iran are now “intermittent” and seemed to downplay the intensity of a war that's cost U.S. taxpayers more than $37.5 billion and left 18 U.S. service members dead.
“I can understand what he's saying,” said Mr. Trump. He added, “I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing." Mr. Vance on Thursday (September 3), during a White House press briefing, rejected the use of the word “war” to describe the US fighting with Iran and steered clear of predicting that the 6-month-old conflict would be over by November's midterm elections, in which Republicans are trying to hang on to their narrow majorities in Congress.
“I wouldn't call it a war,” Mr. Vance said after being asked during a White House press briefing about whether the fighting could end before voters cast their ballots in the November 3 congressional elections. “Right now, there is no active shooting.” Vance's assertion came even as Iran fired at U.S. Gulf ally Kuwait on Thursday in retaliation for rounds of US strikes on Iran earlier in the week.
Mr. Trump, in Friday's exchange with reporters, added that the US death toll in the Iran conflict is relatively lower than in some other recent U.S. wars. The U.S., along with Israel, have only carried out air strikes in the Iran war, which began on February 28, and has not deployed troops into the country.
“We did Venezuela and we did this. In Venezuela, we lost nobody,” said Trump, referring to the January US military operation to seize former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and spirit him to New York City to face federal drug trafficking charges.
“And this, we lost 18 people. And, in Vietnam we lost 100,000 people. And in other conflicts, we lost tens of thousands of people.” A total of 58,220 members of the US armed forces died during the Vietnam War, according to records from the U.S. National Archives.
Pressed by a reporter on describing the conflict as “small potatoes" when 18 U.S. service members have been killed, Trump responded by reiterating his argument that the conflict—one that he said at the outset of the war would last a matter of weeks—has led to the defanging of Iran's nuclear program.
“Iran will not have a nuclear weapon because if they did you probably wouldn't be standing here,” Mr. Trump said.

A common cause given for leg pain is muscle strain, and this may be attributed to standing for a long time, exercising incorrectly, or getting older. But sometimes, there may be something different going on. A pain that begins in the lower back and radiates down the buttock and to the leg, may indicate irritation or pressure on the sciatic nerve, and is referred to as sciatica.
The largest nerve in the body is the sciatic nerve. It extends from the lower back through buttocks and down each leg. If a nerve in the lower back is compressed or inflamed, it may result in pain that radiates down this nerve.
How do you know if you have sciatica pain?
Sciatica isn’t always typical leg pain. It can cause a sudden electric-like, burning or tearing sensation down the back of the thigh and sometimes into the calf or foot from the lower back or buttock.
Some people may also experience tingling, numbness or weakness in the affected leg. The pain can worsen after sitting for prolonged periods, or after coughing, sneezing or certain movements.
In some cases, the discomfort may be primarily experienced in the leg, and there may be very little discomfort in the back. This can be one explanation as to why people may confuse sciatica with leg muscle or joint pain.
What causes sciatica?
A common cause of sciatica is a slipped disc or a bulging disc in the lower portion of the spine. The discs between the bones of our spine work like cushions. If one of them bulges or tears, it can compress an adjacent nerve.
Other reasons include changes in the spine with age, constriction of the spinal canal, bone growth and, less frequently, injury or other spinal diseases.
Not all people suffering from sciatica require a surgery. With the right kind of rest, and the use of the remedies as prescribed by a physician, physiotherapy and a gradual return to normal activity, many people get better. Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the symptoms.
When to det a doctor’s advice
Some back or leg pain may get better over time, but certain symptoms shouldn’t be ignored. You should seek medical advice if the pain is severe, keeps returning, lasts for several weeks or is affecting your ability to walk, work or perform everyday activities.
Numbness or worsening weakness in the leg, trouble with urination or defecation or numbness around the inner thighs and genitals are emergencies.
Avoiding making every leg ache a diagnosis of sciatica is also important. Similar symptoms can occur due to problems involving the muscles, joints, blood vessels or other nerves, which is why it is important to consult a doctor. Your doctor can evaluate your symptoms, motion, muscle strength and reflexes and might suggest imaging if needed.
In addition to this, keeping a healthy weight, being physically active, strengthening core muscles and avoiding long periods of sitting can help keep your spine healthy.
The bottom line is: leg pain that radiates from the back or buttock is not necessarily from the leg and can be from the spine. Early identification of warning signs and proper diagnosis can prevent symptoms from becoming severe and can help to expedite a return to normal life.
(Dr. Kalidutta Das is chief and director of spine services, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. Kaliduttadas@gmail.com)

More than a kilometer underground, in what used to be a gold mine, inside a tank filled with tons of liquid xenon, “something” struck the nucleus of an atom. The tiny collision left an unusual energy signature that researchers are still unable to explain, but the scientists behind the experiment believe this could be the most convincing physical evidence of dark matter to date.
Dark matter is one of the most important and elusive substances in astrophysics. Though it makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe, we can’t observe it directly because it doesn’t interact with light or much else. Most of the evidence for its existence comes from its gravitational effects, the mass of dark matter having tugged on the atoms of the early universe to form stars, galaxies, and the vast web of intergalactic structures visible today.
But the enigma of dark matter is complex. Scientists don’t even know what it is made of, whether it’s a single type of particle or an entire set of particles that interact with one another in ways we do not yet understand. The most fantastical explanations even suggest that it consists of black holes. One of the most widely studied theories on dark matter has dubbed its components WIMPs, short for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, meaning the particles have a mass and thus a gravitational pull but otherwise interact weakly with conventional matter.
If WIMPs exist and are part of the dark matter of our galaxy, enormous quantities of them could be passing through the Earth continuously without leaving a trace. However, it is possible that, very occasionally, one might interact with an atomic nucleus and transfer some of its energy to it, which is why an inexplicable collision is exciting in the world of particle physics.
In the strange disturbance recorded at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in South Dakota, the detector monitoring the tank recorded that a xenon nucleus received energy and recoiled. Though researchers have not yet been able to satisfactorily explain the cause, some models suggest a WIMP could produce such a reaction.
The scientists stated that this single event is statistically too small to be considered the discovery of a new particle. In 220 days of observations conducted between 2023 and 2024, only one such anomaly occurred. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves. We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input,” Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown University and a member of the team leading the project, said in a press release.
The team behind the experiment has published their study as a preprint, meaning it has not yet been peer reviewed. They have, however, presented the results to the scientific community at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics Conference in Japan.
Discoveries made around dark matter tend to elicit this kind of restrained excitement. When in November 2025 a team of Japanese astronomers announced that they had seen signs of dark matter in the Milky Way, they too advised the research community not to count their chickens.
But even if cautious, there are reasons for enthusiasm. If the impact was caused by dark matter, there is enough evidence for researchers to begin characterizing the responsible particle. For example, the team has already calculated that, under the WIMP models they analyzed, the particle is about 200 times more massive than a proton. The impact could help us understand how this type of matter interacts with conventional matter.
The team has also been examining other possible explanations. Paradoxically, in experiments as sensitive as this one, atypical events are not all that uncommon. That’s why SURF has various methods of filtering out background noise and detecting interference caused by known particles or radiation. This event withstood that scrutiny. So far, the researchers have not found an explanation among these known sources that fits what they observed.
“We understand our detector and the backgrounds so well that even a single outstanding event, like the one we found, is important,” said Sam Eriksen, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol and the study’s lead author. “We expect dark matter events to be extremely rare, so only a handful could mark the first detection of WIMP dark matter.”

The world is whiffing on its biggest climate goal
So where, exactly, does the climate fight go next?
For more than a decade, 1.5 degrees Celsius has been the watchword — er, watch temperature? — of climate policy. If the world could hold warming at that level, it could stave off some of climate change’s worst effects, researchers believed.
Well…there’s bad news on that front. A major new assessment from the United Nations concludes the world will inevitably pass the 1.5-degree benchmark within the next few years, barring some celestial intervention. Under current policies, we’re on track to hit 2.6 degrees of warming between now and 2100. And while that’s not quite a Mad Max scenario, it will very much change how humans live. (More on that in just a minute!)
In many ways, the new report formalizes what researchers and policymakers have warned for years. Last November, UN Secretary-General António Guterres made international headlines when he acknowledged that a “temporary overshoot” of 1.5 degrees was “inevitable.”
People understandably fixated on that “inevitable” bit. But “temporary” matters, too. As this new assessment repeatedly stresses, the efforts we make now to cut emissions and remove carbon from the atmosphere will still ultimately determine the size and duration of the much-feared “overshoot.”
Go a little deeper
The realities of a rapidly warming world also point to a second, equally urgent task: Even as we strive to limit climate change, we need to brace for the warming we can no longer prevent.
That approach, known as “climate adaptation,” has not always been popular among advocates or philanthropists. Adaptation is “a kind of laziness, an arrogant faith in our ability to react in time to save our skins,” Al Gore wrote in his 1992 book Earth in the Balance.
Gore has since changed his tune, however, and so have many others. Among the most prominent converts is the billionaire philanthropist Bill Gates, who has gradually made adaptation a larger piece of his climate agenda.
Last October, Gates released a controversial memo arguing that climate policy should measure success by improvements in human welfare “even more than” changes in emissions or temperature. But there’s no reason we can’t advance both goals together.
Many countries and US states already have, in fact. After a 2003 heat wave killed roughly 15,000 people in France, the country created a “robust” national heat plan that included early warnings and checks on vulnerable residents. The system is credited with making subsequent heat waves less deadly (although a historic heat wave earlier this summer still caused 5,700 excess deaths).
Other adaptations will be far more disruptive. Fiji, for instance, has begun relocating coastal villages threatened by rising sea levels. And whatever adjustments society makes, life in a warming world will still be more difficult and more expensive.
Maybe that’s why “climate adaptation” no longer sounds like laziness: There is clearly no easy or low-effort way out of all of this.

➨ Beware the “loneliness economy.” A booming cottage industry of paid apps, meet-ups, and clubs promise they can make you friends…for a fee. But many of these products and services do little more than sell the idea of community.
